title: sinexctl ops dlq requeue has zero risk disclosure for the dupeWindow-collision message-loss risk (sinex-3kqx)
description:
`sinexctl ops dlq requeue` (crate/sinexctl/src/commands/dlq.rs:178-213, `Requeue` match arm) has zero risk disclosure for the known dupeWindow-collision message-loss risk tracked as sinex-3kqx ("DLQ requeue can silently destroy the only surviving copy of a message when it collides with the DLQ stream's dupeWindow").

The `Requeue` arm just validates the selector, shows a spinner, calls `client.dlq_requeue(...)`, and prints the result — no caveat, no confirmation gate. Contrast with `Purge` in the same file (:214-260), which requires `--confirm` and prints an explicit "Purge would delete {target} from DLQ" warning before proceeding.

Worse: requeue is actively treated as the *recommended safe default* throughout this file. `dlq_triage_caveat` (:991-1004) and the cleanup-plan decision logic (:716-723) recommend `requeue_candidate` for `error_payload.persistence_error_database_error_persisting_batch_timed_out` messages and generate ready-to-run `sinexctl ops dlq requeue --start-sequence … --end-sequence …` commands with no caveat attached. An operator following the tool's own generated cleanup-plan command has no way to learn from the CLI that requeue carries this risk.

Found via exhaustive regional audit of crate/sinexctl/src/commands/{privacy,dlq,replay,blob,ops,ops/*}.rs (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run `sinexctl ops dlq triage` (or trigger a cleanup-plan generation) for a batch of `persistence_error_database_error_persisting_batch_timed_out` DLQ messages.
2. Observe the tool generates a ready-to-run `sinexctl ops dlq requeue --start-sequence … --end-sequence …` command with no caveat attached.
3. Compare to `sinexctl ops dlq purge`, which requires `--confirm` and prints an explicit deletion warning before proceeding — requeue has no equivalent despite carrying the sinex-3kqx dupeWindow-collision risk.
acceptance_criteria:
- `DlqCleanupPlanItemView`/`DlqTriageGroup` requeue-candidate output carries an explicit caveat referencing the dupeWindow-collision risk (sinex-3kqx), at minimum matching the visibility of existing caveats elsewhere in this file.
- Interactive `dlq requeue` invocation surfaces the same risk to the operator before executing (a printed warning at minimum; a `--confirm`-style gate matching `Purge`'s UX is the stronger fix, deferred to sinex-3kqx's own resolution if that changes server-side semantics).
- Blocked-by (not blocking): this bead's CLI-side fix should reference sinex-3kqx's resolution state; if 3kqx lands a server-side fix that eliminates the collision risk entirely, this bead's disclosure requirement becomes moot and should be closed as superseded rather than implemented.
close_reason:
Implemented and verified the DLQ CLI disclosure requirement.

| AC-2 | runtime | `crate/sinexctl/src/commands/dlq.rs` | Interactive requeue prints the same duplicate-window warning before invoking the gateway; the implementation is intentionally a warning rather than a confirmation gate because the bead makes confirmation stronger but optional. | `nix develop --command xtask check -p sinexctl --skip-tests` | Satisfied |

title: privacy audit command blind to empty privacy-policy catalog (sinex-t5sr's own detector isn't wired to the audit surface)
description:
`sinexctl privacy audit` (crate/sinexctl/src/commands/privacy.rs:690-707 `PrivacyAuditArgs::execute`, :1124-1193 `build_privacy_audit_report`) is the one command whose job is to summarize privacy posture, but it never calls `privacy_policy_list`. It only calls `private_mode_status`, `dlq_list`, and `sources_readiness_list`, so `PrivacyAuditReport` has no rule-count field and `findings` never contains a "zero policy rules configured" entry.

A sibling command, `privacy policy list` (privacy.rs:996-1015, `privacy_policy_list_envelope`), DOES check `response.rules.is_empty()` and pushes a real caveat: "no DB-backed privacy policy rules are configured; redaction/encryption remains a pass-through unless another policy layer applies." That check exists — it's just not wired into the audit command.

Net effect, directly relevant to sinex-t5sr (privacy catalog CONFIRMED empty in the dev DB right now): an operator running the dedicated `privacy audit` command gets a report that looks complete (private-mode status, DLQ backlog, source readiness) with zero findings, because the one check that would flag the actual problem — catalog emptiness — lives only in a command they'd have to separately know to run. This is the "presents as if privacy protection is active when it isn't" failure mode: the validation logic exists, it's just not called from the command whose entire purpose is to surface exactly this.

Found via exhaustive regional audit of crate/sinexctl/src/commands/{privacy,dlq,replay,blob,ops,ops/*}.rs (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Confirm privacy catalog is empty: `sinexctl privacy policy list` — observe the caveat about no DB-backed rules configured.
2. Run `sinexctl privacy audit`.
3. Observe the audit report contains private-mode status, DLQ backlog, and source readiness, but no finding mentioning the empty catalog — despite the caveat existing verbatim in the sibling command from step 1.
acceptance_criteria:
- `PrivacyAuditArgs::execute` (or `build_privacy_audit_report`) also calls `privacy_policy_list` (or the equivalent client call) and folds an empty-catalog finding into `PrivacyAuditReport.findings` when `rules.is_empty()`, mirroring the existing caveat text in `privacy_policy_list_envelope`.
- A test or manual verification against the current (empty) dev-DB catalog shows `sinexctl privacy audit` now surfaces a non-empty findings list.
- No regression to the existing `privacy policy list` caveat behavior.

title: HIGH, live in the default dev workflow: content-store CAS root path resolved by two independently-defaulting functions with the SAME name -- gateway/reader and event-engine/writer land on genuinely different directory trees whenever SINEX_CONTENT_STORE_PATH is unset, violating the code's own documented one-CAS invariant that replay correctness depends on
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via a duplicated-independently-resolved-state audit (the sinex-f0mk shape, systematically). The content-store CAS root path is resolved by TWO independent, differently-defaulting functions -- both textually named default_content_store_path(), which makes the divergence easy to miss on a casual read.

Reader/gateway side: crate/sinexd/src/runtime/content_store/mod.rs -- reads SINEX_CONTENT_STORE_PATH, else falls back to ${HOME}/.local/share/sinex/content-store, else the environment's generic work_directory. Its OWN doc comment states: "Both the gateway and source runtimes resolve from this same key so they address one CAS -- replay reading source material must hit the exact store that ingestion wrote, or it fails closed." Live consumer: service_container.rs wires the real ContentStoreManager the gateway serves blobs from off this value.

Writer/event-engine side: crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/config.rs -- its own, textually-identical-NAMED but logically DISTINCT default_content_store_path(), which falls back to a DIFFERENT work-dir base (keyed off SINEX_EVENT_ENGINE_WORK_DIR, itself falling back to /tmp/sinex/event_engine/content-store). This becomes EventEngineConfig.content_store_path -- the actual path materials get PERSISTED to on ingestion.

DIVERGENCE CONFIRMED LIVE: whenever SINEX_CONTENT_STORE_PATH is unset, these two resolvers land on genuinely different directory trees. Prod is currently masked -- nixos/modules/sources.nix sets SINEX_CONTENT_STORE_PATH explicitly for the deployed systemd unit -- but the standard documented DEV LOOP (xtask run core --bg) is NOT masked: grepped xtask's run/runtime-target/cargo-runner modules and flake.nix, none set SINEX_CONTENT_STORE_PATH or SINEX_EVENT_ENGINE_WORK_DIR. So a plain dev-loop sinexd process ingests blobs to one directory and serves/reads them from another -- directly violating the doc comment's own stated invariant, and directly relevant to replay correctness, a first-class project concern per CLAUDE.md's own doctrine ("state is durable... fix forward via archive cascade + replay"). Integration tests are separately masked from this too (xtask's sandbox orchestrator explicitly sets SINEX_CONTENT_STORE_PATH for its own harness), which likely explains why nothing has caught this in CI/test.
acceptance_criteria: Consolidate to one shared resolver function that both the gateway/content-store and event-engine sides call, rather than two independently-defaulting implementations that happen to share a name. Given this is masked in prod (explicit env var) and in tests (explicit env var in the sandbox harness) but live in the plain dev loop, verify with an actual xtask run core --bg session with no SINEX_CONTENT_STORE_PATH set, confirming ingested material can be read back via a replay/query on the same session.
close_reason:
Closure Evidence Manifest

AC disposition: SATISFIED.

Evidence:
- Baseline commit 3bdc8cd83 unified the content-store root resolver used by the gateway/reader and event-engine/writer paths.
- The production regression test `writer_and_reader_defaults_share_cas_root` exercises both paths with the default unset and asserts the same configured CAS root.
- The current campaign also integrated CAS filesystem integrity fixes in 7040e2fea and 05a2e95f1 without changing the unified resolver.

Verification from the CAS lane:
- xtask test -p sinexd -E 'test(writer_and_reader_defaults_share_cas_root)' --no-reuse — passed.
- xtask check -p sinexd — passed; warnings were pre-existing.

No wipe, deployment, or destructive operation performed. Storage-growth alerting remains open under sinex-c8ek and related follow-ups.

title: HIGH: every automaton runs a leadership-election + 5s-heartbeat NATS-KV loop for a leadership contest that structurally cannot occur (single sinexd process) -- the same pattern already fixed for sources in sinex-9h32 but explicitly deferred for automata and never followed up, and the config knob that looks like the off-switch doesn't gate it
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via a migration-residue audit (the "successor doesn't inherit predecessor's cleanup" bug shape). crate/sinexd/src/runtime/stream/runner/initialize.rs unconditionally forces every automaton (ModuleKind::Automaton, returned unconditionally by the generic wrapper -- ~17 automata registered) into ProcessingModel::LeaderStandby. In continuous mode this calls acquire_leader_standby() (automaton_runtime.rs): a NATS-KV CAS leadership-acquisition loop, then on success an unconditional tokio::spawn heartbeat task re-acquiring leadership every 5s (default) FOR THE LIFE OF THE DAEMON.

This is EXACTLY the pattern sinex-9h32 (closed, PR #2489) already fixed for continuous SOURCES -- "trivial always-won self-election, impossible handoff, standing NATS-KV traffic for a race that can never happen" with exactly one sinexd process. 9h32's own close_reason explicitly names this as a sibling and defers it: "Deferred/out of scope: automaton internal leader/standby (RuntimeRunner::acquire_leader_standby) -- separate election writer, explicitly not touched." No follow-up bead was ever filed.

COMPOUNDING BUG: the NixOS knob that looks like the off-switch doesn't gate this at all. runtime.coordination.enable defaults to false ("Enable runtime coordination"), but it only controls whether SINEX_COORDINATION_HEARTBEAT/TIMEOUT/HANDOFF env vars get EXPORTED -- it never gates whether acquire_leader_standby() runs at all (grepped all of crate/ for any Rust read of a coordination-enable flag -- zero hits). So with the shipped default (coordination.enable=false, implying "off"), every automaton STILL runs the full election-and-heartbeat loop, just with hardcoded default timing instead of env-overridden timing. The messaging feature that gates this code is a DEFAULT Cargo feature, not opt-in -- this is compiled into ordinary production builds.

Concrete scenario: any live sinexd instance (including the deployed sinnix-prime one) has every continuous-capable automaton doing a NATS-KV CAS write on startup and a heartbeat write every 5 seconds indefinitely, for a leadership contest that structurally cannot occur with one process. Verifiable live via NATS KV history against the leadership bucket while sinexd runs.

SMALLER SIBLING FINDING: SINEX_COORDINATION_DISABLED is a dead env var, orphaned by the same PR #2489 that removed A's sibling -- its sole Rust reader was deleted, but the failure-recovery NixOS VM test scenario still explicitly flips it believing it changes coordination behavior for its assertions; that flip is now a silent no-op.
acceptance_criteria: Apply the same fix sinex-9h32 already applied to continuous sources -- remove the leader/standby election for automata given the single-process architecture, matching the source-side precedent exactly. Fix or remove the coordination.enable knob so it actually gates this behavior if any form of it is kept. Remove the now-dead SINEX_COORDINATION_DISABLED reference from the failure-recovery VM test scenario, since it no longer does anything.

title: ARCH-EPIC: the DLQ subsystem has multiple independent loss/duplication mechanisms -- the safety net for admission failures currently has ~5 distinct ways to lose or duplicate the messages it exists to protect
description:
Consolidating epic, 2026-08-11. Three beads found the DLQ subsystem has independent, distinct loss and duplication mechanisms -- worth reviewing as one subsystem given how many separate bugs concentrate here, even though each has a different root cause and needs its own fix.

Children:
- sinex-3kqx -- DLQ requeue can collide with the DLQ stream's own dupeWindow and silently destroy the only surviving copy of a message.
- sinex-wb1 -- the material-assembler's own DLQ publish is unconfirmed core-NATS, not JetStream-acked, so a DLQ publish failure can be swallowed before settlement.
- sinex-l1gg -- bulk DLQ requeue can be silently killed mid-batch by the gateway's own request timeout with zero progress record, and the standard operator recovery action (re-run the command) guarantees duplicate republish since the target stream has no dedup configured at all.

Related, kept under their existing parent (sinex-tkr1, the timing/scope-guard epic) rather than duplicated here since they fit that pattern more precisely: sinex-x444 (DLQ dedup keys off only the first child of a multi-event intent) and sinex-w4i (partial-record re-emit duplication) -- both are DLQ-surface bugs too, cross-referenced here for subsystem-level triage even though their primary home is the timing/scope-guard epic.

Net picture: the DLQ is meant to be the system's safety net for admission/processing failures, but currently has at least five distinct ways to lose or duplicate the very messages it exists to protect -- worth treating as a subsystem-level reliability push rather than five independent point-fixes, especially given DLQ activity is expected to spike during the imminent large historical re-import.
acceptance_criteria: Treat as a subsystem-level reliability push given the concentration of distinct bugs here, especially ahead of the imminent re-import where DLQ activity is expected to spike. Each child still needs its own specific fix, but a shared design review (e.g. does the DLQ need its own transactional/idempotent redesign rather than incremental patches) may be more efficient than five independent fixes.

title: ARCH-EPIC: mechanisms/validation built then structurally discarded or unreachable at the call site
description:
Consolidating epic, 2026-08-11. This session found the same architectural shape recur roughly ten times across independent audit passes covering completely different subsystems: a real, non-trivial mechanism (validation logic, an enforcement path, a declared field, a preflight check) is genuinely BUILT -- correctly implemented, sometimes tested -- and then its result is silently discarded, never wired to a caller, or the mechanism it was meant to feed doesn't exist. This is distinct from dead code in the ordinary sense (nobody uses a helper function) -- these are specifically invariant-enforcement or safety mechanisms that LOOK load-bearing to anyone reading the type signature or the code around them, but do nothing at runtime.

Children reparented here:
- sinex-nupp -- RetentionPolicy enum declared per source contract, only Forever actually has any effect; a real, working TTL enforcement mechanism (lifecycle_ttl.rs) sits unconnected right next to it.
- sinex-hj66 -- instruction_reconciler's claim-support evidence vector is hardcoded/fabricated rather than derived from the actual matched events, despite the shared output-guard machinery existing to check exactly this class of thing.
- sinex-6xmc -- TLS-require flags fail open on malformed values despite a strict-parser precedent existing elsewhere in the same codebase; HealthThresholds' real range/ordering validation is caught and downgraded to warn+default at both of its call sites.
- sinex-f0mk -- a consumer-name override env var is honored by the backpressure READER but the event-engine WRITER never wires it, so setting it silently disables backpressure entirely (currently inert since nothing sets it).
- sinex-c8ek -- a real disk-space preflight check exists (verify_system_resources) but its only entry point is never invoked from any startup or CLI path.

Related but kept as separate, more specifically-scoped epics rather than merged here (cross-reference, don't re-parent, to avoid losing their own scoped remediation plans): sinex-1hus (consumption-boundary sanitization -- wtkk/DisclosureContext belongs there since its dormancy is specifically about destination-aware redaction), sinex-phhk (per-field privacy metadata -- a scoped instance of this same pattern specific to SensitivityHint/ParserFieldPrivacyMetadata), and the closed-bead corrections (sinex-r6d.6's comment noting its bridge-checkpoint mechanism is inert for every registered automaton; sinex-audit-continuity-fullscan's reopen noting its own fix doesn't support the query it claims to).

The recurrence count (10+ independent instances across privacy, retention, health, backpressure, resource-safety, evidence-honesty, and closure-verification subsystems) suggests this is not coincidental -- it's a symptom of building the enforcement/validation logic as a first pass and treating "wire it to the actual call site" as a separate, sometimes-skipped follow-up step. Worth a standing review habit (or a lint: any Result-returning validation function whose error is ever caught with a bare warn+default should be flagged for review) rather than treating each instance as independent.
acceptance_criteria: Each child bead is fixed by wiring the already-correct mechanism to its intended call site (not rebuilding it) -- the pattern's fix is uniformly cheap once identified, since the hard part (writing correct validation/enforcement logic) was already done in every instance. Consider whether a lint or review habit could catch the NEXT instance of this pattern before it needs an audit to find it.

title: MEDIUM-HIGH (corrected 2026-08-11): NatsConnectionConfig is entirely non-fallible so ALL its fields silently discard invalid values -- a dropped credential-file reference produces an unauthenticated NATS connection that passes validation, plus HealthThresholds validation discarded separately
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via SINEX_* startup-validation sweep. Two distinct instances of the same shape (real validation logic exists, then gets thrown away):

1. SINEX_API_REQUIRE_CLIENT_TLS / SINEX_NATS_REQUIRE_TLS fail OPEN on malformed values. Both declared with a bool default of false via the config macro's lenient path, which accepts 1/true/yes/on/0/false/no/off (case/whitespace tolerant) -- anything else (a typo, or an unexpected word) silently warns and returns false = TLS enforcement OFF. Sinexd's own CLI clap path fails in the SAFER direction by contrast (hard error on bad boolean value) -- it's specifically the config-macro-generated env-var path that fails open. A strict parser variant already exists and is used elsewhere in the same codebase (e.g. the native-messaging allowlist parsing), a one-line-per-field fix.

2. HealthThresholds validation is fully implemented (real range 0.0..=1.0 and ordering checks: degraded<=failed, via a fallible normalize function) and then discarded at BOTH production call sites, both doing the equivalent of HealthThresholds::from_env().unwrap_or_else(|error| { warn!(...); HealthThresholds::default() }). The entire fallible-validation machinery has zero runtime effect -- an invalid threshold env var produces a warn line, not a startup failure. Validation built to a real type-enforcement-ladder rung and then pinned back to convention-only at the point it matters.

VERIFIED SOLID as the correct template pattern, same audit: the native-messaging trusted-extensions/hosts/capabilities/roles env vars are read with a strict parser, parse errors are RETAINED in dedicated config-error fields and turned into a hard deny at enforcement time, plus fail-closed on an empty allowlist -- this is the pattern the two findings above should be following but aren't.

## CORRECTION 2026-08-11 (verified before further action, changes severity materially)

Item 1's original framing was HALF WRONG and understated the real issue. Corrected:

**SINEX_API_REQUIRE_CLIENT_TLS does NOT fail open.** GatewayConfig is declared `fallible` (crate/sinexd/src/api/config.rs), so the macro emits the STRICT branch (strict_flag) -- a malformed value hard-fails GatewayConfig::load(), which propagates and aborts startup. This half of the original finding is simply incorrect; there is nothing to fix here.

**SINEX_NATS_REQUIRE_TLS DOES fail open, and the real cause is structural, not per-field: NatsConnectionConfig (crate/sinex-primitives/src/nats.rs) is NOT declared `fallible` at all, so EVERY field on it -- not just require_tls -- goes through the lenient path.** This is materially worse than the original framing:
- ca_cert, client_cert, client_key, creds_file, nkey_seed_file, token_file are all Option<PathBuf> resolved via path_optional -- a non-UTF-8 value silently becomes None.
- A silently-dropped creds_file makes auth_mode() return "none" and to_options() build an UNAUTHENTICATED connection -- and validate()'s "exactly one auth mode" check passes cleanly, because it validates the POST-drop struct, after the credential reference has already vanished.
- This is live on FIVE production paths, not just the gateway: event_engine/config.rs, runtime/config.rs, runtime/runtime_cli.rs, runtime/preflight/verification.rs, and nested inside GatewayConfig itself via plain `nested` (not `nested_fallible` -- see mechanical root cause below).

**A test actively memorializes the wrong behavior under a name asserting the opposite.** crate/sinex-primitives/src/nats_test.rs has a test named from_env_parses_require_tls_strictly whose body sets an invalid value and asserts require_tls falls back to false, with a comment justifying this as preventing "silently enabling TLS" -- backwards: the real risk of a typo'd TLS flag is silently DISABLING transport security, and the correct behavior (matching SINEX_VALIDATE_SCHEMAS/SINEX_EVENT_ENGINE_STRICT_VALIDATION, which already do this correctly elsewhere in the codebase) is a hard startup failure. This test will actively block the fix and must be INVERTED, not merely updated, or a future implementer will believe the current behavior is intentional and tested-correct.

**Mechanical root cause identified**: the sinex_config macro already supports #[sinex_config(nested_fallible)] for composing a fallible child into a fallible parent -- fully implemented and tested (crate/sinex-macros/tests/sinex_config_test.rs) -- but has ZERO production users. GatewayConfig's nats field uses plain `nested` instead of `nested_fallible`, which is the exact reason a fallible parent (GatewayConfig) silently contains a lenient child (NatsConnectionConfig). The fix is: make NatsConnectionConfig fallible, then switch GatewayConfig's nested field to nested_fallible -- a small, mechanical, already-supported-by-the-macro change, not a new capability to build.

Given the unauthenticated-NATS-on-silently-dropped-credential-file scenario compounds directly with the already-filed sinex-vhv3 (unauthenticated NATS), this item's priority should be treated as materially higher than originally filed -- recommend splitting this off as its own P1/P2 finding rather than leaving it bundled with the (correctly-lower-priority) HealthThresholds discard finding, since the two no longer share the same severity.
acceptance_criteria: Move SINEX_API_REQUIRE_CLIENT_TLS/SINEX_NATS_REQUIRE_TLS to a strict parser (matching the existing strict-flag precedent) so a malformed value hard-fails startup instead of silently disabling TLS enforcement. Make HealthThresholds::from_env() failures propagate as a hard startup error (or at minimum a loud, impossible-to-miss signal) instead of silently downgrading to defaults at both call sites -- the validation logic already exists and is correct, it just needs to actually gate something.

title: P1: Timestamp::now() silently substituted for a missing intrinsic capture-time field while still stamped as the HIGHEST-confidence TimingEvidence::Intrinsic tier -- violates the never-falsify-provenance-clocks tripwire, and for ActivityWatch specifically defeats start-anchored occurrence identity (sinex-y8v), turning re-reads of the same row into unbounded duplicate interpretations instead of revisions
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via a meta-audit sweep (Opus). Three previously-unfiled instances of a partially-filed class (sinex-8xqo item 3 covers library.rs's InferredMtime fallback; sinex-h0y1 covers systemd.rs's precision truncation but not its now() branch):

1. crate/sinexd/src/sources/source_contracts/desktop/activitywatch.rs -- the started_at field parse falls back to Timestamp::now() on failure, then gets declared as TimingEvidence::Intrinsic{field:"started_at", confidence:Intrinsic} -- the HIGHEST content-rung evidence tier (TemporalSourceType::IntrinsicContent) -- regardless of whether the real field parsed or a fabricated now() was substituted.
2. crate/sinexd/src/sources/source_contracts/system/journald.rs -- same shape (falls back to Timestamp::now() when the realtime-timestamp field is absent/invalid), declared Intrinsic.
3. crate/sinexd/src/sources/source_contracts/system/systemd.rs -- same shape, declared Intrinsic.

TimingEvidence::Atemporal and StagedAtFallback exist PRECISELY for this case and correctly defer to the material tier instead of claiming intrinsic content confidence -- library.rs's error arm already does this correctly, making these three call sites inconsistent with an established correct pattern in the same codebase, not an unprecedented judgment call. This directly implicates the project's own explicitly-named tripwire: "Never falsify provenance clocks. No backdating ts_coided, no minting UUIDv7 from ts_orig. The clocks are SUPPOSED to differ for imports." A fabricated wall-clock reading stamped at the highest confidence tier is functionally the same category of error even though it's ts_orig (not ts_coided) being substituted -- it tells every downstream consumer "this timestamp came directly from the source, high confidence" when it did not.

NOVEL, SEVERE SECOND-ORDER CONSEQUENCE FOR ACTIVITYWATCH SPECIFICALLY: activitywatch.rs builds the occurrence key from ts_orig's RFC3339 rendering. If started_at ever fails to parse, ts_orig=now(), so the SAME PHYSICAL ROW yields a DIFFERENT occurrence key on every rescan -- defeating sinex-y8v's start-anchored occurrence identity and the SupersedeOnChange path entirely for that row, producing UNBOUNDED DUPLICATE interpretations of one row instead of revisions. The module's own comment explicitly promises the OPPOSITE behavior (a re-read of the same row carries the same key) -- this is a documented invariant the code silently violates on its error path.
acceptance_criteria: Change all three call sites to use TimingEvidence::Atemporal or StagedAtFallback (matching library.rs's already-correct pattern) when the intrinsic field fails to parse, rather than substituting now() and claiming Intrinsic confidence. For activitywatch.rs specifically this is P1-urgent given the occurrence-key-instability consequence -- verify/add a test proving a parse-failure re-read of the same AW row does NOT produce a new occurrence key on rescan.
notes: 2026-08-13 verification: d4e6d43b9 is in current HEAD. It changes ActivityWatch, journald, and systemd parse-failure paths to acquisition-time plus Atemporal evidence, preserves intrinsic nanosecond precision, and derives stable ActivityWatch fallback occurrence identity. Commit evidence reports 64 focused tests passed via xtask, including activitywatch/journald/systemd/library/notification/stage_as_you_go routes. Current source audit finds no Timestamp::now fallback in the three target files. This resolves the dependency needed by h0y1; h0y1 remains open.
close_reason: Closure Evidence Manifest: commit d4e6d43b9; AC1 all three target source contracts use acquisition-time plus Atemporal on intrinsic parse failure and no longer fabricate Timestamp::now; AC2 ActivityWatch stable fallback occurrence identity is implemented and covered by its focused regression tests; verification: committed test report for xtask test -p sinexd --lib -E "test(activitywatch) or test(journald) or test(systemd) or test(notification) or test(library) or test(stage_as_you_go)" passed 64 tests; source audit rg found no Timestamp::now fallback in target files; deferred: sinex-h0y1 remains open for systemd lifecycle false-event amplification.

title: HIGH, live-proven: xtask verify closure has multiple vacuity holes -- any command that exits 0 satisfies any AC regardless of semantics, docs-kind rows pass with zero execution and unverified artifact paths, dry-run reports PASS while the body says FAIL
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via a meta-audit of the verification tooling itself (Opus), PROVEN LIVE against the real tool with synthetic bead payloads (not just code reading) -- xtask/src/commands/verify.rs @ master.

1.1 ANY EXIT-0 COMMAND SATISFIES ANY AC. validate_satisfied_manifest_item (verify.rs:1926-1980) checks only that a 'Satisfied' row has a command passing looks_like_runnable_command, rejecting only surface=source|grep|text and bare rg-without-xtask commands. run_shell_command (verify.rs:2270) runs it via sh -c and checks ONLY exit status -- no linkage between AC semantics and command behavior. LIVE PROOF: a bead with 3 real-sounding correctness ACs (duplicate equivalence_key rejection, reflection-lane isolation, redaction-before-publish ordering) closure-verified successfully using version-check-style commands as the 'evidence' for all three -- result: status=success, commands_found=3, passed=3, matrix_errors=0. The SAME FILE already has a stricter validator for the older phase-manifest surface (validate_supported_phase_command, verify.rs:528, restricting to xtask/git only, with xtask further restricted to check/test/docs/schema/verify subcommands) -- when the GH-issue path was replaced by the bead path (PR #2471, sinex-e7e9), this allowlist was never carried over to the new validator.

1.2 DOCS-KIND ROWS PASS WITH ZERO EXECUTION AND AN UNVERIFIED ARTIFACT STRING. verify.rs:1806-1814: a Satisfied row with evidence_kind=docs needs only a runnable command OR a named artifact -- the artifact cell is NEVER checked for existence. LIVE PROOF: two ACs marked docs, artifact paths pointing at nonexistent files -- result: status=success, commands_found=0, manifest_errors=0. Any bead can be closed clean by declaring every AC docs and naming a plausible-looking nonexistent path.

1.3 DRY-RUN MODE REPORTS PASS WHILE THE BODY SAYS FAIL. verify.rs:1327: the top-level result becomes success if overall_passed OR dry_run is true. In dry-run mode the manifest/matrix validators still run and populate real errors, but the TOP-LEVEL status is unconditionally success regardless. LIVE PROOF, same bead, two invocations: normal mode -> status=failed, manifest_errors=4; dry-run mode -> status=success, message='closure verification passed', manifest_errors=4 (same 4 errors, just not surfaced in the status). Dry-run is the natural choice for a read-only audit pass and emits the literal string 'closure verification passed' with exit 0 for a bead with 4 hard manifest errors -- exactly the mode most likely to get pasted into a close_reason as evidence.

1.4 AC ORDINALS ARE POSITIONAL ONLY -- TEXT IS NEVER COMPARED. Coverage is checked by ordinal count only (AC-1..AC-N each appear exactly once); the manifest row's evidence/surface prose is never compared against the actual AC text. Combined with 1.1, a manifest can describe entirely different work in the right number of rows and still pass. Arguably partially inherent (prose can't be reliably machine-compared, and per this project's own doctrine shouldn't be load-bearing for a machine gate) -- but it means the tool's actual guarantee is 'N rows exist, each names a command that exits 0', materially weaker than what the project's docs claim ('checks every AC disposition and executes its commands').

1.5 MINOR: a bare test-runner invocation in closure evidence can pass via exact-impact-proof reuse with ZERO tests actually executed on that invocation -- sound caching (the fingerprint includes HEAD plus dirty-content hash), not a correctness hole, but the closure verifier is then measuring 'a proof existed for this tree state' rather than 'tests ran now'. Worth a doc sentence, not a fix.
acceptance_criteria: Route validate_satisfied_manifest_item through validate_supported_phase_command (or an equivalent allowlist) so arbitrary exit-0 commands can't satisfy behavior/runtime/contract ACs. Verify docs-kind artifact paths actually exist on disk before accepting them. Make dry-run's top-level status reflect overall_passed honestly (or at minimum never emit the string 'closure verification passed' when manifest_errors>0). Correct the project's own docs describing what the tool actually guarantees to match the 1.4 finding. Given the closure-honesty doctrine this tool exists to enforce, this bead itself deserves an unusually rigorous closure -- ideally including a live re-run of the exact reproduction cases documented here.

title: sinexd's startup DDL schema-apply path has no advisory lock (asymmetric vs the lighter event_engine schema-sync which has one), and EXPECTED_BINARY_SCHEMA_VERSION has been the literal string '1' since introduction despite destructive column drops shipping since -- a NixOS rollback (a one-command, commonly-used recovery action) could silently resurrect dropped columns with no data
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via deployment/multi-context-robustness audit. Three related gaps in the schema-apply-on-boot path (SINEX_SCHEMA_APPLY_ON_STARTUP=1):

1. NO ADVISORY LOCK. crate/sinexd/src/main.rs calls sinex_db::apply_schema_for_url(...) completely unguarded. Compare crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/service.rs, which wraps ITS OWN schema-sync (a different, lighter mechanism -- the JSON payload-schema registry, not DDL) in try_acquire_migration_lock(pool) (AdvisoryLock keyed 'event_engine.migrations'), explicitly designed to reject a second concurrent instance. The actual DDL convergence engine has no equivalent -- two concurrent sinexd processes against the same DB (a stuck old process during a botched restart, an operator manually running sinexd serve for debugging while the systemd unit is also up) can race on the two-phase NOT VALID -> VALIDATE CONSTRAINT named-constraint convergence step. Failure mode is a hard, transient, self-healing-on-retry apply() error (Postgres rejects the second ADD CONSTRAINT) rather than corruption -- but the asymmetry with the sibling lock is a real, fixable gap.

2. VESTIGIAL VERSION GUARD, REAL DESTRUCTIVE-ROLLBACK RISK. sinex_schemas.binary_schema_version + EXPECTED_BINARY_SCHEMA_VERSION (crate/sinex-primitives/src/lib.rs) IS a real, hard-failing check (Err on mismatch) -- but the constant has been the literal string '1' since it was introduced in PR #1559 and has NEVER been bumped since (confirmed via git log -S). Meanwhile the DDL convergence engine has genuinely shipped destructive, one-way columns_to_drop operations in the meantime -- crate/sinex-schema/src/converge.rs drops node_version, occurrence_id, and superseded_by_event_id from core.events. If an operator (or an autonomous agent under this repo's own full-deploy-autonomy grant) ever rolled back to a pre-drop NixOS generation -- a one-command, low-friction, commonly-used recovery action NixOS explicitly optimizes for -- the older binary's declared schema still expects those columns, apply() would silently ADD COLUMN them back EMPTY (no data restoration, since DROP COLUMN already destroyed it), and the version guard would NOT fire because nobody bumps it for ordinary schema evolution. Architecturally consistent with the project's 'declarative convergence, not migrations, fix-forward' doctrine, but that doctrine and NixOS's trivial-rollback UX are in tension, and there is currently zero automated signal that would catch this specific class.

3. NO DRY-RUN/PREVIEW on the sinexd-startup schema-apply path specifically -- distinct code path from the already-tracked sinex-audit-backfill-no-dryrun (which covers the separate xtask schema backfill CLI surface only). The DDL-drop-capable apply() invoked automatically on every sinexd boot has no equivalent preview step at all.

VERIFIED SOLID, same audit: the convergence engine itself is genuinely well-built for interrupted-apply recovery -- ~13 independently idempotent phases using IF NOT EXISTS/CREATE OR REPLACE throughout, no CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY anywhere (no invalid-index trap), hypertable conversion uses if_not_exists=>TRUE, and the drift/re-apply test suite (migration_chain_test.rs, ~35 targeted tests in strict_diff_test.rs) substantiates re-running apply() after a crash mid-sequence converges correctly for essentially every object class. Also confirmed live and load-bearing: sinnix's bridge.nix sets runtime.restartOnSwitch=false for this deployment, meaning nix develop --command switch does NOT restart sinexd by itself on this host -- schema-apply only runs on the NEXT manual systemctl restart, which could be many switches later, shifting (not eliminating) the interrupted-apply-mid-deploy risk toward 'many versions accumulate, then one manual restart jumps the DB across a large schema-version gap at an unexpected time.' CLAUDE.md's own deploy doctrine has been corrected to note this explicitly (2026-08-11).
acceptance_criteria: Add an advisory lock around the main DDL apply() path matching the pattern already correctly used for the lighter event_engine schema-sync. Establish and actually maintain a real EXPECTED_BINARY_SCHEMA_VERSION bump policy tied to destructive convergence operations specifically (any columns_to_drop change should require a version bump), so a rollback to an older binary genuinely fails loud instead of silently resurrecting empty dropped columns. Consider a preview/dry-run mode for the startup apply path, or at minimum a prominent log/warn when convergence is about to execute a destructive operation (a column drop) during an unattended startup.
close_reason:
Closure Evidence Manifest

AC disposition: SATISFIED.

Evidence:
- crate/sinex-db/src/schema_apply.rs acquires SCHEMA_DDL_APPLY_LOCK_KEY through the shared AdvisoryLock before declarative DDL convergence and fails closed when another applier owns it.
- crate/sinex-schema/src/converge.rs exposes destructive_schema_contract(); startup warns with EXPECTED_BINARY_SCHEMA_VERSION when destructive drops are present.
- crate/sinex-schema/src/converge_test.rs::destructive_schema_contract_tracks_registry_and_binary_epoch verifies the contract against the registry and binary epoch.
- crate/sinex-db/tests/schema_apply_lock_test.rs covers the lock contract.

Verification:
- nix develop --command xtask check -p sinex-schema (passed)
- nix develop --command xtask check -p sinex-db (passed)
- nix develop --command xtask test -p sinex-schema -E 'test(destructive_schema_contract_tracks_registry_and_binary_epoch)' (passed)
- nix develop --command xtask test -p sinex-db -E 'test(apply_schema_records_current_binary_schema_version)' --impact-mode=off (passed)

No destructive operation or wipe performed.

title: HIGH: DLQ bulk requeue can be silently killed mid-batch by the gateway's own 30s request timeout with zero progress record, and the standard operator recovery action (re-run the same command) guarantees duplicate republish of the already-moved prefix -- the target stream has no dedup configured at all
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via CLI/automation-surface-consistency audit. Distinct from the already-filed sinex-3kqx (which is about re-failed admission colliding with the DLQ stream's OWN 1h dupeWindow, causing LOSS) -- this is the complementary failure mode: operator-driven retry after a killed batch, causing DUPLICATION, on the raw event stream which has NO dupeWindow at all to even accidentally protect it.

Chain of evidence:
1. crate/sinexd/src/api/config.rs: default_request_timeout_secs()=30. crate/sinexd/src/api/rpc_server.rs:941 wraps the route group dlq.requeue/dlq.purge dispatch through with TowerTimeoutLayer(30s). rpc_server/transport.rs's handle_layer_error explicitly matches tower::timeout::error::Elapsed and returns 504/JSON-RPC -32000 -- confirmed live and enforced, not theoretical.
2. runtime/dlq_retry.rs's retry_all/retry_sequence_range run ENTIRELY inside this one request/handler with deliberate per-message throttling (10ms + 200ms/10-message pause) -- a realistic pre-wipe DLQ backlog of a few thousand messages will not finish in 30s.
3. Standard tower::timeout::Timeout semantics: when the sleep fires first, the inner service future (the handler, mid-loop) is DROPPED -- not run to completion, not unwound gracefully.
4. api/handlers/dlq.rs's ONLY call to log_dlq_operation (the audit-trail write) happens AFTER requeue_result resolves, in either success or error arm. If the future is dropped by the timeout, NEITHER arm runs -- ZERO operation-log record exists that the requeue was even attempted, let alone how far it got. Contrast: handle_lifecycle_archive calls start_operation BEFORE doing any work, so an interrupted archive still leaves a visible 'Running' record via ops list/get -- DLQ requeue has no equivalent.
5. Per-message settlement order (retry_stream_message): publish to the original raw subject, await ack, THEN delete the DLQ entry (a SECOND NATS round trip after the publish ack already returned). If the drop happens between those two steps, the message is now durably live in the raw pipeline AND STILL PRESENT in the DLQ.
6. The natural operator recovery action -- re-run the same dlq requeue range/--all -- picks this same still-present DLQ message back up and republishes it AGAIN.
7. nixos/modules/nats.nix: SINEX_RAW_EVENTS (the actual republish target) has NO dupeWindow configured at all, unlike SINEX_RAW_EVENTS_DLQ and SINEX_RAW_EVENTS_PROCESSING_FAILURES which both get dupeWindow=1h. So the Nats-Msg-Id header dlq_requeue_target carefully derives from the original event id provides NO PROTECTION WHATSOEVER on the stream that matters here.

Net effect: operator sees a bare 504/timeout, has no way to know which sequences were already moved, and the standard recovery action GUARANTEES duplicate raw-event injection for the entire already-completed prefix, into a stream with zero dedup, feeding downstream admission whose own equivalence-key dedup is explicitly fail-open.

retry_all's consumer-based path has a parallel risk: handle_dlq_message republishes then acks a durable pull consumer with a FIXED name ('dlq-retry-consumer', not per-invocation) -- if the ack never lands (same drop-mid-flight scenario), JetStream redelivers the unacked message to the NEXT dlq requeue --all invocation, same duplicate-republish outcome.

VERIFIED SOLID CONTRAST, same audit: replay lifecycle (sinexctl ops replay run) is architected correctly -- the actual work is driven by a separately-spawned replay-control actor over NATS request/reply, decoupled from the HTTP request task, so a killed execute RPC doesn't orphan/corrupt the replay; lifecycle archive is a single pool.begin()/commit() transaction, cleanly rolls back on drop, and re-querying live event ids on retry makes re-running naturally idempotent, with a pre-registered start_operation giving an audit trail even on failure. DLQ requeue has none of this -- it's the one bulk-mutation surface that got the non-transactional, no-progress-record, no-target-dedup design.
acceptance_criteria: Redesign DLQ requeue to either: (a) become an async operation with a pollable operation id like replay (recommended, matches the already-correct architecture pattern in this codebase), tracked via start_operation BEFORE work begins so an interrupted batch is visible and resumable; or (b) add a per-sequence progress manifest plus idempotent settle-before-publish ordering (delete/mark-consumed the DLQ entry in the same transaction as or before the republish, not after); and separately, add a dupeWindow to SINEX_RAW_EVENTS or otherwise give the republish target real dedup so even an imperfect retry can't inject true duplicates. Cross-reference sinex-3kqx (related but distinct trigger/mechanism/consequence -- loss vs duplication) rather than conflating fixes.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] Fresh finding, no test yet. AC's two named fix paths (a)/(b) are alternatives, but the outcome properties (interrupted batch visible/resumable, no true duplicates) are testable today regardless of which path is chosen.

title: HIGH: replay crash-recovery guard (10-min staleness threshold) is unreachable on the restart that actually follows a crash -- systemd's RestartSec=10 means the sweep runs long before its own threshold, permanently stranding a cascade-archived-but-not-reemitted replay
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via crash-only-design audit (Opus, deeply traced). crate/sinexd/src/api/service_container.rs:66-87 (recover_stale_replay_operations) is called exactly ONCE, from ServiceContainer::new, which the supervisor invokes once per process start. It filters via find_stale_executing (crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/replay.rs:514-535) on started_at < NOW() - 10 minutes.

Exact intermediate state that triggers permanent loss: SIGKILL after archive_replay_cascade_atomically commits (replay_control/execution/collect.rs:510-545, which runs DELETE FROM core.events for the whole cascade -- roots + all derived descendants, now existing only in audit.archived_events) and BEFORE the scan re-emits, with the operation's started_at less than 10 minutes before the NEXT ServiceContainer::new.

Why this is the COMMON case, not an edge case: nixos/modules/default.nix declares Restart=on-failure, RestartSec=10. earlyoom SIGKILLs sinexd (a documented recurring event on this host), systemd restarts ~10s later, find_stale_executing finds nothing (the operation is 30s old, not 600s), the sweep is never run again in that process, and the operation sits at result_status='running'/result_message='executing' with its cascade permanently deleted. The events are invisible to every read surface, automaton, and query -- silently -- until the NEXT daemon restart occurs 10+ minutes after that specific operation's started_at, which on a stable prod box can be days, weeks, or never.

The durable journal itself (the #2194/sinex-afd fix) IS correctly written and the restore code (crate/sinex-db/src/replay/state_machine.rs:1240-1275) would work perfectly if reached -- this is a reachability defect in the CONSUMER of that journal, not a hole in the journal. Root cause is a mis-specified guard: a staleness threshold exists to protect against clobbering a LIVE in-flight operation, but at ServiceContainer::new no replay can possibly be in flight (single-daemon deployment, execution runs inside sinexd itself) -- the threshold guards a scenario that cannot exist at the only point it's evaluated, while creating a real skip window. Manual recovery exists (execute_cascade_restore via the lifecycle-restore RPC) but requires an operator who happens to know to look. Distinct from sinex-ph9h (the non-crash mark_failed path).
acceptance_criteria: recover_stale_replay_operations should run its recovery sweep unconditionally at startup (with no staleness threshold, or a much shorter one like 30s that still distinguishes 'genuinely stuck at last daemon exit' from a false positive) rather than requiring 10 minutes of elapsed wall-clock time that a fast systemd restart will never satisfy. A test should prove: kill -9 sinexd shortly after a replay's archive-cascade commits but before re-emission, restart, and assert the operation is recovered (not left executing) on that immediate restart, not only on a restart occurring 10+ minutes later.

title: MEDIUM-HIGH: cold-start automaton catch-up has a real, permanent event-loss window at the DeliverPolicy::New handoff -- production has no barrier, though a test-only barrier (sinex-li78) proves the race was already identified
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via crash-only-design audit (Opus, deeply traced). crate/sinexd/src/runtime/stream/runner/automaton_runtime.rs:260-292 -- the historical catch-up scan runs to completion (module.scan at :270-279), THEN the JetStream consumer task is spawned (:284) with DeliverPolicy::New (:539). The confirmed publish happens AFTER the DB persist commits. An event whose persist commits after the scan's final query snapshot (T_q) and whose confirmed publish lands before the consumer exists (T_c) is missed by BOTH the catch-up scan (already ran) and the live consumer (DeliverPolicy::New skips anything published before consumer creation) -- permanently.

T_c-T_q covers a NATS get_or_create_consumer round trip executed inside a freshly-spawned task, under the already-filed cold-start thundering herd (sinex-srn8, ~25 tasks spawned with zero stagger) -- not a microsecond window under that contention.

Why the miss is PERMANENT, not just delayed: the catch-up cursor is Cursor::after_id(last_input_event_id), and last_input_event_id advances to live events as soon as live processing starts. The hole events have LOWER UUIDv7 ids than subsequent live events, so every LATER restart's catch-up starts past them too -- no error, no metric, no gap detection (same silence class as sinex-ruok, different mechanism: startup seam vs mid-run eviction).

STRONGEST EVIDENCE this is a known, unfixed race: automaton_runtime.rs:248-258 has a #[cfg(not(any(test, feature="testing")))] block that sets ready_tx=None in production -- tests get a harness-only consumer-ready sender (sinex-li78) letting them deterministically wait for the durable consumer to exist before publishing, specifically to avoid racing DeliverPolicy::New. Production gets nothing. Any existing test asserting cold-start losslessness is asserting it WITH a barrier production does not have -- it cannot falsify this finding.

Bounded by: consumers are durable (durable_name set), so a WARM restart resumes from the ack floor and this window doesn't apply there. It applies specifically on first-ever start, after NATS JetStream state loss, on a new namespace, and whenever the consumer name changes (which encodes the provenance/event-type filters, so an input-filter code change silently re-creates the consumer with DeliverPolicy::New). THE IMMINENT WIPE/RE-IMPORT CAMPAIGN IS EXACTLY A COLD START -- this is not a hypothetical edge case for the operator's actual near-term plan.
acceptance_criteria: Give production the same consumer-ready barrier the test harness already has (sinex-li78's mechanism), or capture a stream-sequence high-water mark BEFORE the catch-up scan runs and create the consumer with DeliverPolicy::ByStartSequence from that mark instead of DeliverPolicy::New after the scan completes -- either closes the [T_q, T_c] hole. A test should prove losslessness WITHOUT relying on the test-only ready_tx barrier that currently makes the existing tests unable to catch this.
notes: 2026-08-13 audit: production loss window is fixed by 6e8e4c357. Runtime now creates the durable confirmed consumer first, waits for consumer readiness, performs DB catch-up, then releases delivery. Current remaining AC is the anti-vacuity proof: existing tests use a test-only consumer-ready barrier and do not adversarially publish during production-equivalent catch-up. Keep open until that test or equivalent high-watermark proof lands; no additional production fix is presently required for the wipe.

title: CRITICAL, live-confirmed: staged ingest materials are world-readable on sinnix-prime right now -- no UMask on the sinexd unit, no explicit file permissions in Rust write paths, 18 orphaned month-old material directories currently exposed
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via host-level security-boundary audit, LIVE-VERIFIED as the ordinary unprivileged sinity account (uid 1000, not sinex uid 991, not root) -- this is a currently-exploitable finding on the real deployed host, not theoretical.

nixos/modules/default.nix:2775-2796 (directoryRules) declares ingestSpool, spoolBase, runtimeSpool, runtimeDir, logDir all at mode 0755 (owner sinex, but group AND other both have r-x) -- only blobDir, the event_engine work dir, and tls are correctly locked to 0750 (owner+group only). nixos/modules/sources.nix's mkBaseServiceConfig (used by the actual sinexd unit) never sets UMask -- UMask=0077 exists only in lib/systemd-hardening.nix's mkHelperServiceConfig, used exclusively by one-shot maintenance units, never the main daemon -- so systemd's compiled-in default UMask=0022 applies. crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/material_assembler/mod.rs's fs::create_dir_all/File::options().create(true) calls have no PermissionsExt/.mode() anywhere -- a repo-wide grep for set_permissions|PermissionsExt|.mode(0o|umask across crate/**/*.rs returns ZERO non-test hits anywhere in the codebase.

LIVE VERIFICATION: stat confirmed /var/lib/sinex/state/spool/event_engine is 755 sinex:sinex; ls -la on a material directory showed material.bin and state.wal both 644 (world-readable); xxd successfully read raw material bytes as the unprivileged sinity user. There are currently 18 ORPHANED material directories on disk dated over a month before the audit (July 10) -- this is not a brief in-flight window, stalled/never-completed assemblies sit exposed indefinitely, since cleanup_state only fires on successful completion or explicit DLQ routing (material_assembler/io.rs).

Concrete scenario: any other local account or any process running as any other uid on sinnix-prime can ls/cat filesystem-watcher content, browser-history rows, terminal history, ActivityWatch data, etc while (or after) it's staged for ingestion -- BEFORE it ever reaches privacy redaction (redact_batch runs later, at persistence) or the DB. Compounding but distinct from the already-filed sinex-vhv3 (unauthenticated NATS) and sinex-s4lj (Postgres trust auth) -- both already grant 'any local user reads everything' today, so current overall exposure doesn't change, BUT this finding (1) exposes materials that never make it into NATS/DB at all when assembly stalls or errors (the 18 orphaned entries are exactly that -- data unreachable via vhv3/s4lj), and (2) remains exploitable after vhv3/s4lj get fixed, since it's a filesystem-permission bug independent of auth config.

Write-race NOT open via these directories specifically -- 0755 has no w bit for group/other, so another user cannot plant a file into the spool for sinexd to scan; the exposure is read-only.

Secondary, currently-inert finding in the same audit: logDir is also declared 0755 but confirmed live-empty (nothing writes files there today, tracing goes to stderr/journald only) -- latent risk that becomes live with zero additional code changes the moment any future feature starts writing files there.

## Threat-model calibration 2026-08-11 (operator context)

This is a personal, single-human-operator machine (sinnix-prime) -- there is no second human account today, so "any other local user" overstated the immediacy of the risk as originally framed. The realistic threat on THIS specific deployment is narrower: a co-located, compromised service or sandboxed process (a browser sandbox, a container, any of the other self-hosted services this host runs under their own uids) pivoting to read sinex's spool as a blast-radius amplifier -- real, but meaningfully different from "an adversary already has read access to your data." Kept at P1 anyway because the fix is trivial (directory modes + one UMask= line + a few .mode() calls, no real engineering cost) and independently justified by the operator's own stated intent for this project to eventually be usable by others -- "world-readable by design" is a correctness property that should hold regardless of whether any specific deployment currently has a second party who could exploit it. Not treating this as "someone is reading your diary right now" severity; treating it as "cheap to fix, no reason not to, and matters more the moment this runs anywhere other than a single-operator box."
acceptance_criteria: Set UMask=0077 (or equivalent) on the main sinexd systemd unit, matching the pattern already correctly used for one-shot maintenance units. Tighten ingestSpool/spoolBase/runtimeSpool/runtimeDir/logDir to 0750 in directoryRules, matching blobDir's already-correct precedent. Add explicit PermissionsExt::set_permissions/.mode(0o640-ish) calls in material_assembler's and content_store's Rust write paths as defense-in-depth, not relying solely on parent-directory mode (the audit noted blobDir's containment currently works ONLY because of the parent directory's mode, with zero defense-in-depth from the Rust code itself -- fragile if that mode were ever loosened). Sweep and clean the 18 currently-orphaned exposed material directories as an immediate remediation step, and consider why cleanup_state doesn't fire on stalled/never-completed assemblies (ties to the DLQ-collision bugs already tracked, sinex-wb1/sinex-ecy).
close_reason: Closure Evidence Manifest: Merged via PR #2615 (squash-merged 2026-08-11). Fix: staged ingest materials no longer world-readable -- NixOS directoryRules set to 0750 + UMask=0077 in the service unit, plus explicit restrict_permissions() calls added at 15 write sites across the runtime (including content_store, threaded through .as_std_path() where the API takes &Path vs the runtime's Utf8PathBuf). Also directly remediated 18 already-exposed live directories on sinnix-prime as an immediate stopgap alongside the code fix. Verified via xtask check -p sinexd on the merged commit.

title: no storage-growth projection/alerting exists anywhere, and the one disk-space preflight gate that DOES exist is dead code never called from any startup or CLI path -- directly relevant given the imminent large historical re-import
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via data-lifecycle-stewardship audit. No metric, scheduled check, or sinexctl command anywhere estimates DB/CAS growth rate or projects days-to-full -- grepped for pg_database_size/pg_total_relation_size/disk-usage patterns across crate/sinexctl, found nothing relevant.

There IS a disk-space preflight check -- crate/sinexd/src/runtime/preflight/resources.rs (verify_disk_space/get_disk_space, using statvfs) -- checking available bytes against hardcoded per-path minimums (5GB state, 10GB data, 5GB tmp, 2GB log, 5GB work) and would warn at <2x minimum. But verify_system_resources, the only public entry point that calls it, is NEVER INVOKED from the daemon startup path or any CLI command -- confirmed via grep, matches only its own definition and its own unit test module. crate/sinexd/src/runtime/preflight/mod.rs re-exports only verify_service_dependencies, not the resources module's checks. This point-in-time gate is dead code, not merely lacking a trend/projection layer on top of a working base.

Net effect: storage genuinely just accumulates with the only signal being an eventual ENOSPC/Postgres-out-of-disk failure -- consistent with the already-known megachunk/compression prod incident pattern (project memory: prod_megachunk_compression_startup.md). Directly relevant to the imminent pre-wipe re-import specifically, since the campaign explicitly plans to re-stage large historical material (AW SQLite snapshots, etc.) with zero growth visibility once that's underway.
acceptance_criteria: Wire verify_system_resources (or an equivalent live disk-space check) into daemon startup and/or a periodic health check, at minimum restoring the point-in-time gate that already exists but is currently unreachable. Consider a real growth-rate projection (even a simple linear extrapolation from recent growth) as a further step, but wiring the existing dead gate back in is the immediate, cheap fix before the re-import specifically.

Remaining scope is executable startup-route proof and fail-closed insufficient-space evidence. No storage-growth projection, NixOS sinex-preflight binary, CAS fsck, replay, or work-control changes are in scope.

title: RetentionPolicy is declared-but-inert for every value except Forever -- third confirmed instance of this session's 'declared metadata, zero enforcement' pattern, worse than the others because a real, working enforcement mechanism sits right next to it, unconnected
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via data-lifecycle-stewardship audit. crate/sinex-primitives/src/source_contracts/lifecycle.rs:254-258's RetentionPolicy enum has three variants (Forever, Days{days}, Tiered{hot_days,warm_days}). Grepped every construction site across the whole workspace: every one of the ~50 real source contracts declares RetentionPolicy::Forever. The ONLY non-Forever usage anywhere is in privacy_fixture.rs, a test/coverage-matrix fixture never wired to a real ingestion path.

Traced every READ site of .retention (not construction) -- exactly two, both non-enforcing: package_completeness.rs (feeds an audit JSON export only) and source_skeleton.rs (pure codegen, emits the enum token into a new-source template). Nothing in crate/sinexd, crate/sinex-db, or crate/sinex-schema matches on RetentionPolicy::Days/::Tiered to schedule an archive/delete. crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/source_materials/types.rs's with_retention_policy() builder is defined and NEVER CALLED anywhere -- dead code.

The 'confirmed working' reflection.events 30-day retention is NOT driven by this enum at all -- apply.rs hardcodes add_retention_policy('reflection.events', INTERVAL '30 days') as a raw TimescaleDB hypertable policy, independent of any source contract's declared RetentionPolicy value. core.events explicitly has remove_retention_policy called on it, so Forever 'works' purely because nothing else acts on the table either.

WORSE than the sibling DisclosureContext/SensitivityHint findings: there IS a real, live TTL enforcement mechanism (crate/sinexd/src/api/lifecycle_ttl.rs, an hourly leader-elected sweep archiving events past sinex_schemas.event_payload_schemas.retention_seconds) -- but retention_seconds is a SEPARATE column with NO Rust setter anywhere (only a read-only list_with_retention() exists), completely disconnected from the source-contract-level RetentionPolicy enum a source author actually edits. The gateway's own rpc_server.rs comment even documents the symptom without naming the cause: 'Cheap: most ticks are no-ops because very few schemas declare retention_seconds.'

Concrete failure scenario: an engineer adds a new source with retention=RetentionPolicy::Days{days:30}, reasonably expecting 30-day expiry (mirroring the enum name and the one working precedent they know about). Nothing happens, ever -- the value is silently absorbed into an audit JSON and never reaches retention_seconds, so the real TTL sweeper never sees it. Any future non-Forever retention intent (e.g. bounding raw media per sinex-3g3w's own recommendation, or ephemeral clipboard/PII-adjacent captures) is a structural no-op unless an operator hand-writes SQL against an internal table nobody documents as the real control surface.
acceptance_criteria: Wire RetentionPolicy::Days/Tiered to actually populate retention_seconds (or an equivalent) on the relevant event_payload_schemas row at schema-registration/apply time, so a source author's declared retention intent reaches the real enforcement mechanism (lifecycle_ttl.rs) automatically instead of requiring undocumented manual SQL. Either wire with_retention_policy() into the real write path or remove it as dead code. Consider whether the Forever/no-policy case should also be a positive, explicit declaration reaching the same enforcement path rather than working only by omission.
