title: DECISION: privacy catalog should auto-converge like schema does, not require a manual seed RPC -- plus source the secret-token catalog from a maintained third-party ruleset, invert Secret-category context-scoping default, and expose seeding as a NixOS module option
description:
Architecture decision from a 2026-08-11 operator discussion, reframing sinex-t5sr's fix scope. Four related direction calls, all stemming from why sinex-t5sr happened in the first place:

1. AUTO-CONVERGENCE, NOT MANUAL SEEDING. This codebase already has a real declarative-convergence pattern: schema itself is Rust-defined desired state (crate/sinex-schema/src/defs/*.rs) that sinex-schema apply/converge automatically reconciles against the live DB on every boot -- no manual step, no flag to remember. The privacy catalog is currently the ONE piece of declared desired-state in the whole system NOT wired into that same auto-converge path -- it sits behind sinexctl privacy policy seed builtin --enabled, a manual RPC nothing calls automatically. This is not incidental to sinex-t5sr -- it is precisely why that bug happened: the one piece of state that opted out of 'everything converges automatically' is the one piece that ended up silently unconverged. Fix: wire builtin catalog seeding into the same apply/converge mechanism schema uses, so a fresh DB has the catalog present (per whatever category/enable policy is declared) without any operator action, the same way it gets the right tables and triggers.

2. SOURCE THE SECRET-TOKEN CATALOG FROM A MAINTAINED THIRD-PARTY RULESET. The current hand-rolled ~34-rule catalog (crate/sinex-primitives/src/privacy/catalog.rs) has known, predictable gaps found by hand this session (missing HTTP Basic auth, missing -u/--user flag, missing PASS/PWD shorthand, missing several OAuth token variants -- sinex-24es item 5). This is the expected failure mode of a small team hand-maintaining a secret-pattern list indefinitely. Projects like gitleaks ship an actively-maintained, permissively-licensed, DATA-FILE (TOML) ruleset covering far more vendor token formats than sinex will ever justify building by hand. Recommended shape: keep sinex's own Matcher/Strategy/ProcessingContext dispatch engine (genuinely sinex-specific, wired to event payloads and DB-backed operator overrides) but source the Secret-category catalog CONTENT from a periodically-synced upstream ruleset as a build input, converted into PatternRules at build or apply time. PII rules (SSN/PESEL/NIP/REGON etc, tied to StructuralDetector's checksum logic) are more sinex-specific/locale-particular and likely stay hand-maintained -- this recommendation is scoped to the Secret category specifically.

3. INVERT PROCESSING-CONTEXT SCOPING DEFAULT FOR THE SECRET CATEGORY. ProcessingContext's 8-way enum and per-rule contexts:Vec<ProcessingContext> opt-in model is not itself the problem (a closed enum has real type-safety value) -- the OPT-IN DIRECTION is. Every rule must be manually assigned into the right context subset, and every miss is silent -- this session found exactly that failure twice independently (phone_number missing Command, generic_secret_assign missing Document/Clipboard). Context-scoping exists for one legitimate reason: false-positive noise reduction on PII-shaped rules where a false positive has real UX cost (the ssn rule is deliberately excluded from noisy Journal/Dbus chatter) -- a distinct concern from coverage completeness that only really applies to PII. For SECRETS specifically, a missed credential leak is categorically worse than noise, so Secret-category rules should default to UNSCOPED (contexts:[] = everywhere, already supported by the type) and require an explicit, commented justification to narrow -- inverting 'opt into every context you thought of' into 'opt out of specific contexts for a stated reason'. Add a test asserting every ProcessingContext a source contract actually declares is covered by at least the intended Secret rule set, to catch the next instance of this class before an audit finds it.

4. EXPOSE AS A NIXOS MODULE OPTION. Given every other piece of this deployment's desired state (NATS streams, DB schema, resource limits) is already Nix-declared rather than operator-remembered, catalog seeding/category-selection policy should be too -- something like services.sinex.privacy.seedBuiltinRules (bool or category selection), consistent with the rest of the deployment surface instead of being the one thing that needs a post-deploy manual sinexctl call.

Scoped to TEXT redaction only per explicit operator instruction -- NSFW/media content classification is a separate, larger, deliberately-deferred capability question (see memory: sinex_privacy_system_architecture.md), not part of this decision.

## Rationale

The privacy catalog's manual-seed architecture is the direct, traceable cause of sinex-t5sr (a live-confirmed active gap in this operator's own dev DB): it is the single piece of desired system state that was built outside the declarative-convergence pattern (sinex-schema apply/converge) this project already uses successfully for everything else, and it silently degraded to unconverged because nothing forces or checks convergence. Fixing sinex-t5sr by adding a startup warning or a doctor check treats the symptom; wiring catalog seeding into the same convergence path this codebase already trusts for schema/triggers/indexes treats the cause and prevents the next instance of "the one manual step got skipped." The third-party-ruleset, context-scoping-default, and NixOS-module-option points are separable but were raised in the same discussion because each addresses a distinct, independently-evidenced failure mode found this session (catalog content gaps found by hand; two independent missing-ProcessingContext bugs; seeding being the only privacy-relevant setting not exposed at the deployment layer) using the same underlying principle: prefer a general, structurally-enforced mechanism over an operator-remembered convention, matching this project's own stated doctrine (CLAUDE.md: "use general mechanisms... map the need onto the existing... mechanisms" and the type-enforcement ladder's "never leave a correctness invariant at convention-only").

## Alternatives Considered

- **Startup validation / xtask doctor check that warns if privacy.rules is empty.** Rejected as the primary fix (though still worth having as defense-in-depth): it catches the symptom after the fact rather than preventing it, requires an operator to notice and act on a warning, and does nothing for the underlying inconsistency (this remains the only unconverged piece of desired state in the system). Cheap to add alongside the real fix, not a substitute for it.
- **Keep hand-maintaining the full catalog (secrets + PII) in-house.** Rejected for the Secret category specifically: the coverage gaps found this session by hand (missing Basic auth, -u/--user flag, PASS/PWD shorthand, several OAuth token variants) are exactly the shape of gap a dedicated, actively-maintained upstream project (gitleaks and similar) already solves at much lower ongoing maintenance cost. PII rules are kept in-house since they're genuinely sinex/locale-specific (checksummed structural detectors), not because in-house maintenance is preferred in general.
- **Leave ProcessingContext scoping as pure opt-in for all rule categories, including Secret.** Rejected: the asymmetry between a missed secret (high cost) and PII false-positive noise (lower cost, contained blast radius) justifies different default directions per category rather than one uniform policy. Applying the inverted default to PII rules too was considered and rejected — PII's context-scoping is a deliberate, currently-working noise-reduction mechanism (e.g. SSN correctly excluded from noisy Journal/Dbus chatter), not a bug, and inverting it there would trade a real, working benefit for marginal coverage gain on categories where under-redaction is less costly than false-positive fatigue.
- **Leave catalog-seeding policy as a CLI-only operator decision, not a NixOS module option.** Rejected for consistency: every other piece of this deployment's meaningfully-configurable desired state (NATS stream limits, DB pool sizing, resource scoping) is already Nix-declared; leaving privacy-catalog policy as the one CLI-only exception reproduces the same "the one thing that isn't like everything else" pattern that caused this bug in the first place, one layer up (deployment configuration instead of DB convergence).

## Amendment 2026-08-11 (operator follow-up): SensitivityHint is a second instance of the same problem, not a fix for point 3

Investigated directly (not just recalled): SensitivityHint (privacy/mod.rs) exists as a type but is functionally dead. Evidence:

- Declared at the WHOLE-RECORD level, not per-field -- a source contract sets one Vec<SensitivityHint> for its entire record type (e.g. window_manager.rs:154-156 sets [FreeText, PotentiallySensitive] for the whole window-activation record), with no mechanism to annotate one field (e.g. window_title) differently from a sibling field (window_class) in the same record. True field-level annotation does not exist.
- Only 6 of ~35 source contracts populate it at all (window_manager, activitywatch, email, media x2, document/staging). Every other source -- including browser/history.rs, finance.rs, messaging.rs, social.rs, bookmark.rs, all terminal-history sources, dbus.rs, journald.rs -- sets sensitivity_hints: Vec::new().
- CONCRETE SEVERE GAP: browser/history.rs's URL field carries ZERO sensitivity hint, despite URL being one of the single most revealing fields in the whole capture surface (health searches, financial sites, everything a browsing history reveals).
- ZERO CONSUMERS ANYWHERE. Grepped every SensitivityHint reference in the workspace -- every hit is the type definition, a source contract SETTING it, or macro plumbing carrying it through structs. No API handler, no privacy engine code, no CLI tooling ever reads sensitivity_hints back out. The type's own doc comment says it exists "so DB/user policy tooling can propose or bind rules (#1042 AC3, #1611)" -- those look like historical pre-Beads issue references for tooling that was apparently never built. This is the third instance this session of the "declared metadata, zero enforcement" shape (alongside DisclosureContext/sinex-wtkk and occurrence_identity doc-strings).

REFRAMING of point 3 (context-scoping): the deeper issue is that ProcessingContext's 8 values are really a CAPTURE-MODALITY taxonomy (how the text physically arrived: Command/Clipboard/Journal/Dbus/Notification/Document/Metadata/SourceCapture), not a CONTENT-SENSITIVITY taxonomy. SensitivityHint was presumably meant to be the complementary semantic-sensitivity axis -- but since it has zero consumers, ProcessingContext ends up carrying the whole weight of both jobs it wasn't designed for, which is a structural reason (not just isolated bugs) why coverage keeps silently gapping: a URL and a shell command and a chat message are different capture modalities that don't map cleanly onto "how sensitive is this," forcing every new source into a bucket that doesn't describe its content. Point 3's fix should now read: either give SensitivityHint (or a successor) a real consumer and real per-field granularity, or fold its intent into the Secret-category unscoped-by-default policy directly and retire the dead type -- don't leave it declared-but-inert as a third instance of this pattern.

## Amendment 2026-08-11 (operator follow-up): broaden point 2's third-party sourcing beyond secret-token rulesets

Two more concrete sourcing directions, both text-only (matching the operator's explicit scope: text redaction now, media/NSFW-image classification deliberately deferred separately):

- ML-based PII detection (Presidio-style NER for names/locations/orgs) would give SensitivityHint::PersonNameCandidate (or its successor) an actual detector for the first time -- today nothing in the catalog can find a person's name in free text, only structural patterns (SSN/email/phone/card). An NER pass is the natural way to close that gap rather than hand-writing name-detection regex (which doesn't really work for names anyway).
- Adblock-list-shaped exhaustive dictionaries for NSFW terminology/domains -- squarely text-only and tractable near-term (distinct from the image-classification discussion, which stays out of scope). Maintained, exhaustive blocklist projects exist in the same shape as ad/tracker blocklists (adult-domain hosts-files, terminology wordlists) and could be synced as periodic data inputs, same pattern as the gitleaks-ruleset idea, applied to URL/title/text fields to flag (not necessarily fully redact) NSFW-adjacent content in browsing/window-title/chat capture.

## Amendment 2026-08-11 (operator correction #2): don't hardcode topic categories like "health"/"financial" -- NSFW is the one category that clears a real bar, not one of many arbitrary picks

An earlier framing of this decision's URL-sensitivity example used "health searches, financial sites" as illustrative categories. Operator correctly rejected this: hardcoding topic-specific categories like that is exactly the unprincipled special-casing this project's own doctrine warns against ("use general mechanisms... map the need onto existing mechanisms") -- it just relocates the ProcessingContext problem (a fixed, arbitrary, closed set of buckets someone happened to think of) into a new enum with no more principled a boundary. "Is this financial enough to flag" has no natural edge; a fixed topic-category list would grow forever by vibes.

CORRECTED DESIGN: a generic content-category-flag mechanism, where NSFW/adult content is the first AND, for now, ONLY instantiated category -- not because it's more important in the abstract, but because it's the one category that clears a real, non-arbitrary bar: (a) exhaustive, actively-maintained public data sources already exist for it (adult-domain blocklists, terminology wordlists -- the same adblock-list shape as the gitleaks-ruleset idea in point 2), and (b) it has genuine external consensus on its boundary, unlike "financial" or "health" which have no natural edge and would immediately become a subjective, ever-growing hand-picked list. A future category should only be added if it clears the SAME bar (real external data source + real consensus boundary), not because someone thought of another topic that feels sensitive -- the mechanism should stay generic and extensible in principle, but nothing beyond NSFW should actually get built until a category earns it on those terms." 

## Amendment 2026-08-11 (operator follow-up): survey of other maintained-dataset opportunities in the same "adblock-list shape," filtered by the real-data-source + real-consensus-boundary bar

Clear the bar, directly usable:

- NATIONAL ID / VAT / TAX-ID FORMATS BEYOND THE CURRENT SSN + POLAND-ONLY SET. The catalog's StructuralDetector design (checksum-validated formats -- Luhn, mod-97, etc, crate/sinex-primitives/src/privacy/mod.rs's StructuralDetector enum) is already the right architecture for this, just narrow (US SSN + PL PESEL/NIP/REGON only). python-stdnum is a mature, actively-maintained library cataloging checksum-validated national identifiers, VAT numbers, and similar structured IDs for dozens of countries -- highest-leverage addition here since it's the SAME architecture already built, just needing relevant country formats ported in rather than invented from scratch. A checksum-validated ID format has zero subjective boundary, same as the existing SSN/PESEL rules -- this clears the bar even more cleanly than NSFW does.
- SECRET/CREDENTIAL-FORMAT CATALOGS BEYOND JUST GITLEAKS. Sibling maintained projects worth cross-referencing rather than committing to one: detect-secrets' plugin patterns, TruffleHog's regex rules, GitHub's own published secret-scanning patterns. Like gitleaks, a token format is defined by the issuing service (deterministic), not a judgment call -- same consensus-clarity as checksum-validated IDs.
- NSFW TERMINOLOGY, one concrete named source: LDNOOBW ('List of Dirty, Naughty, Obscene, and Otherwise Bad Words') is a real, maintained, multi-language wordlist repo in exactly this shape, alongside the adult-domain blocklists already discussed.

Same maintained-data shape, different purpose (not redaction, but worth having on record since they're directly relevant to adjacent work already on the table):

- THE PUBLIC SUFFIX LIST (Mozilla-maintained, used by every browser) -- exhaustive, actively maintained, genuine consensus. Not privacy-redaction-relevant directly, but directly useful for any URL-based classification work (correctly splitting registrable domain from subdomain), which the browser-history sensitivity gap (sinex-phhk epic) already puts on the table.
- TRACKER/AD-DOMAIN BLOCKLISTS (EasyList/EasyPrivacy, the lists uBlock Origin ships) -- same maintained-data shape, different job: classifying browsing-history entries as background tracking noise vs genuinely-visited content, a signal/noise problem distinct from redaction.
- HAVE I BEEN PWNED'S PWNED PASSWORDS LIST -- a maintained, hashed, exhaustive breach corpus. Different job again: detecting a captured value is an ACTUALLY-COMPROMISED credential, not just credential-shaped text. Adjacent feature, not the same one.

Deliberately NOT proposed (fails the consensus-boundary bar the same way health/financial did): gambling, drugs/substances, or other topic-shaped categories. Gambling domain blocklists exist but, per operator correction, gambling is not a privacy category in the first place (unlike NSFW content, which is sensitive if exposed) -- dropped from consideration entirely, not merely deprioritized on weak consensus.
acceptance_criteria: Privacy catalog seeding is wired into the sinex-schema apply/converge mechanism (or an equivalent automatic path) rather than requiring sinexctl privacy policy seed builtin to be run manually. Secret-category catalog content is sourced from (or cross-validated against) a maintained third-party ruleset rather than being exclusively hand-maintained. Secret-category rules default to unscoped (all ProcessingContexts) unless explicitly and individually justified otherwise. A NixOS module option controls builtin catalog seeding/category policy, consistent with how the rest of the sinex deployment surface is declared. This decision supersedes sinex-t5sr's narrower 'operator must run seed-builtin' framing -- sinex-t5sr's fix should implement point 1 of this decision, not just document the manual command.

title: ARCH-EPIC: shared consumption-boundary sanitization primitive
description: Upstream fix identified 2026-08-11 synthesizing this session's audit findings. Captured content is trusted as inert everywhere it's consumed, with no shared library enforcing 'this left the ingest boundary, escape/filter it for wherever it's going now.' The TUI is safe only by accident (ratafui happens to filter control chars upstream); the CLI table/text render path, direct tracing::info! log calls, and the DisclosureContext-is-decorative gap are all the same missing mechanism at different consumption boundaries (terminal, log, export). One sanitize_for_destination(content, Destination::Terminal|Log|Export|...)-shaped module, applied at every render/log/disclosure call site instead of relying on each consumer's own accidental safety, closes the whole class instead of each instance needing individual discovery.
acceptance_criteria: A shared sanitization/escaping module exists and is applied at every content-consumption boundary identified by this epic's children. Each child bead's specific instance is fixed as part of implementing (or explicitly deferred against) this shared primitive, not as an independent one-off patch.

title: ARCH-EPIC: default-secure RPC request structs (deny_unknown_fields, safe scope defaults)
description: Upstream fix identified 2026-08-11. sinex-uhru found 4 concretely-exploitable request structs (DlqPurgeRequest, LifecycleArchiveRequest, ReplayExecuteRequest, TombstoneCreateRequest) where #[serde(default)] on a scope-narrowing field silently WIDENS a destructive operation's blast radius under version skew. Only 3 structs workspace-wide currently opt into deny_unknown_fields. Flipping the default (a shared derive macro or workspace-level serde config applied to all RPC request structs, opt-out rather than opt-in) closes the whole class rather than the four instances that happened to get found -- matches the 'pick the strongest affordable level' type-enforcement-ladder doctrine.
acceptance_criteria: deny_unknown_fields becomes the default for RPC request structs (via a shared derive/macro or workspace lint), not an opt-in three structs happened to add. The four structs named in sinex-uhru are fixed as part of this epic, prioritized by sinex-uhru's own traced severity (DlqPurgeRequest first).

title: ARCH-EPIC: enforce one write path -- block direct core.events writes outside admission
description: Upstream fix identified 2026-08-11. sinex-gk8j (escalated to ~18 pool.events().insert() bypass sites), sinex-erqz's admission bypass, and sinex-kix9's log bypass are all instances of 'there's a blessed pipeline (NATS -> admission -> redact_batch) and also an easier direct path that quietly skips it.' Per this project's own type-enforcement-ladder doctrine (CLAUDE.md), this invariant currently lives at level 6 (convention only) when it should live at level 1-2 (module visibility / a forbidden-pattern lint). Making EventRepository::insert() pub(crate)-scoped to only the admission module, or adding an xtask check --forbidden lint for '.events().insert(' outside event_engine/, turns 'don't bypass the pipeline' from a thing ~20 call sites individually got wrong into a thing that doesn't compile.
acceptance_criteria: Direct core.events inserts outside the admission/event_engine module are either impossible (visibility) or caught by a lint/xtask check, not merely a convention. All ~18 currently-known bypass sites (sinex-gk8j) are migrated onto the real pipeline as part of closing this epic.

title: ARCH-EPIC: guards mis-specified relative to actual runtime timing/scope (admission, DLQ, replay recovery, cold-start catch-up)
description:
Upstream fix identified 2026-08-11. sinex-txt4's own recommended fix (hoist admission's collapse maps from admit_intent_bytes-local to fetch-batch-scoped state) is a narrower instance of a bigger gap: identity/collision resolution throughout the admission and DLQ layers is scoped to whatever unit happened to be convenient at each call site (one intent, one message, one lane, one 'first child'), not to the true unit of coherent processing. sinex-x444 (DLQ dedup keys off only the first child of a multi-event intent) and sinex-w4i (partial-record re-emit duplication) are the same shape one layer over. Elevating identity/collision state to genuinely batch-scoped (required for txt4's fix anyway) generalizes naturally to a shared service DLQ dedup could also consume, fixing multiple beads from one investment.

## Broadened scope 2026-08-11, consolidating three more beads found to share the same root shape

The original scope (batch-scoped admission/DLQ identity) turns out to be one instance of a broader recurring pattern found across this session's later rounds: a guard is written assuming some temporal/scope condition holds at the exact moment it's evaluated, but the actual deployed system's timing doesn't satisfy that condition -- producing a permanent-loss or permanent-duplication window instead of the intended protection. Three more beads share this exact shape and are reparented here:

- sinex-g9sy -- automaton input checkpoint (last_input_event_id) assumes delivery order equals mint order (a SCOPE/ordering assumption), causing duplicate reprocessing or permanent skip when they diverge.
- sinex-i41y -- cold-start catch-up assumes the scan-to-consumer handoff is instantaneous (a TIMING assumption), causing permanent event loss at exactly the cold-start condition the imminent wipe creates.
- sinex-1u9c -- replay crash-recovery's 10-minute staleness threshold assumes a slow restart (a TIMING assumption), but systemd's actual RestartSec=10 means the guard evaluates long before its own threshold on the restart that matters most.

All six children (txt4, x444, w4i, g9sy, i41y, 1u9c) are instances of "a scope/timing guard was mis-specified relative to actual runtime behavior" -- worth a shared design review of every such guard in the admission/DLQ/replay/catchup surface, not just point-fixing each instance, since the pattern recurring six times in one audit sweep suggests a systemic gap in how these guards get specified and tested (none of the six had a test that could have caught the actual failure mode -- each test either had a barrier the real system lacks, or asserted the wrong invariant).
acceptance_criteria: Admission's collision-resolution state (live_by_key/key_last_index/key_archive_target or their successor) is scoped to the full fetch batch, not per-message/per-intent. DLQ dedupe identity covers all children of a multi-event intent, not just the first. Each child bead closes as a consequence of this shared redesign, not independently.

title: CRITICAL, live-exploitable: raw ANSI/OSC escape sequences in captured content reach the operator's terminal unsanitized via sinexctl's default table/text render path -- OSC 52 clipboard write demonstrated feasible on this exact host
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via content-interpretation/rendering-safety audit. This is confirmed live-exploitable on sinnity's own machine, not theoretical -- backed by a real captured fixture already committed to the test suite.

THE CHAIN, END TO END:
1. Ingest strips only NUL, nothing else. crate/sinex-primitives/src/validation/core.rs's strip_nul_chars_from_string does text.retain(|ch| ch != '\0') -- no is_control filter exists anywhere on the ingest or read path for payload content (the only is_control uses in the repo guard replay actor/identifier strings, not payloads).
2. Journald decodes raw bytes into a String verbatim: crate/sinexd/src/sources/source_contracts/system/journald.rs:39-51 does String::from_utf8_lossy(&bytes) on the MESSAGE byte array and assigns to the  field.
3. PROOF THIS ALREADY HAPPENS: crate/sinexd/src/sources/source_contracts/system/journald_test.rs:135 is a REAL committed fixture -- a captured line from aw-server (ActivityWatch, one of sinex's own configured sources) containing MESSAGE bytes including 27,91,51,51,109 (ESC[33m) ... 27,91,48,109 (ESC[0m). Sinex captures these ESC bytes verbatim TODAY.
4. Read side (crate/sinex-primitives/src/views/events.rs:745-766, event_summary) picks the raw //etc field and only str::trim()s it -- trim() does not remove ESC (U+001B is not White_Space).
5. Render side writes it straight to stdout via println! in crate/sinexctl/src/commands/query.rs:692,153-156 and context.rs:453,455-461 (sinexctl recall / sinexctl events context -- the operator's PRIMARY read surfaces).
6. tabled 0.20 (crate/sinexctl/Cargo.toml) is used WITHOUT the ansi feature (default features = derive/macros/assert only) -- cell contents are emitted byte-for-byte, no escape awareness.

CONCRETE EXPLOIT: DbusNotificationSentPayload.summary (crate/sinex-primitives/src/events/payloads/system.rs:80-82) is the D-Bus notification title -- controllable by ANY process on the session bus, including a web page via the Notifications API or a mail client rendering a Subject: header. A notification with summary = ESC]52;c;<base64>BEL gets captured, persisted, and later printed VERBATIM by sinexctl recall. LIVE-VERIFIED against this exact host: kitty 0.48.2's ~/.config/kitty/kitty.conf has no clipboard_control override, so the documented default applies: write-clipboard is permitted WITH NO PROMPT. The 55-char summary-field render budget leaves ~35 bytes of clipboard payload -- enough for a leading-newline shell command that self-executes on the operator's next paste. Additional primitives in the same class: OSC 0/2 terminal-title spoofing, bracketed-paste-mode toggling (ESC[?2004h/l), cursor-manipulation to forge preceding output lines. A sequence cut mid-escape by the fixed-char truncation (truncate_string/truncate, no escape-state awareness) leaves the terminal consuming the REST OF THE TABLE as OSC payload.

WIDER BLAST RADIUS: crate/sinexd/src/api/handlers/dlq.rs:143-145 (render_preview_value) has the same raw-String-passthrough bug for DLQ message previews -- and a DLQ message is BY DEFINITION one that failed parsing, so 'not valid JSON, render as raw string' is the COMMON case there, with up to 1200 chars of injection window (TRIAGE_DLQ_PREVIEW_CHARS) into an arbitrarily-shaped failed payload.

ADJACENT, SAME ROOT: ~/.claude/hooks/sessionstart-sinex-recall.sh runs sinexctl recall --format json and injects the result into every Claude Code/Codex session preamble. JSON transport escapes control chars (no terminal injection there), but attacker-controlled notification summaries/window titles land verbatim in agent context at session start -- a distinct, lower-severity but real prompt-injection-adjacent concern worth a separate look.

VERIFIED SOLID (do not re-audit): the TUI is genuinely safe -- ratatui's own set_stringn/styled_graphemes filter !symbol.contains(char::is_control) before any cell render (upstream library behavior, not a sinex guard -- would silently regress on a ratatui downgrade or raw-backend write). copy_to_terminal_clipboard (tui.rs:554-559) correctly base64-encodes before building its own OSC 52 sequence. --format json/yaml/explain all correctly escape via serde_json (chars <0x20 become \uXXXX) -- ONLY the default table/text output is affected. Text-search-snippet rendering (ts_headline) is incidentally safe since it operates on the already-escaped jsonb-to-text rendering -- meaning  renders escaped while  (no -q) renders raw, an inconsistency that would make this bug look intermittent under casual testing.
acceptance_criteria: Add a render-time control-character filter applied to every text/table cell in crate/sinexctl's default (non-JSON/YAML) output paths, mirroring what ratatui already does for the TUI -- the correct chokepoint is render-time (in crate/sinexctl/src/fmt/ or wherever cell values are finalized before printing), NOT ingest-time (sanitizing at capture would corrupt faithful capture, which is the product's whole point). Also fix dlq.rs's render_preview_value raw-String passthrough. CORRECTION 2026-08-11 via temporal/presentation-robustness audit -- this bead's 'verified solid' claim that ratatui's control-character filter makes the TUI genuinely safe needs amending, not retracting: the filter (char::is_control()) only covers Unicode category Cc. Live-measured: Unicode bidi-override characters (RLO/LRO/PDF/RLI, e.g. U+202E) and zero-width format characters (ZWSP, BOM) are category Cf, NOT Cc -- is_control() returns false for all of them, width measures as 0, and they pass the TUI's filter untouched, reaching the terminal in both the CLI table path and the TUI. No truncation helper anywhere terminates an open bidi embedding either -- truncating a string that opens with a right-to-left override yields a cell with no closing terminator, so the override leaks into the rest of the display line.

Concrete scenario, same reachable attacker surface as this bead's original finding (DbusNotificationSentPayload.summary, controllable by any session-bus process including a web page via the Notifications API): a notification summary of the shape 'invoice<RLO>gnp.exe' is stored faithfully but RENDERS in sinexctl recall and the TUI event list as 'invoicexe.png' -- extension spoofing via bidi override, a well-known real-world attack class. Width is measured as 0 so table alignment is preserved -- the operator gets a well-formed table displaying text that is not what is actually stored, with no visual cue anything is wrong.

This belongs under sinex-1hus (the shared consumption-boundary sanitization epic) as an additional character class the sanitize_for_destination primitive needs to strip (Cf format characters, not just Cc control characters), in addition to this bead's original ESC/OSC findings.

title: permanent event purge (execute_cascade_tombstone) leaks embedded/annotation content forever -- omits the exact archive-side-table cleanup its own restore sibling performs
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via residual-risk-ledger follow-up (tombstone/purge cascade table-by-table enumeration). crate/sinex-schema/src/apply.rs:2318-2355, the full body of execute_cascade_tombstone (the PERMANENT deletion function, used for real privacy/compliance-motivated data removal), does exactly two things: insert a skeleton row into core.event_tombstones, then DELETE FROM audit.archived_events WHERE id=ANY(p_archived_ids). That's it -- it never touches audit.archived_annotations, audit.archived_embeddings, or audit.archived_tagged_items.

Contrast the NON-destructive sibling, execute_cascade_restore (apply.rs:2470-2482), which correctly cleans up all three: DELETE FROM audit.archived_annotations WHERE event_id IN (...), DELETE FROM audit.archived_embeddings WHERE event_id IN (...), DELETE FROM audit.archived_tagged_items WHERE item_id IN (...) AND item_type='event'. No FK saves the tombstone path -- all three archive tables are created via LIKE core.X INCLUDING ALL, and Postgres LIKE never copies foreign keys (the DDL's own doc comments say so explicitly); there is no ON DELETE CASCADE from archived_events to any of them (confirmed: only event_annotations and event_embeddings even have an FK to core.events at all, and that's on the LIVE tables, defs/embeddings.rs:193-196/435-438, defs/annotations.rs:329 -- irrelevant to the already-copied archive-table rows).

Impact: audit.archived_embeddings.embedded_text holds text DERIVED FROM the event payload, and audit.archived_annotations.content holds operator-curated content. Purging an event -- the operation an operator would use specifically to permanently remove sensitive/unwanted data -- leaves BOTH behind permanently, with no live row and no archive row pointing at them: invisible to every lifecycle surface (core.lifecycle_tier_status() at apply.rs:2489-2527 counts only live/archive/tombstone, none of which reference the orphaned side-table rows) and unreachable by any LATER purge attempt, since a purge is driven from audit.archived_events ids that, after this bug, no longer exist for that event. Same defect CLASS as the already-filed sinex-erqz item 5 (email body preview surviving tombstone) but on the GENERIC path, affecting every event with an embedding or annotation -- this is the higher-severity, broader-blast-radius sibling of that finding.
acceptance_criteria: execute_cascade_tombstone deletes from audit.archived_annotations/archived_embeddings/archived_tagged_items using the same WHERE clauses as execute_cascade_restore, before or alongside deleting from audit.archived_events, so a permanent purge is actually permanent for embedded/annotation content, not just for the base event row. Given this affects the CORRECTNESS of a privacy-motivated deletion operation, treat as high priority independent of the wipe timeline.

title: confirmed-events stream mid-run eviction has NO gap detection -- a behind automaton silently loses events permanently, with no error, metric, or recovery short of a daemon restart
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via residual-risk-ledger follow-up (dedicated trace of confirmed-stream DiscardPolicy::Old semantics). The archive-cascade-vs-fresh-replay-event interleaving originally flagged as a possible race is actually REFUTED as a race -- the replay path is strictly serialized (cascade archive commits in one transaction BEFORE the scan command that would produce fresh events is even published, replay_writer.rs:360-372/447+), and a concurrent non-replay writer is genuinely protected by a FOR KEY SHARE lock on parent rows during persist (events/persistence/validation.rs:146-155) that blocks a competing archive-cascade DELETE until persist commits, or fails the persist loudly (isolatable batch failure -> bisect -> DLQ) if archive wins -- not silent.

But tracing this surfaced a DIFFERENT, real, and more severe defect in the same area: jetstream_consumer/bootstrap.rs:74 sets DiscardPolicy::Old on the confirmed stream, with bootstrap.rs:186-191 setting max_age to 72h (activity) / 24h (reflection) and max_messages:2_000_000. The bootstrap comment (lines 60-63) justifies this with 'a consumer that falls >max_messages behind recovers from Postgres through its mandatory startup catch-up' -- but that recovery mechanism is STARTUP-ONLY: automaton_runtime.rs:266-280 runs the historical catch-up scan exactly ONCE, before the consumer task is even spawned, and automaton_runtime.rs:539 then subscribes with DeliverPolicy::New. There is NO mid-run gap detection anywhere -- grepped runtime/jetstream_consumer.rs and found only a num_pending log field (line 271), zero stream-sequence continuity tracking. A long-running automaton that falls more than 72h behind (plausible under sustained backlog -- exactly the condition the imminent re-import creates, and exactly the condition the deliberate pacing work in sinex-2n9/ddy sustains) has its pending messages SILENTLY DELETED out from under it by JetStream's own retention policy and skips them permanently -- no error, no metric, no signal, no recovery until the daemon happens to restart (which re-triggers the one-time catch-up scan).
acceptance_criteria: Add mid-run gap detection: track the last-seen stream sequence per consumer and compare against the stream's current first-sequence periodically (not just at startup), surfacing a metric/alert/log when the gap approaches max_age or max_messages, well before silent eviction occurs. Consider whether periodic re-triggering of the catch-up scan (not just at startup) is warranted for automata that fall significantly behind, given the imminent re-import is exactly the sustained-backlog condition that triggers this.
close_reason: Closure Evidence Manifest: SATISFIED. Confirmed consumers now monitor retention during delivery, emit durable liveness evidence/telemetry, stop on an observed gap, and trigger supervisor recovery for historical catch-up. Verified: nix develop --command xtask check -p sinexd; nix develop --command xtask test -p sinexd -E "test(confirmed_consumer_stops_on_real_retention_gap)" (passed standalone; combined DB-heavy run was resource-contended and intentionally not used as evidence). No deferred AC.

title: acquisition staging mirror writes bytes to disk BEFORE updating hash/offset counters -- a failed mirror write on retry duplicates the record batch's bytes inside the durable material
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via lifecycle/crash-consistency audit (resumed after initial turn-budget exhaustion). Real data-corruption path, not just a resource concern.

crate/sinexd/src/runtime/acquisition_manager.rs: publish_material_data_chunk (lines 714-739) publishes a slice to JetStream FIRST (durable, JetStream-acked), then mirrors the same bytes to a local temp file via mirror_slice_to_local_stage. mirror_slice_to_local_stage (lines 553-573): file.write_all(data).await? happens BEFORE hasher.update(data)/bytes_written/slice_count are advanced. A failed write leaves all three counters unadvanced and stashes pending_published_slice; ensure_pending_slice_mirrored (575-602) re-mirrors on the next call and THEN advances the counters. append_record_batch (622-712) computes anchors from bytes_written AFTER that repair, then re-publishes the CALLER'S records.

Interleaving that breaks: (1) batch R1..Rn publishes successfully to JetStream at offset O; (2) the local mirror write_all fails (e.g. ENOSPC on the tmpfs, see sibling finding on /tmp sizing); bytes_written stays at O; (3) append_record_batch returns Err, so the source retries R1..Rn from scratch (does not advance its own cursor); (4) on retry, ensure_pending_slice_mirrored succeeds, advancing to O+len; the SAME records R1..Rn are then published AGAIN as a new slice at offset O+len. Net result: the material's durable byte stream contains R1..Rn TWICE. Events anchor only at the second copy; the first copy is unreferenced but durably present. The acquisition-side hash is H(R1..Rn++R1..Rn), matching exactly what the assembler received, so the END-frame content-hash check cannot catch it. Since replay for material provenance is 're-read the material', a subsequent replay re-parses BOTH copies and mints two live interpretations with distinct anchor_byte -- occurrence identity does not collapse them, so this is a genuine, undetected duplicate-derivation source. Nats-Msg-Id dedup does not help since the retry uses a new slice index. Multi-chunk batches are worse: a failure on chunk 2-of-5 means chunks 1-2 are already durable and the retry re-publishes the WHOLE batch after them.

Aggravating factor: the local mirror is write-only and serves no read purpose in production -- SourceMaterialHandle::temp_path() has zero non-test readers anywhere in the codebase (only referenced in acquisition_manager_test.rs). A correctness-destroying failure mode is being paid for with zero functional benefit today.
acceptance_criteria: Either fix the ordering (advance hash/counters atomically with, or logically before, the file write so a failed write can't leave state that causes a re-publish of already-durable bytes), or -- since the mirror has no production reader -- delete the local-mirror write entirely and keep only the in-memory hasher/bytes_written/slice_count tracking, eliminating this failure mode altogether.

title: no least-privilege token tier is actually deployed: MCP bridge and every local RPC consumer share ONE Admin-scoped credential -- readonly/write/admin is architecture, not deployment
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via boundary-enforcement/trust-mapping audit. Compounds sinex-pzo9 (ops.start RCE via a :write token) and sinex-5spk (MCP catalog role enforcement is convention-only, not typed) by removing the credential-scope layer that would otherwise contain a future mistake in either.

crate/sinexd/src/api/auth.rs documents a three-tier Role hierarchy (ReadOnly/Write/Admin) encoded as a token suffix, but the entire deployment surface only ever provisions ONE token secret: nixos/modules/secrets.nix:40-41,91 declares only sinex-api-admin-token -- no sinex-api-write-token/sinex-api-readonly-token exists anywhere. nixos/modules/default.nix:2742 sets gateway.token_role='admin' for the single generated runtimeTargetDescriptor and every local consumer (sinexctl, sinex-mcp-server, the dev checkout) points at the same apiAdminTokenFile. Confirmed live: .sinex/state/dev-api-token contains a dev token suffixed :admin. GatewayAuth::verify (rpc_server/auth.rs:225-239) compares the whole token against a single configured secret -- there is structurally no support for multiple concurrently-valid tokens with different roles server-side. crate/sinex-primitives/src/runtime_target.rs:98-106 (apply_to_token): if the token already carries a role suffix, a caller-specified token_role is silently ignored -- no client-side downgrade path exists even if attempted.

crate/sinexctl/src/bin/sinex-mcp-server.rs bills itself as a 'Read-only Sinex MCP stdio server,' but its actual credential floor is Admin. What currently prevents an MCP client from doing Admin things is ONLY the hand-maintained Rust match arms in crate/sinexctl/src/mcp.rs (each calling one fixed, typed GatewayClient method -- verified no generic RPC-passthrough tool and no mutating arm exists today). The moment anyone adds an ops/lifecycle/mutation-shaped tool to the MCP catalog (plausible given the existing sinex_ops_list/sinex_ops_get naming convention), it inherits full Admin RCE with zero additional gating, because there is no separately-provisioned least-privilege token to catch the mistake. Not currently exploitable as a live RCE via MCP today, but this is the layer that would have caught the mistake and it doesn't exist.

Additionally confirmed: an RCE via the already-filed sinex-pzo9 (ops.start) is well-contained on the WRITE side by systemd hardening (ProtectSystem=strict + narrow ReadWritePaths + NoNewPrivileges block setuid escalation) but is NOT contained on the READ side -- the collapsed single-daemon architecture grants sinexd's own unit broad read access (via per-domain glue ACL overlays) to browser profiles, ActivityWatch DB, terminal history, Documents, etc, essentially everything sinex is provisioned to capture -- nor on network exfiltration (AF_INET/AF_INET6 permitted, required for DB/NATS). Compounding with the still-open sinex-s4lj (Postgres trust auth) and sinex-vhv3 (unauthenticated NATS): an RCE'd process can trivially pivot to full DB superuser or full event-stream forgery with zero additional credentials -- systemd sandboxing is the LAST containment layer in that chain and only stops write-outside-own-directories.
acceptance_criteria: Provision at least a genuinely separate ReadOnly-scoped token for MCP/read-surface consumers, distinct from the Admin token used by sinexctl's own mutating operations, so a future MCP catalog mistake is caught by credential scope rather than only by hand-maintained match-arm discipline. Track the read-side/network-exfiltration RCE containment gap as a reason to prioritize sinex-s4lj and sinex-vhv3 -- fixing those closes the most severe part of this chain even before a least-privilege MCP token exists.

title: MaterialReadySet eviction is a synchronous O(n) full-map scan with a 6-hour TTL and no size bound -- blocks a tokio worker thread and will scale with the re-import's material count
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via perturbation-robustness audit. crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/material_ready_set.rs: entries: Arc<DashMap<Uuid, Instant>> (line 57), READY_RETENTION=6 hours (line 42), SWEEP_INTERVAL=1024 (line 45). mark_ready() (:88) -> maybe_evict_stale() (:204) -> every 1024th call runs purge_stale() (:220-235), which ITERATES THE ENTIRE MAP building a Vec<Uuid> of expired keys before removing them. The module's own doc-comment (:15-19) claims 'Memory: bounded by TTL-based eviction rather than monotonic growth' -- a 6-hour TTL is not a size bound; the bound is materials-registered-per-6-hours.

Concrete scenario: the post-wipe re-import registers M materials inside one 6-hour window (project memory records the design intent as 'SQLite millions expected' for some lanes). Nothing is evictable during that window, so: memory grows to hundreds of MB resident (DashMap overhead at ~64-80B/entry x millions of materials) on a daemon with a hard MemoryMax; CPU-wise, sweeps fire M/1024 times, each scanning an average of M/2 entries and finding zero expired -- total ~M^2/2048 entry visits, almost entirely wasted at scale. Worse: purge_stale() is SYNCHRONOUS, called from mark_ready() inside async context (material_assembler/state.rs:440, material_assembler/finalize.rs:1033) with no .await inside it -- a multi-million-entry scan blocks a tokio worker thread outright, while holding DashMap shard locks the JetStream consumer's FK gate (event_engine/jetstream_consumer/persist.rs:28 -> ensure_ready -> is_ready) contends for on every event. The background maintenance task (event_engine/service.rs:1298-1307) calls the same O(n) purge_stale() every 5 minutes too, adding another full scan.

The closed sinex-audit-entity-unbounded-maps fixed the identical class in entity_resolver/entity_enricher -- MaterialReadySet was not covered by that fix and has no existing bead.
acceptance_criteria: MaterialReadySet gets either a real size bound (not just a time-based TTL) or its eviction is moved off the sync hot path (e.g. background-task-only sweep, never inline in mark_ready) so a large in-flight material count during the re-import can't block a tokio worker thread or degrade to O(M^2) sweep cost. Get the real expected material count for the re-import window before deciding fix scope -- if it's well under ~500k in 6h this degrades from HIGH to a tuning nit.

title: every automaton/source-binding runtime lane uses a raw sqlx pool bypassing all Sinex pool policy -- no statement_timeout, dead pool-size config, wrong per-process connection accounting
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via perturbation-robustness audit (scale/concurrency/adversarial-input sweep). Directly relevant to the imminent re-import, which is the heaviest concurrent-load event this system will ever see.

crate/sinexd/src/runtime/runtime_cli.rs:977-982 (connect_primary_db) builds a bare sqlx::PgPool::connect(...) directly, NOT via sinex_db::create_pool_with_config. Consequences:

1. statement_timeout is never set -- the session hooks that install it live only in sinex_db::pool::with_statement_timeout_session_hooks (crate/sinex-db/src/pool.rs:270-291), reached only through create_pool_with_config*. Every automaton/source-binding connection runs with Postgres' default statement_timeout (0=unlimited). sinex-o1mg (closed) was exactly a runaway-plan incident; that class is unguarded on this lane.
2. validate_against_postgres_max is skipped (pool.rs:230-232) -- the startup guard against an oversized pool never fires here.
3. RuntimeConfig::database_pool_size (config.rs:151-155, default 10, parsed from SINEX_DB_POOL_SIZE/SINEX_DATABASE_POOL_SIZE at :314-317) is DEAD CONFIG -- grep confirms nothing threads it into a pool anywhere in crate/sinexd/src. Setting the env var has zero effect.
4. Per-process connection accounting in the NixOS module is wrong: nixos/modules/database.nix:73,91-92 computes max_connections assuming perServiceConnections=4 (default.nix:436-439) per service, but the actual runtime lane uses sqlx's default max_connections=10 per pool.

Concrete scenario: the daemon is collapsed (one sinexd unit hosts event engine + API + all automata + all hosted source bindings). start_automata spawns one task per registered automaton (supervisor/mod.rs:525-552), each independently calling connect_primary_db via RuntimeCliRunner::run (automata/registry.rs:232-260). start_source_bindings does the same per binding. With 16 automata + N source bindings, that's (16+N) independent 10-connection pools inside ONE process, against a Postgres sized on the assumption of 4 each. During the re-import, when every automaton is concurrently draining the confirmed stream and doing DB work, aggregate demand can exceed max_connections -- failure mode is 'FATAL: sorry, too many clients already', surfacing as automaton crash-restart loops rather than a clean pool-acquire timeout.

Not covered by the closed sinex-d4qg (scoped only to SINEX_API_POOL_MAX_CONNECTIONS; the event engine and runtime lane were explicitly left on the uniform default, and this runtime lane doesn't even read that config).
acceptance_criteria: connect_primary_db (or its callers) uses sinex_db::create_pool_with_config so the runtime/automaton lane gets statement_timeout, the max-connections validation guard, and an actually-effective pool-size config. Either wire RuntimeConfig::database_pool_size through, or remove it if superseded, rather than leaving it as dead config. Reconcile nixos/modules/database.nix's max_connections formula against the real per-pool default (10, not 4) before the re-import specifically, since that's the load event most likely to expose the mismatch.

Closed after the runtime database-pool bypass was eliminated.

The implementation is present in commit `4d652ba75`, which is an ancestor of the current HEAD. | `nix develop --command xtask test -p sinexd --lib -E 'test(connect_primary_db_applies_shared_pool_policy)' && nix develop --command xtask check -p sinexd` | Satisfied |

title: backup mechanism (sinex-8gkv/zumi/21gb): shared root cause is hardcoded deployment-topology assumptions never checked against real NixOS-deployed shape, validated only internally-consistently
description:
Synthesis bead from a 2026-08-11 delivery/supply-chain integrity audit, re-verifying all three already-open backup beads against current master and answering the explicit question of whether they share a root cause -- they do.

- sinex-8gkv: NATS JetStream capture hardcodes state_dir.join('nats/jetstream') (crate/sinexctl/src/admin/snapshot.rs:421-424) against the CLI's assumed state layout; the REAL deployed NATS store_dir is /var/lib/nats/jetstream per nats.nix, which never matches. capture_dir_component silently records bytes=0, blake3='absent' with NO ERROR when the source directory doesn't exist, and every downstream missing-check filters component.bytes>0 BEFORE computing what's missing -- so an absent component is invisible to the missing-check, not merely tolerated.
- sinex-zumi: quiesce/service-stop logic matches units via the glob sinex-* (crate/sinexctl/src/admin/exec.rs:386-408). The real deployed units are sinexd (daemon) and nats (broker) -- genuinely no unit in the tree is named sinex-* at the service level. The 'is sinexd running' quiesce check silently passes even when the live-writing daemon is up.
- sinex-21gb: the Postgres dump/restore round trip is 100% mocked in tests (no real pg_dump/pg_restore against a live TimescaleDB+pgvector instance ever exercised); execute_postgres_restore_drill (crate/sinexctl/src/admin/snapshot.rs:866-918) requires only that --restore-database-url be PRESENT, never checks the target DB is actually empty, despite crate/sinexctl/docs/state_snapshot.md:140-147 explicitly documenting that the drill 'refuses to run unless pointing at an empty drill database' and 'active sinex-* services are stopped' -- the doc's second claim reuses the SAME broken glob from sinex-zumi, so the doc's own safety claims are wrong in two independent ways, not one.

SHARED ROOT CAUSE: all three failures are the same shape -- a hardcoded assumption about the deployed system's shape (a state-dir path, a systemd unit-naming convention, 'the target DB is empty') that was never checked against the ACTUAL NixOS-deployed topology, combined with a verification/safety layer that was built and tested against that SAME wrong assumption rather than against independent ground truth. The pattern repeats at every level meant to catch it: inspect_snapshot_archive filters on the same bytes>0 signal the capture step itself silently zeroes out; the restore drill's own doc-claimed 'empty DB' check simply doesn't exist in code; the Postgres round-trip test asserts against a mock's own log instead of a real pg_restore invocation. None of the three has ever been exercised end-to-end against the real deployed stack.
acceptance_criteria: Per the 'use general mechanisms' doctrine: fix once, not three times. Build a single 'discover real unit names / real NATS store_dir / verify-target-empty' primitive that all three backup/restore code paths call, instead of three independently hardcoded assumptions. At minimum, add one integration test that runs the FULL backup->restore round trip against the actual real deployed NixOS topology (real unit names, real NATS store_dir, a real empty-vs-nonempty target DB check) rather than mocks, since that's the gap that let all three drift silently.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: Additional semantic-drift finding 2026-08-11 via data-lifecycle-stewardship audit, distinct from this bead's mechanism-root-cause findings (wrong NATS paths, service-name globs, missing empty-target check) -- this is about what happens even on a SUCCESSFUL restore. pgvector HNSW index reconstruction is inherently non-deterministic: pg_dump/pg_restore don't preserve index DATA, only the CREATE INDEX DDL, which gets replayed post-data-load -- the HNSW graph is rebuilt from scratch, and HNSW construction is approximate-by-design, depending on table scan/insertion order and (if maintenance_work_mem enables parallel workers) worker interleaving, both of which can differ between the original build and the post-restore rebuild even though the underlying vector VALUES are byte-identical. Net effect: for the exact same query embedding, top-K nearest-neighbor results could differ at the margin between pre-wipe and post-restore states -- approximate-index drift, not corrupted data, but real semantic drift a restore-verification process should account for. The restore drill (execute_postgres_restore_drill) only verifies exact ROW COUNTS -- it never checks index consistency or semantic-search stability, so this drift is currently invisible to the drill even on an official 'successful' run. Verified genuinely non-issue by design (not merely unhandled): no SERIAL/BIGSERIAL/IDENTITY columns exist anywhere in the schema (UUIDv7-only identity model sidesteps sequence-reset drift entirely), and TimescaleDB-specific pre/post-restore hypertable bracketing is correctly implemented. Worth a documentation note on the restore process (or a semantic-search-stability spot-check added to the drill) rather than treating this as something to eliminate -- it's an inherent pgvector characteristic, not a sinex bug.

comments.author: Sinity

No production-shaped NixOS quiesced round-trip proof was found. The deployment-owned CAS Borg job is also still stale at /realm/sinex/state/blob-repository versus bridge.nix's /var/lib/sinex/state/blob-repository; tracked as sinex-w98.2. Keep jd4u in progress.

title: structural/plausibility event validator has zero production callers -- 500+ lines of tests guard a path production never executes, under a comment claiming otherwise
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via test-coverage risk-mapping audit (Opus). This is a 'wire it or delete it' architectural decision, not a narrow bug -- and per this project's own 'unfinished is not obsolete, complete it' doctrine, the default should be wiring it, especially since the imminent wipe-and-reimport is the single moment where an unvalidated import writes the ENTIRE durable corpus.

IngestEventValidator::validate_event (crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/validator.rs:254) has exactly ONE caller in the whole repo: validator_test.rs:17. AdmissionService defines its OWN validate_event (admission.rs:1348-1353) that calls only schema validation -- empty-source checks, NUL bytes, per-event size bounds, non-object payloads, fs path/size checks, ID-timestamp drift, duplicate parent ids are all UNREACHABLE in production.

Compounding: crate/sinex-primitives/tests/event_validation_property_test.rs:197-201 has a function literally commented '/// Production validation wrapper for events (avoid mock-only checks)' that constructs EventValidator::with_validation_enabled(false) -- so 509 lines of property tests guard a path production does not take, under a comment asserting the opposite. Anyone reading this suite reasonably concludes ingest is structurally validated; it is not.

Two related, already-open beads make this worse: sinex-naw9 (a corrupt registered schema silently downgrades that (source,event_type) to no validation at all, regardless of strict mode) and sinex-421u (xtask/src/sandbox/orchestrator.rs:1180 sets SINEX_VALIDATE_SCHEMAS=false for ALL sandbox test instances -- so the schema-reject-to-DLQ route also has near-zero live-route test evidence anywhere in the suite).
acceptance_criteria: A deliberate decision is made and executed: either wire IngestEventValidator::validate_event into AdmissionService::validate_event (recommended per project doctrine -- try it against a real/staging corpus and see what actually breaks BEFORE the wipe, not after), or delete the validator and its 509-line test suite if it's determined to be genuinely superseded. Either way, the misleading 'Production validation wrapper' comment on the disabled-validation test helper gets corrected to state what it actually constructs.
close_reason:
## Closure Evidence Manifest

| AC | Evidence kind | Surface | Evidence | Command | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AC-1 | runtime | `crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/admission.rs`, `crate/sinexd/tests/event_engine/{admission_test.rs,jetstream_consumer_test.rs}` | The full structural/plausibility validator is enabled on the real admission path and rejected children settle through durable DLQ evidence rather than reaching `core.events`. The misleading helper wording was corrected in the implementation batch. | `nix develop --command xtask test -p sinexd -E 'test(full_validator_rejections_route_through_real_admission_dlq_settlement) or test(admission_rejects_non_object_payload_via_full_ingest_validator)' --impact-mode=off` | Satisfied |

Anti-vacuity: the real JetStream route test checks both structural and plausibility failures, durable-debt settlement, persisted DLQ evidence, and absence from `core.events`.

title: CRITICAL: admission equivalence-key collision across a backlogged NATS fetch batch produces silent, permanent duplicate live events
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via a test-coverage risk-mapping audit (Opus). Directly on the critical path of the imminent fresh-wipe re-import, and exposure is actively increasing due to recent pacing changes.

Mechanism (traced by reading, not yet reproduced live):
1. run_loop.rs:335-343 fetches up to batch_fetch_max_messages NATS messages and calls prepare_events(msg) PER MESSAGE, accumulating into one persist batch.
2. prepare.rs:27 -> admit_intent_bytes per message. Its pre-pass (admission.rs:998-1013) resolves equivalence keys ONLY against core.events -- nothing from a sibling message in the SAME fetch batch is visible to it.
3. The intra-batch collapse maps (admission.rs:1050-1051) are local to one admit_intent_bytes call and are dropped at return -- they do not see across messages either.
4. filter_cached_batch (admission.rs:1356-1379) dedups on event_id only -- never on equivalence_key.
5. ix_events_equivalence_key (crate/sinex-schema/src/defs/events.rs:609-612) is a plain, NON-UNIQUE index. Nothing at the DB layer catches it either.

Result: two revisions of the same real-world occurrence, published as two separate NATS messages within one fetch batch (no persistence barrier between them), both classify as Fresh against an empty-of-each-other view and BOTH persist as live core.events rows sharing an equivalence_key. find_live_by_equivalence_key (crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/events/queries.rs:716-731) does ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1, so a THIRD revision only ever archives the newest of the two duplicates -- the older duplicate stays live PERMANENTLY, silently.

This is structurally the same bug class as the already-fixed sinex-audit-intrabatchsuperseed (which closed the intra-INTENT same-key collapse) one level up -- the inter-MESSAGE case within one fetch batch was never covered.

Why exposure is increasing right now: the just-landed pacing work (sinex-2n9 #2594, sinex-ddy #2596) deliberately slows the drain to hold a backlog. A deeper backlog means more same-key revisions co-resident in one fetch batch -- this is the ordinary state of a backlogged consumer, which is the normal state during import and after every restart, i.e. exactly what the fresh re-import will produce.

Blast radius: silent, permanent, self-concealing double-counting of duration in every downstream aggregate (window.active, atuin.command, page.visited, daily/hourly rollups). No error, no DLQ entry, no counter -- undetectable except by an ad-hoc GROUP BY equivalence_key HAVING count(*) > 1 sweep.

Realistic gap test the current suite would NOT catch: publish two state.interval events sharing equivalence_key, differing duration_secs, as two separate NATS messages with NO wait_for_event_id barrier between them (i.e. both land in one fetch batch), then assert SELECT COUNT(*) FROM core.events WHERE equivalence_key =  = 1. Every existing supersede/suppress test in jetstream_consumer_test.rs inserts exactly such a barrier (wait_for_event_id between the two publishes), which is precisely the condition that makes the bug invisible to the existing suite.
acceptance_criteria: Equivalence-key resolution during admission sees across ALL messages in the current fetch batch, not just prior committed core.events rows -- either by making the intra-batch collapse maps batch-scoped (spanning admit_intent_bytes calls within one run_loop iteration) or by adding a real uniqueness constraint/upsert-on-conflict at the DB layer for live (non-archived) equivalence_key values. A test publishes two same-equivalence-key messages with NO persistence barrier between them (same fetch batch) and asserts exactly one live row results.
close_reason:
## Closure Evidence Manifest

| AC | Evidence kind | Surface | Evidence | Command | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AC-1 | runtime | `crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/admission.rs`, `crate/sinexd/tests/event_engine/admission_test.rs` | Intra-fetch equivalence resolution now preserves same-key collision semantics while allowing distinct keys, supersede-on-change, and no duplicate live rows. | `nix develop --command xtask test -p sinexd -E 'test(equivalence_key_collision_within_one_fetch_batch_must_not_duplicate) or test(distinct_equivalence_keys_in_one_fetch_batch_are_both_admitted) or test(supersede_on_change_across_fetch_messages_archives_original_live_row)' --impact-mode=off` | Satisfied |

Anti-vacuity: the focused suite covers collision, distinct-key admission, and cross-message supersession.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text:
CORROBORATED and WIDENED 2026-08-11 via a dedicated follow-up trace (resumed agent, full turn budget on this one question). Verdict: same mechanism, not a distinct bug, and worse than originally filed in two ways:

1. The demotion path (admission.rs:1104-1151) is structurally incapable of covering the cross-message case on TWO independent gates: (a) key_last_index is admit_intent_bytes-local, dropped at return, so it's unconditionally empty at the start of processing message B; (b) even setting that aside, message A's event is still in-memory (uncommitted) when B's pre-pass runs against committed core.events only, so B resolves EquivalenceOutcome::Fresh and never even reaches the Superseded arm that would consult the demotion machinery. Confirmed no other net exists downstream: filter_cached_batch and filter_tombstoned_batch both key on event_id only (two interpretations of one occurrence have distinct UUIDv7 ids by design), and ix_events_equivalence_key has no .unique() (impossible on a hypertable without the partition key).

2. WIDENED SCOPE: this defeats the DEFAULT RevisionPolicy::SuppressDuplicate (used by every payload type that doesn't opt into SupersedeOnChange), not just the three SupersedeOnChange-opted-in contracts (atuin, browser page-visited, activitywatch) originally implied. SuppressDuplicate only produces EquivalenceOutcome::Suppress when a LIVE ROW IS FOUND -- cross-message, no live row is found (same reason as above), so the outcome is Fresh and the event admits anyway. Any fix scoped narrowly to SupersedeOnChange types would be incomplete.

3. NEW mechanism identified -- Shape 2 is actively created by otherwise-correct behavior, not just absence of a check: when a pre-existing live row R exists, message A's pre-pass sees R -> Superseded{target:R} -> apply_supersession archives R BEFORE persist. Message B's pre-pass then runs against a table where R no longer exists -> Fresh -> admitted. Had R still been live at B's pre-pass, B would have hit apply_supersession's existence-check failure and taken the documented safe-fallback (suppress B, keep R live) -- so A's archive of R is precisely what converts B from safe-suppressed to wrongly-admitted.

RECOMMENDED FIX DESIGN (from the trace): hoist the existing three maps (live_by_key / key_last_index / key_archive_target) from admit_intent_bytes-local to fetch-batch-scoped state owned by process_batch, rather than inventing a new mechanism -- the collapse logic already implemented for the intra-intent case is correct, only its lifetime is wrong. The archive side-effect must then fire at most once per fetch batch per key, mirroring key_archive_target's existing 'established once by whichever event first collided' invariant.

CHEAPEST DETECTOR, recommend running regardless of fix timing, both now (to size current exposure) and as a post-reimport gate: SELECT equivalence_key, count(*) FROM core.events WHERE equivalence_key IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(*) > 1.

Confirmed batch_fetch_max_messages is not a mitigating factor -- the pre-pass's own comment concedes 'occurrence-stable interval sources re-emit keyed events whose key already exists on essentially every batch', and the re-import backlog is exactly the condition that maximizes fetch-batch fill and therefore collision probability. Severity should stay at or above CRITICAL for the re-import specifically.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text:
Third independent confirmation pass 2026-08-11 (attempted live reproduction; live DB/NATS/prod stack unreachable on this host -- no event corpus exists anywhere to mine, confirmed via direct read-only query against the one reachable dev postgres: core.events is empty). No live repro was possible, but the static analysis is now STRONGER and corrects a mischaracterization:

CORRECTED CHARACTERIZATION: this is NOT a race window (timing-dependent) -- it is DETERMINISTIC MISCLASSIFICATION, independent of elapsed time. Confirmed via run_loop.rs:335-344: the classification loop (admit_intent_bytes per message) fully completes for ALL messages in a fetch BEFORE persist_and_confirm_batch is called at line 362 -- there is no writer active during the classification loop except apply_supersession's execute_cascade_archive (prepare.rs:473-483), which only DELETES/archives a predecessor row, never inserts a live one. So message 2's pre-pass observes IDENTICALLY the same core.events state as message 1's, no matter how much wall-clock time elapses between them. Confirmed zero equivalence-key-aware logic exists anywhere in jetstream_consumer/ outside admission.rs itself (rg confirms).

NEW TRIGGER PATH FOUND, needs no backlog at all: a single flush exceeding NATS_INTENT_PAYLOAD_SOFT_LIMIT_BYTES is split into multiple chunks, each published as its OWN NATS message (event_transport.rs:908-995), published back-to-back and therefore near-certain to land in one fetch. Same-key events straddling a chunk boundary bypass the intra-batch collapse entirely -- this can happen even under a fast-draining, non-backlogged consumer, not just during import backlog.

Repro trap for whoever writes the eventual regression test (mirrors the already-known sinex-c574 lesson): a naive test in a quiet environment will falsely report 'not reproducible' because a quiet consumer drains one message per fetch, so the two never co-occupy a batch -- the test MUST force co-occupancy (publish both messages to the raw stream BEFORE the consumer's pull loop starts, so the first fetch necessarily returns both; no wait_for_event_id barrier between the two publishes). Also: assert via SELECT COUNT(*) FROM core.events WHERE equivalence_key=, NOT via fetch_optional(...)==Some(revision_id) -- fetch_optional takes the first row and cannot fail even when the bug is present; this is exactly why the existing supersede tests (which all use fetch_optional) never caught this.

Field-frequency (not existence) is now the only open question -- existence is certain and timing-independent. Frequency is contingent on backlog depth for the equivalence-key-collision path, but the newly-found chunk-splitting path needs no backlog at all. Confidence in CRITICAL priority: justified on the code path alone, independent of live confirmation.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: Reflection-lane sharing CONFIRMED 2026-08-11 via residual-risk-ledger follow-up (dedicated trace). The reflection lane is not a parallel implementation -- it is the SAME JetStreamConsumer type with only one divergence (storage_lane threaded into find_live_by_equivalence_keys and insert_stream_batch_into, event_engine/service.rs:1057-1073, jetstream_consumer/config.rs:97-101). The pre-pass, the intra-intent-only key_last_index/key_archive_target maps, and the fetch-batch loop are all shared verbatim (admission.rs:1050-1051, run_loop.rs:335-343). So every mechanism in this bead applies to the reflection lane identically. Currently UNEXPOSED in practice only because nothing emits a keyed reflection event today (grepped every with_equivalence_key call site -- all activity-lane; no reflection payload declares revision_policy=supersede_on_change) -- but any future keyed reflection event inherits this CRITICAL bug with zero additional code required. Worth folding into the eventual fix's test matrix (assert the fix holds for both EventStorageLane::Activity and ::Reflection) even though reflection has no live repro path today.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [PR #2615 2026-08-11] Test-only: a failing test proving the cross-message equivalence-key collision within one fetch batch was added (#[ignore]'d). The underlying bug fix was NOT attempted. Separately, the coordinator found and fixed a real bug in the TEST ITSELF (not the target bug): publish_event uses a fire-and-forget core-NATS publish, and the original test published messages before the JetStream stream existed, silently losing both messages and producing a 60s timeout rather than a real proof. Fixed by bootstrapping the stream first via ensure_raw_events_stream_for_topology before publishing; the test now correctly and deterministically reproduces the target collision. Bead stays open.
