title: rpc_server.rs: TTL task excluded from shutdown-wait set (can leak past server stop); accept_loop's error path skips shutdown signaling/waiting entirely; batch handler violates JSON-RPC notification-response spec
description:
Three bugs in crate/sinexd/src/api/rpc_server.rs found via narrate-through audit (gpt-5.3-codex-spark, wave128-047):

1. MEDIUM -- rpc_server.rs:787 the TTL enforcement background task is spawned and immediately dropped/detached (`let _ttl_task = RpcServer::monitor_background_task(...)`) rather than being included in the shutdown-wait set: `RpcServer::wait_for_background_tasks(metrics_task, cleanup_task, sse_bus_task).await?` only waits for three tasks, omitting the TTL task. If the TTL task exits early, panics, or hangs during shutdown, nothing observes or treats it as a failure, and it can continue running past server stop.

2. MEDIUM -- rpc_server.rs:822 the accept_loop hard-error path bypasses background-task shutdown signaling: `let accept_result = RpcServer::accept_loop(...).await; ... accept_result?; // signal + wait sequence below` -- if accept_loop returns Err (e.g. a listener accept failure), the `?` short-circuits before the shutdown_tx.send(true) and wait_for_background_tasks sequence runs, so background cleanup/metrics/SSE tasks are never told to stop and never awaited on this path.

3. LOW-MEDIUM -- rpc_server.rs:594 the batch RPC handler emits a response for every entry, including JSON-RPC notification-style requests that per spec should get no response (id absent/null). Clients expecting spec-compliant "no response for notifications" behavior get unexpected extra entries in a batch response, breaking correlation/result-streaming logic that assumes strict JSON-RPC 2.0 semantics.

Found via narrate-through audit of crate/sinexd/src/api/rpc_server.rs (2026-08-11, wave128 batch).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Trigger a TTL background task panic/hang during a normal server shutdown -- observe the shutdown sequence completes without any indication the TTL task is still running or failed.
2. Force accept_loop to return an early Err (e.g. simulate a listener accept failure) -- observe the shutdown_tx signal and wait_for_background_tasks call never run.
3. Send a JSON-RPC batch request containing a notification-style entry (no id) -- observe the batch response still contains an entry for it.
acceptance_criteria: The TTL task is included in wait_for_background_tasks (or an equivalent monitored-task set) so its failure is observable at shutdown. accept_loop's error path still signals shutdown and awaits background tasks before propagating its error (e.g. via a defer/guard pattern, or restructuring the ? to run cleanup first). The batch handler omits responses for notification-style requests (no id) per JSON-RPC 2.0.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] All 3 findings (TTL task excluded from shutdown-wait set, accept_loop error path skips shutdown signaling, batch RPC responds to notifications) are directly testable against rpc_server.rs's shutdown/batch-handling logic. None have tests yet.

Not tested this pass: all 3 require either full server-lifecycle harness (bind+shutdown sequence) or a full AppState (DB pool, auth, rate limiter, services) to reach handle_rpc_batch -- existing rpc_server_test.rs's build_test_router is a synthetic layer-only router, not wired to the real batch handler. title: domain.rs: EventName Display/FromStr aren't true inverses for dotted sources (identity round-trip bug); HostName::new vs from_static disagree on lowercasing; ContentKey::from_static accepts shapes validate() rejects
description:
Three compile-time-vs-runtime validation divergences in crate/sinex-primitives/src/domain.rs, found via narrate-through audit (gpt-5.3-codex-spark, wave128-009):

1. HIGH -- EventName's Display/FromStr are not true inverses for dotted sources. domain.rs:821 (Display: `write!(f, "{}.{}", self.source, self.event_type)`) and :813 (FromStr: `s.split_once('.')`). For source="desktop.input", event_type="file.created" (valid per EventSource, which allows dots), Display emits "desktop.input.file.created" but FromStr on that string parses source="desktop", event_type="input.file.created" -- a real round-trip identity mismatch, not just style, that can route to the wrong stream/subject class or fail downstream validation expecting true identity.

2. MEDIUM -- HostName canonicalization diverges between constructors. domain.rs:918 (`HostName::new` lowercases: `s.into().to_lowercase()`) vs :926 (`HostName::from_static` does not: `Self(Cow::Borrowed(s))`). The same logical hostname compares unequal depending on which constructor built it, breaking canonical map/set-key and dedup assumptions.

3. MEDIUM -- ContentKey::from_static accepts a shape that ContentKey::validate rejects. domain.rs:~1313 (from_static: only checks a "--" separator is present, no exact-count check) vs :2045 (validate: `splitn(3, "--")`, errors if parts.len() > 2, i.e. requires exactly one "--"). A compile-time key like "a--b--c" passes from_static but validate("a--b--c") fails -- split-brain between compile-time-allowed constants and runtime validation.

Found via narrate-through audit of crate/sinex-primitives/src/domain.rs (2026-08-11, wave128 batch).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Construct EventName{source: "desktop.input", event_type: "file.created"}, format it via Display, then parse the resulting string back via FromStr -- observe the round-trip produces a different (source, event_type) pair than the original.
2. Compare HostName::new("Host-A") against HostName::from_static("Host-A") -- observe they don't canonicalize identically.
3. Call ContentKey::from_static("a--b--c") (should be rejected per the exactly-one-separator rule) and confirm it passes, then call ContentKey::validate("a--b--c") and confirm it fails.
acceptance_criteria: EventName's FromStr uses rsplit_once or an unambiguous delimiter/length-prefixed encoding so Display/FromStr become true inverses for all valid EventSource values (which may contain dots). HostName::from_static either lowercases identically to new(), or the divergence is documented as intentional (compile-time-known-already-canonical) with a comment explaining why. ContentKey::from_static enforces the same exactly-one-separator rule as validate().

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] Display/FromStr non-inverse bug is a textbook round-trip property test on EventName. No test exists yet.

title: sinex-primitives utils/validation cluster: barrier timeout uses 1/10th budget instead of full budget; FileChangeKind::Moved never constructed; existing single-file watch paths rejected; retry multiplier truncated to integer; NUL-stripped JSON keys can silently collide
description:
Five bugs in crate/sinex-primitives/src/{utils,validation}/ found via narrate-through audit (gpt-5.3-codex-spark, wave128-022):

1. HIGH -- utils/coordination.rs:188 barrier waits can time out far earlier than requested: `tokio::time::timeout(timeout_duration / 10, self.notify.notified())` inside wait() for non-last participants, returning on the FIRST 1/10th-duration chunk timing out rather than the full budget. A 5-party barrier with timeout_secs=60 where the first participant arrives at t=0 and nobody else joins within 6s fails after 6s instead of the intended 60s.

2. MEDIUM -- utils/file_watcher.rs: FileChangeKind::Moved is declared (line 46) but the conversion mapping (line 170) only handles Create/Modify/Remove/Other -- rename/move events can never surface as Moved; a caller filtering for Moved gets nothing even when files are renamed.

3. MEDIUM -- validation/file_watching_security.rs:161,192 existing single-file watch paths can be rejected during count estimation: `if path.exists() { total_estimated_files += estimate_file_count(path, ...) }` calls read_dir(path) without checking file-vs-directory, so watching a specific existing FILE (a valid `notify` use case) errors out during validate_watch_paths.

4. MEDIUM -- utils/wait_helpers.rs: retry multiplier configuration is inconsistently interpreted -- line 260 does `let factor = config.multiplier as u64;` (truncates fractional/sub-1.0 multipliers to an integer, including to zero) while line 86's backoff_for_attempt uses float power with the real multiplier. A configured multiplier=0.5 becomes factor=0 in one path, producing degenerate/bursty retry timing that diverges from the other path's intended behavior.

5. MEDIUM -- validation/core.rs:322 stripping NUL bytes from JSON object keys can silently merge distinct keys: the object branch of strip_postgres_jsonb_nul_chars rebuilds the map after mutating keys via map.insert(key, nested) with no collision check. Input like {"a\0": 1, "a": 2} can collapse to a single "a" entry, silently dropping payload information before persistence.

Found via narrate-through audit of crate/sinex-primitives/src/utils/{coordination,file_watcher,wait_helpers}.rs and crate/sinex-primitives/src/validation/{file_watching_security,core}.rs (2026-08-11, wave128 batch).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run a 5-party coordination barrier with timeout_secs=60, only 1 participant joins -- observe it fails around t=6s not t=60s.
2. Rename a watched file -- observe no FileChangeKind::Moved event is ever produced.
3. Call validate_watch_paths on a path pointing at an existing single file -- observe it errors instead of succeeding.
4. Configure a retry multiplier of 0.5 and observe wait_helpers.rs's two call sites (line 86 vs 260) computing materially different backoff behavior.
5. Persist a JSON payload with keys "a\u0000" and "a" -- observe one value silently overwrites the other after NUL-stripping.
acceptance_criteria: Barrier wait() waits the full configured timeout (polling in smaller chunks internally is fine, but the overall budget must be respected, not the first chunk). FileChangeKind::Moved is actually constructed from the underlying notify crate's rename events, or the variant is removed if genuinely unsupported. file_watching_security's count-estimation branches on file-vs-directory before calling read_dir. wait_helpers.rs's two multiplier-interpretation sites are unified to the same (float-preserving) semantics. strip_postgres_jsonb_nul_chars detects and errors (or logs loudly) on a post-strip key collision instead of silently overwriting.

title: cascade_analyzer.rs: dead include_weak_dependencies config, unvalidated max_depth i32 downcast, self-loop not detected as a cycle, phantom IDs can appear in a cascade plan; plus sinexctl mcp.rs schema/handler mismatches and one wrong RPC method wiring in ops/debt.rs
description:
Several bugs found via narrate-through audit (gpt-5.3-codex-spark, wave128-031/039/038):

1. MEDIUM -- ops/debt.rs:365-372 wires the wrong RPC method for a remediation action: source-material detail rows label an action "source_material.remediation_plan" but call `.with_rpc_method("sources.list")` instead of the correct "sources.remediation_plan" (used correctly by the sibling constructor at debt.rs:270-277). A caller using machine-readable ActionAvailability to execute actions via rpc_method calls the wrong RPC and gets the wrong view.

2. HIGH -- cascade_analyzer.rs:99 `include_weak_dependencies: bool` (from SINEX_CASCADE_INCLUDE_WEAK env) is parsed but never read by any later branch or query -- a dead control-plane value. Operators setting this env var get no behavior change with no signal.

3. MEDIUM -- cascade_analyzer.rs:379 `max_depth as i32` downcasts a usize-parsed SINEX_CASCADE_MAX_DEPTH without validation; a very large configured value can overflow to negative when cast, producing unpredictable traversal bounds instead of a clean cap.

4. MEDIUM -- cascade_analyzer.rs:465 self-referential parent edges aren't detected as cycles: Tarjan SCC returns a size-1 component for a self-loop node (`parent_event_ids` containing itself), and the code filters `if scc.len() > 1`, discarding it. `detect_circular_dependencies_tx` reports no cycle even though a hard cycle exists via malformed/crafted data.

5. LOW/MEDIUM -- cascade_analyzer.rs:531 `plan_cascade_order` can return a plan containing IDs not present in core.events: non-existent IDs remain in `in_degree` initialization and can still be emitted by the topological walk, producing a misleadingly "successful" plan with phantom IDs.

6. MEDIUM -- sinexctl/mcp.rs: three MCP tool-schema/handler mismatches -- (a) :1450-1463 handler accepts `source_identifier` but the exposed tool schema omits it, making the filter unreachable from schema-validating clients; (b) :1202-1220 `sinex_tasks_list` schema is missing `external_system`/`external_id` that the handler expects, same unreachability; (c) :1870-1905 transport-unavailable handling is inconsistent -- only the runtime-analytics tool group degrades gracefully to a gateway_unavailable_envelope on transport failure, all other tool groups (events/sources, ops/infra) propagate a hard RPC error for the identical outage condition, breaking uniform failure-observability expectations across read-only MCP tools.

Found via narrate-through audit of crate/sinexctl/src/commands/ops/debt.rs, crate/sinexd/src/api/cascade_analyzer.rs, crate/sinexctl/src/mcp.rs (2026-08-11, wave128 batch).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Set SINEX_CASCADE_INCLUDE_WEAK=true and run any cascade analysis -- observe no behavior change.
2. Set SINEX_CASCADE_MAX_DEPTH to a value large enough to overflow i32 on cast -- observe unpredictable traversal depth instead of a clean error/cap.
3. Craft an event row whose parent_event_ids array contains its own id -- observe detect_circular_dependencies_tx reports no cycle.
4. Call an MCP tool client that validates arguments against the exposed schema, e.g. sinex_source_materials with source_identifier, or sinex_tasks_list with external_system/external_id -- observe the argument is rejected by schema validation even though the handler supports it.
5. Trigger a gateway-transport-unavailable condition and compare sinex_system_health's response shape (degraded envelope) against sinex_search_events's response shape (hard -32000 error) for the identical outage.
acceptance_criteria: include_weak_dependencies is either wired into the cascade query or removed. max_depth is validated/clamped before the i32 cast. Self-loop parent references are detected as cycles (or explicitly documented as an accepted limitation with a reason). plan_cascade_order filters out or errors on IDs absent from core.events rather than silently including them. MCP tool schemas for the three named tools expose the fields their handlers already support. Transport-unavailable handling is consistent across all read-only MCP tool groups, not just runtime analytics. The ops/debt.rs remediation-plan action uses with_rpc_method("sources.remediation_plan").

title: TombstoneOperation's state and phase fields are independent with no coupling invariant -- a producer updating only one can leave contradictory lifecycle status on a destructive operation
description:
TombstoneOperation carries both `state` (TombstoneOperationState) and `phase` (TombstoneOperationPhase) as independent fields with no invariant guard, constructor, or serde-level coupling forcing them to stay consistent, despite both representing the same underlying lifecycle concept per their doc comments.

crate/sinex-primitives/src/rpc/lifecycle.rs:223-255 defines the two enums separately; :360-367 puts both fields on the same wire record. If any producer path updates only one field (or they diverge via migration/fallback logic), clients/operators can observe contradictory lifecycle status from the same record -- e.g. state says "previewed" while phase says "completed" -- and status-driven UI/automation could branch on the wrong axis, leading to invalid approvals/cancellations or incorrect operator visibility during a destructive tombstone operation.

Found via narrate-through audit of crate/sinex-primitives/src/rpc/lifecycle.rs (2026-08-11, wave128 batch).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Read lifecycle.rs:223-255,360-367 -- confirm TombstoneOperationState and TombstoneOperationPhase are two full independent enums on the same record with no constructor enforcing consistency.
2. Audit every write site of a TombstoneOperation record -- confirm whether any path updates one field without the other (a migration path, a fallback branch, an error-recovery path).
acceptance_criteria: Either collapse to one canonical field with the other derived/computed, or add an explicit invariant check (a constructor, a debug_assert, or a DB CHECK if persisted) that state and phase can never diverge for a live record.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] Concrete missing-invariant bug (state/phase fields can diverge); testable via a property/unit test on the coupling invariant.

title: declarative parser silently saturates out-of-i64-range JSON integers instead of rejecting them; llm.rs composite key uses unescaped delimiter-joined strings, allowing collisions
description:
Two bugs found via narrate-through audit (gpt-5.3-codex-spark, wave128-014):

1. HIGH -- declarative.rs:783-789 integer coercion from JSON Number can silently corrupt out-of-range values via float saturation: `(FieldType::Integer, Value::Number(n)) if n.is_f64() => n.as_f64().filter(|f| f.fract() == 0.0).and_then(|f| { let i = f as i64; ... })`. A JSON value like `9.22e18` (or any integer-like float outside i64 range) has zero fractional part, so `f as i64` saturates/truncates and the parser silently accepts an incorrect value instead of rejecting it. Can corrupt parsed payloads, occurrence-key fields, or any integer field used in routing/validation.

2. MEDIUM -- llm.rs:191-196 model-effect composite key is built via unescaped string concatenation: `format!("{}|{}|{}|{}|{}", self.provider, self.model, self.prompt_hash, schema, self.input_hash)`. Two different tuples can collapse to the same material string if provider or model contains `|` (e.g. `("a","b|c",...)` vs `("a|b","c",...)`), producing an identical composite_key -- distinct model-effect requests could share a replay key and incorrectly reuse each other's recorded output (if/when the model-effects subsystem, currently tracked as inert in sinex-330i, is wired up).

Found via narrate-through audit of crate/sinex-primitives/src/{parser/declarative.rs,llm.rs} (2026-08-11, wave128 batch).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Parse a JSON field declared FieldType::Integer with value 9.22e18 (or any integer-valued float outside i64 range) -- observe it's accepted as a saturated/truncated i64 instead of a ParserError.
2. Construct two ModelEffectRecord composite keys where provider or model contains a literal '|' character such that the concatenation collides -- observe identical composite_key strings for distinct logical tuples.
acceptance_criteria: Relate to sinex-330i (model-effects subsystem currently inert) since this collision risk only bites once that subsystem gets wired to a real caller.

title: sinexctl: verify --demo seeds via a subprocess that doesn't inherit runtime context; Json output format is actually line-delimited (breaks true-JSON consumers); malformed config.toml silently downgrades to hardcoded defaults
description:
Three bugs in sinexctl found via narrate-through audit (gpt-5.3-codex-spark, wave128-037):

1. HIGH -- verify/mod.rs:1326+ `verify --demo` invokes `ops demo` in a fresh subprocess via `Command::new(std::env::current_exe()?)` without propagating the active runtime context (SINEX_RUNTIME_TARGET_CONFIG, custom token/URL flags, non-default env overrides). When sinexctl runs with non-default runtime settings, the parent verifies against one target but the subprocess seeds data via ops demo on potentially a different/default target -- producing false negatives and seeding the wrong system.

2. MEDIUM -- fmt/output.rs:25-28 `CommandOutput::list` emits JSON as line-oriented records for OutputFormat::Json (same branch shared with Ndjson): `{"a":1}\n{"a":2}\n...` is not a single valid JSON value, despite a separate format_json_lines API implying Json and Ndjson should be distinct.

3. MEDIUM -- main.rs:188-191 config parse/load failures silently downgrade to Config::default(), dropping env-derived runtime config: `Config::load().unwrap_or_else(|e| { tracing::debug!(...); Config::default() })`. A malformed/unreadable config.toml causes fallback to hardcoded defaults rather than preserving env-based runtime/auth overrides or surfacing a hard error -- operators relying on env credentials/runtime can get silently redirected to defaults.

Found via narrate-through audit of crate/sinexctl/src/{commands/verify/mod.rs,fmt/output.rs,main.rs,config.rs} (2026-08-11, wave128 batch).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run sinexctl verify --demo with a non-default SINEX_RUNTIME_TARGET_CONFIG set -- observe the spawned ops demo subprocess doesn't receive it.
2. Call any command with CommandOutput::list(...).display(OutputFormat::Json) on multiple items -- observe newline-delimited JSON objects, not a single valid JSON value.
3. Point sinexctl at a malformed config.toml -- observe it silently falls back to Config::default() with only a debug-level log line, dropping any env-derived overrides that path would have applied.
acceptance_criteria: verify --demo passes effective runtime/auth/context arguments into the spawned subprocess (or invokes an internal demo routine directly). OutputFormat::Json renders a single valid JSON array/object; Ndjson keeps the line-delimited behavior. Config::load() failures either fail fast with a clear error or explicitly preserve env-derived overrides on top of defaults, with a non-debug-level warning.

title: document_search.rs: parameter-index collision breaks natural_key_prefix searches; vector/hybrid search API is declared but never wired (always falls through to FTS/trigram)
description:
Two real bugs in document_search.rs found via narrate-through audit (gpt-5.3-codex-spark, wave128-001):

1. Parameter index collision breaks searches with natural_key_prefix, in both FTS and trigram paths. document_search.rs:281-311 and :381-408: `if query.natural_key_prefix.is_some() { predicates.push(format!("d.natural_key LIKE (${bind_index} || '%')")); }` -- no bind_index increment after this branch, so limit_bind reuses the same index. A search with natural_key_prefix set compiles SQL where the prefix placeholder and LIMIT placeholder share an index (e.g. $2) while bound values differ types (string vs i64) -- query preparation/execution fails with a parameter type error.

2. Vector/hybrid search API surface is declared but never wired. document_search.rs:67-79 and :169-208: `pub vector_params: Option<VectorSearchParams>` and `SearchMode::{Fts, TrigramFallback, Vector, Hybrid}` are declared, but `search()` always executes only search_fts then search_trigram -- no branch reads query.vector_params, no path returns SearchMode::Vector/Hybrid. A caller passing vector_params expecting vector/hybrid behavior gets silently misrouted to FTS/trigram logic with incorrect result sets.

Found via narrate-through audit of crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/document_search.rs (2026-08-11, wave128 batch).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Call search() with natural_key_prefix set -- observe a SQL parameter-type error from the bind_index collision with the LIMIT placeholder.
2. Call search() with vector_params set and search_mode expecting Vector/Hybrid -- observe it silently falls through to FTS/trigram logic instead.
acceptance_criteria: The natural_key_prefix predicate increments bind_index correctly so LIMIT gets its own placeholder. Either vector/hybrid search is actually implemented and wired to query.vector_params, or the declared API surface (fields, SearchMode variants) is removed/documented as not-yet-implemented so callers don't silently get wrong behavior.

title: embeddings.rs register_model dimension-check race (concurrent registrations can silently mask a mismatch); privacy_policy.rs list_dictionary_terms returns disabled terms despite its enabled-only contract
description:
Two real bugs found via narrate-through audit (gpt-5.3-codex-spark, wave128-002/005):

1. embeddings.rs:44,65 register_model has a dimension-validation race distinct from the UPDATE-SET-clause race already checked clean in an earlier audit pass: the pre-check (`if let Some(existing_dimensions) = ...fetch_optional... && existing_dimensions != dimensions { return Err(...) }`) runs before the `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE` -- two concurrent registrations for the same (provider, model_name) with different dimensions can both pass the pre-check before either inserts, so the second caller gets Ok(id) even though its dimensions weren't actually applied (silently masks a registration contract mismatch until later embedding writes fail validation).

2. privacy_policy.rs:668-670 list_dictionary_terms returns disabled terms despite its API contract implying "enabled terms": `SELECT id, dictionary_id, term, metadata, enabled FROM privacy.dictionary_terms WHERE dictionary_id = $1 ORDER BY term` has no `AND enabled = true`, diverging from the enforcement-time loader (load_dictionary_terms_for_rule, which does filter enabled=true). Management/read surfaces can show terms that are actually disabled, leading to incorrect operator pruning/remediation decisions based on false positives.

Found via narrate-through audit of crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/{embeddings,privacy_policy}.rs (2026-08-11, wave128 batch).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run two concurrent register_model calls for the same (provider, model_name) with different dimensions -- observe the second returns Ok(id) despite its dimensions not being applied.
2. Call list_dictionary_terms on a dictionary with both enabled and disabled terms -- observe disabled terms are included, contradicting load_dictionary_terms_for_rule's enabled=true filter.
acceptance_criteria: register_model's dimension check and insert happen atomically (single query with a CHECK, or an advisory lock spanning both). list_dictionary_terms filters to enabled=true, or is renamed/documented to clarify it intentionally returns all terms with a separate enabled-only variant for management UIs that need to show disabled terms explicitly.

title: api handlers curation.rs+runtime_registry.rs: swallowed finalization error leaves control ops stuck Running, event-insert-before-validation in curation finalize, non-atomic proposal+judgment insert pair, one missing KV key hard-fails whole runtime listing
description:
Four issues in previously-unread handler files flagged by this session's earlier audit-api-handlers-rest pass (source_status.rs/telemetry.rs/tasks.rs/semantic.rs/curation.rs/runtime_registry.rs were explicitly triaged out for time, not for low value):

1. crate/sinexd/src/api/handlers/runtime_registry.rs:120 -- `let _ = finalize_runtime_control_operation(...).await; return Err(error);`: if a NATS publish for a runtime-control operation fails, the already-created "Running" operation record's finalization error is discarded. The caller gets the publish error, but the operation row remains stuck in Running state -- audit/state visibility becomes permanently incorrect since operators can't see the actual terminal failure.

2. crate/sinexd/src/api/handlers/curation.rs:707-722 (handle_curation_finalize) -- the finalized event is inserted via pool.events().insert(event) BEFORE extract_lane_id(&proposal.candidate_payload) is called; if candidate_payload.lane_id is malformed, extract_lane_id errors AFTER the event is already persisted. The request fails but the side effect (event insert) already happened with no operation logging, so a client retry can produce duplicate finalization artifacts.

3. crate/sinexd/src/api/handlers/curation.rs:555-600 -- duplicate-judgment insertion is two sequential non-transactional inserts (proposal_event then judgment_event); if the judgment insert fails after the proposal insert succeeds, the API returns an error but a proposal event remains without its paired judgment, creating dangling state and risking extra proposals on retry instead of a clean atomic pair.

4. crate/sinexd/src/api/handlers/runtime_registry.rs:220-234 (handle_runtime_list) -- a KV key deleted between the initial keys() scan and the subsequent get() turns ONE missing key into a hard failure for the ENTIRE listing request, rather than skipping that key and returning partial results -- avoidable API-level failures under ordinary concurrent runtime-module churn.

Found via a narrate-through audit of crate/sinexd/src/api/handlers/curation.rs and runtime_registry.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Inject a NATS publish failure for a runtime-control operation, then inject a finalize_runtime_control_operation failure on the cleanup path -- observe the operation row is stuck Running with no visible failure record.
2. Send a curation-finalize request with a malformed candidate_payload.lane_id -- observe the event is already inserted before the error is returned.
3. Inject a failure on the second (judgment) insert of a duplicate-judgment pair -- observe an orphaned proposal event with no paired judgment.
4. Delete a runtime-module KV key between handle_runtime_list's scan and fetch -- observe the whole listing request fails instead of returning partial results.
acceptance_criteria: Finalization failures after a publish error are at minimum logged with the operation id so stuck-Running rows are discoverable. curation finalize validates candidate_payload.lane_id before inserting the event, or wraps both steps in a transaction. The duplicate-judgment insert pair is wrapped in a transaction. handle_runtime_list skips a concurrently-deleted key rather than failing the whole request.

title: event_engine: redact_batch (the persistence chokepoint) doesn't refresh the privacy-policy cache like disclosure paths do; from_args()/default() resolve the same config values via two error-handling policies (strict vs lenient) and from_args skips its own validator
description:
Two related findings in sinexd's event_engine privacy-policy and config modules:

1. crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/policy.rs:752-763 -- redact_batch (the central persistence-chokepoint redaction function) does NOT call self.ensure_fresh().await at its start, unlike every disclose_* method (lines 778,804,881) which does. Privacy rules updated in the DB within the system's intended ~30s refresh window are not seen by the persistence chokepoint -- newly ingested events in redact_batch can be persisted under a STALE policy cache until process restart or an external refresh path fires, even though the read-side disclosure paths correctly auto-refresh. This directly compounds the privacy-catalog concerns already tracked this session (sinex-t5sr): even once the catalog is populated, this cache-staleness gap means newly-added rules may not apply to fresh ingestion for up to the refresh window.

2. crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/config.rs:363,370 vs 842 (and the same pattern repeated for default_consumer_fetch_timeout_ms/default_consumer_max_ack_pending/default_material_slices_max_ack_pending) -- the SAME env-var-derived config values are resolved via two different constructor paths with contradictory error handling: EventEngineConfig::from_args does a strict parse (bad value -> hard startup failure via ?), while EventEngineConfig::default()'s helper functions do a lenient parse (bad value -> logged warning, numeric fallback kept). Setting e.g. SINEX_EVENT_ENGINE_CONSUMER_FETCH_MAX_MESSAGES=oops behaves completely differently depending on which construction path a caller uses. Separately, from_args() (config.rs:490) returns its built config WITHOUT invoking the struct's own declared validator chain (visible on fields like pool_size / consumer_* ranges) -- a caller trusting from_args() and proceeding directly to create_db_pool can get an invalid config (e.g. pool_size=0) reaching runtime instead of failing at construction time.

Found via a narrate-through audit of crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/policy.rs and crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/config.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Add a new privacy rule to the DB, then immediately admit an event via redact_batch (not through a disclose_* read path) -- observe the new rule may not apply until the refresh window elapses or a restart happens.
2. Set SINEX_EVENT_ENGINE_CONSUMER_FETCH_MAX_MESSAGES to an unparseable value, construct config via from_args vs via default() -- observe one hard-fails and the other silently falls back.
3. Construct config via from_args() with an out-of-range field (e.g. pool_size=0) -- observe it's never run through the declared validator chain.
acceptance_criteria: Relates to sinex-t5sr (privacy catalog currently empty) -- this cache-staleness gap will matter once the catalog is populated and rules start changing at runtime.

title: material_assembler: one unexpected directory under state_root aborts the WHOLE orphan-cleanup pass; route_material_error_then_finalize_failed always returns Ok even when terminal settlement fails
description:
Two issues in sinexd's material-assembler maintenance/finalize modules, found on a second narrate-through pass (the original event-engine audit this session read finalize.rs only ~35% and maintenance.rs only ~20%):

1. crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/material_assembler/maintenance.rs:595-600 (check_orphaned_folder, called from cleanup_orphaned_temp_files) -- if an unexpected directory exists under the assembler state root (an operator artifact, a corrupted entry, anything not a valid material-id-named folder), the function returns Err, which propagates up and aborts the WHOLE cleanup pass. Every other genuinely orphaned temp folder in that run is skipped until the one bad entry is manually removed -- a single unrelated file/directory under state_root can silently stall orphan cleanup indefinitely.

2. crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/material_assembler/finalize.rs:258 (route_material_error_then_finalize_failed) -- calls route_material_error via ?, then unconditionally calls finalize_failed_material and returns Ok(()) regardless of that call's actual outcome. finalize_failed_material itself ALSO only warn!()-logs its own settlement failures rather than returning them. Concrete scenario: DLQ publish succeeds, but the subsequent DB write (mark_as_failed) fails transiently -- the caller of route_material_error_then_finalize_failed receives Ok(()) even though terminal settlement never actually completed, so a recovery loop relying on propagated errors to drive retries won't trigger, and the material can be left in limbo depending on caller semantics.

Found via a second narrate-through audit pass of crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/material_assembler/maintenance.rs and finalize.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Place an unexpected (non-material-id-named) directory under the assembler state root, then trigger cleanup_orphaned_temp_files -- observe the whole pass aborts on the first bad entry, skipping all other genuinely orphaned folders.
2. Inject a DB write failure into finalize_failed_material after a successful DLQ publish -- observe route_material_error_then_finalize_failed still returns Ok(()).
acceptance_criteria: check_orphaned_folder's per-entry failure is logged and skipped (continue to the next entry) rather than aborting the whole cleanup pass. route_material_error_then_finalize_failed propagates finalize_failed_material's real settlement outcome instead of unconditionally returning Ok(()).

title: acquisition_manager: BufferedAppendStreamWriter reports success when its background worker is already dead; AppendStreamAcquirer::finalize drops the handle before attempting finalize, losing retry-ability on failure
description:
Two issues in sinexd's material acquisition/append-stream writer (crate/sinexd/src/runtime/acquisition_manager.rs), found on a second narrate-through pass (flagged by the durability-checkpoint audit's finding 8 as needing outside-region verification of AcquisitionManager::cancel semantics):

1. Lines 1613,1638,1665 (BufferedAppendStreamWriter::prime/finalize/flush) -- `if send_result.is_err() { return Ok(()); }`: if the background writer task has already ended (sender dropped), these operations return Ok(()) instead of an error, so callers assume begin/finalize/flush succeeded when it did not. Concrete impact: orphaned open materials, missing BEGIN frames, missing END frames on shutdown/error paths despite the API call reporting success.

2. Lines 1319-1320 (AppendStreamAcquirer::finalize) -- `if let Some(handle) = self.current_handle.take() { self.manager.finalize(handle, reason).await?; }`: the active handle is taken (removed from self) BEFORE the finalize call; if manager.finalize fails partway through (after partial remote publication succeeded), current_handle has already been dropped and the caller cannot retry against the same material identity -- a transient publish failure forces a hard cutover to a new material id, making recovery of that specific in-flight material impossible from this stream path.

Found via a second narrate-through audit pass of crate/sinexd/src/runtime/acquisition_manager.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Kill/end the background writer task, then call prime/finalize/flush on the same BufferedAppendStreamWriter -- observe Ok(()) is returned despite the operation never actually happening.
2. Inject a failure in manager.finalize() after current_handle.take() has already removed the handle -- observe the caller cannot retry against the same material identity.
acceptance_criteria: prime/finalize/flush surface a distinguishable error when the background worker channel is closed, rather than silently reporting Ok(()). AppendStreamAcquirer::finalize retains the handle (or a way to reconstruct equivalent state) until finalize genuinely succeeds, so a transient failure doesn't force an unrecoverable cutover to a new material id.
close_reason: Closure Evidence Manifest: SATISFIED. Buffered writer prime/flush/finalize now surface closed-worker errors, and AppendStreamAcquirer retains the same material identity across transient finalize failure until retry succeeds. Verified: nix develop --command xtask test -p sinexd -E "test(append_stream_retains_handle_until_finalize_succeeds)"; nix develop --command xtask test -p sinexd -E "test(buffered_append_writer_reports_closed_worker_channel)". No deferred AC.

title: event_engine::service.rs: readiness can be signaled right before a JetStream consumer task immediately fails on bad config; schema-broadcast failure at boot is downgraded to a warning
description:
Two issues in sinexd's core event-engine service bootstrap/lifecycle (crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/service.rs), found on a second narrate-through pass (the original event-engine audit this session read this file only ~65% -- startup/monitor/task-spawn, not the sections below):

2. Make NATS unavailable at boot -- observe service init still succeeds with schema broadcast silently skipped.

title: sinex-schema apply.rs has a diff/apply blind spot for telemetry view/aggregate body-only changes and can't self-heal a telemetry relation accidentally created as a table; strict_diff.rs hard-fails on overloaded functions or duplicate view names
description:
Two findings in sinex-schema's declarative convergence/drift-detection engine:

apply.rs (crate/sinex-schema/src/apply.rs):
1. Lines 109-124,315-365,1311-1317,1722-1747 -- telemetry view/continuous-aggregate drift detection only checks relkind (relation exists and is the right kind), with NO definition-hash check for TELEMETRY_VIEW_RELATIONS or TELEMETRY_CONTINUOUS_AGGREGATES_SQL objects (hash reconciliation is only wired for current_health via ensure_view_sql). A body-only change to a telemetry view's SQL (fixing metric logic, without changing relkind) leaves drift empty, so apply skips recreation and the OLD definition stays live indefinitely -- silently serving stale telemetry output after a fix is deployed.
2. Lines 351-365,1429-1433,1311-1317 -- recreate_telemetry_read_models's drop loop only handles relkind='m' (materialized view) or 'v' (view); if a telemetry relation was ever accidentally created as a table (relkind='r'), drift is detected but the recreate step silently does nothing for it, so the subsequent CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW/CREATE VIEW collides with the existing table object and apply hard-fails requiring manual intervention instead of self-healing.

strict_diff.rs (crate/sinex-schema/src/strict_diff.rs):
3. Line 517,608 -- function/view existence checks use fetch_optional against a schema+name predicate that assumes uniqueness; if a function is legitimately overloaded (same name, different signature) or a view name collides unexpectedly, fetch_optional errors on multiple rows and the ENTIRE strict-diff check hard-fails with a SQL row-multiplicity error rather than reporting a clean/handled drift result.

Found via a narrate-through audit of crate/sinex-schema/src/apply.rs and crate/sinex-schema/src/strict_diff.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Change the SQL body of a telemetry continuous-aggregate definition without changing its name/relkind, then run schema apply -- observe drift stays empty and the old definition remains live.
2. Manually create a table where a telemetry view is expected, then run apply -- observe it hard-fails with a naming collision rather than dropping and recreating.
3. Add an overloaded function under a schema strict_diff checks, then run strict_diff -- observe the whole check errors on SQL row-multiplicity.
acceptance_criteria: Telemetry view/aggregate definitions get the same hash-based drift detection current_health already has. recreate_telemetry_read_models handles unexpected relkinds by dropping them regardless of kind before recreating. strict_diff's function/view existence checks use fetch_all or an explicit ambiguity check instead of fetch_optional.

title: sinex-primitives file-watching security validator has four real enforcement gaps: 1000-entry-capped file-count estimator, symlink policy fails open on metadata errors, directory paths pass as file paths, max_depth=0 skips counting root contents
description:
Four issues in sinex-primitives' file-watching security validator (crate/sinex-primitives/src/validation/file_watching_security.rs), which is meant to enforce real security boundaries (max watched files, symlink policy, path depth) for filesystem source configuration:

1. Line 197 -- `for entry in entries.take(1000)`: file-count estimation for a watch-path is capped at the first 1000 directory entries per directory; validate_watch_paths can approve a watch root whose real file count vastly exceeds max_watched_files because the estimator never sums beyond 1000, defeating the policy's own resource-exhaustion guard.
2. Lines 129-133,244-248 -- symlink-policy enforcement checks `if not follow_symlinks and let Ok(metadata) = symlink_metadata(path) and metadata.is_symlink() then reject`: if symlink_metadata itself fails (permissions, transient FS error), the let-Ok pattern silently treats it as "not a symlink" and validation succeeds -- under a restrictive follow_symlinks=false policy, a path that should be rejected can pass purely because the metadata lookup errored.
3. config_validation.rs:97-112 -- validate_file_path only rejects empty paths, invalid normalization, or an explicit trailing slash/backslash as a directory indicator; a bare directory path with no trailing separator (e.g. /tmp) passes as if it were a valid file path, violating the function's stated intent to validate FILE (not directory) paths.
4. file_watching_security.rs:185-188 -- with max_depth=Some(0), the estimator returns 0 for the root directory's own contents rather than counting them, making max_watched_files checks ineffective for zero-depth ("no descent") watch configurations that should still count root-level files.

Found via a narrate-through audit of crate/sinex-primitives/src/validation/config_validation.rs, file_watching_security.rs, query_validation.rs, validation_chains.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Point a watch root at a directory with >1000 files and max_watched_files set below the real count -- observe the estimator's 1000-entry cap lets it pass.
2. Inject a symlink_metadata failure on a symlinked path under follow_symlinks=false -- observe validation succeeds instead of rejecting.
3. Pass /tmp (a directory, no trailing slash) to validate_file_path -- observe it's accepted as a valid file path.
4. Set max_depth=Some(0) on a non-empty watch root -- observe the file-count estimate is 0 rather than counting root-level files.
acceptance_criteria: File-count estimation sums the true count or fails safe when capped. symlink_metadata failures fail closed under a restrictive symlink policy, not open. validate_file_path rejects paths that are actually directories via a stat check. max_depth=0 still counts root-level entries.

title: sinex-db validation.rs: payload-size guard silently treats serialization failure as zero bytes; schema_apply.rs skips explicit pool.close() on apply error
description:
Two issues in sinex-db's validation/schema-apply helpers:
1. crate/sinex-db/src/validation.rs:583 -- `serde_json::to_vec(payload).map(|v| v.len()).unwrap_or_default()` collapses a payload-serialization FAILURE to a byte length of 0, which makes the payload-size guard think the payload is tiny -- a payload that cannot be serialized bypasses the size check entirely rather than being rejected/flagged.
2. crate/sinex-db/src/schema_apply.rs:68 -- `apply_schema(&pool).await?; pool.close().await;`: pool.close() is only reached on the success path; an early return on apply_schema's error leaves the temporary pool's explicit close skipped (cleanup then relies solely on Drop-path timing rather than the deterministic close this admin CLI path presumably wants for short-lived invocations).

Found via a narrate-through audit of crate/sinex-db/src/query_helpers.rs, schema_apply.rs, validation.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Construct a payload that fails serde_json::to_vec -- observe the size guard treats it as 0 bytes and passes.
2. Inject an apply_schema failure in apply_schema_for_url -- observe pool.close() is skipped on that path.
acceptance_criteria: Serialization failures in the size guard are treated as a hard rejection (or at minimum a large/unknown size), not silently as 0. pool.close() runs on both success and error paths (e.g. via a guard or explicit match on both branches).

title: sinexctl admin snapshot/restore: row-count query failure makes restore verification vacuously pass, NATS component hash asymmetry between capture and restore, live-mode top-level file copy isn't vanish-tolerant, quiesce gate silently no-ops on systemctl failure
description:
Four issues in sinexctl's admin snapshot/exec (backup/restore) tooling -- these directly affect the integrity of sinex's own disaster-recovery snapshot/restore path:

1. crate/sinexctl/src/admin/snapshot.rs:579 -- `exec::pg_row_counts(database_url).unwrap_or_default()` silently converts any pg_row_counts failure (permissions, transient DB error) into an empty {} row-count map. Snapshot capture "succeeds" but restore verification then has no authoritative expected_postgres_row_counts, so postgres_row_counts_match can become VACUOUSLY TRUE (nothing to compare against) and real integrity drift during restore goes undetected.
2. snapshot.rs:599-622,438-441,1322-1329 -- capture computes the NATS component's blake3 hash from component_root AFTER try_nats_stream_summary writes nats/streams.summary.json into that same root, so the manifest hash includes that file -- but restore observation explicitly EXCLUDES streams.summary.json when computing its own hash. This asymmetry means expected_component_blake3_matches can report a NATS mismatch even when the restored content is byte-identical to what was actually captured.
3. snapshot.rs:676-701 -- in `--mode live`, top-level state files use plain `std::fs::copy` (not tolerant of NotFound), while directories use the live-tolerant `cp_tree_live`; if a top-level file is removed between read_dir and copy (a normal occurrence under live-mode's own stated "tolerates vanished files" intent), the snapshot fails unexpectedly instead of skipping the vanished file as live mode is supposed to.
4. admin/exec.rs:386-405, snapshot.rs:331-346 -- `active_sinex_services()` returns an empty Vec on ANY systemctl spawn failure or non-zero exit; snapshot's quiesce-mode gate relies on a non-empty vector to know it must block/stop services. A transient systemctl failure makes quiesce mode silently proceed AS IF no services were active, potentially capturing a snapshot while live services are still running and mutating state underneath it.

Found via a narrate-through audit of crate/sinexctl/src/admin/{exec,manifest,mod,snapshot,staging}.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Inject a pg_row_counts failure during snapshot capture -- observe the restore drill's row-count check has nothing to compare against and can pass vacuously.
2. Capture a snapshot with a NATS stream summary present, then restore -- observe expected_component_blake3_matches can report a false mismatch due to the summary-file inclusion asymmetry.
3. Remove a top-level state file mid-snapshot in --mode live -- observe the snapshot fails instead of tolerating the vanished file per live mode's stated intent.
4. Inject a systemctl failure during quiesce-mode's active-services check -- observe snapshot proceeds as if no services were running.
acceptance_criteria: pg_row_counts failures propagate as a snapshot-capture warning/failure rather than silently becoming an empty comparison baseline. The blake3 hash computation is symmetric between capture and restore for the NATS component (both include or both exclude streams.summary.json). Live-mode top-level file copy tolerates NotFound the same way directory copy does. active_sinex_services() distinguishes 'genuinely no services' from 'could not determine' and quiesce mode fails closed (blocks) on the latter rather than proceeding as if clear.
close_reason:
Implemented and verified on master/current branch; no deferred scope.

title: sinexctl auth: token-file reads don't trim trailing newline, empty explicit --token silently wins over configured fallbacks, MCP server silently defaults on config-load failure
description:
Three issues in sinexctl's auth/token handling and MCP-server entrypoint:
1. crate/sinexctl/src/auth/token.rs:36-37 -- `fs::read_to_string(path).map(|s| apply_runtime_role(&s, token_role))` does NOT trim the file contents; token files commonly end with a trailing newline, which then becomes part of the bearer token sent to the gateway, causing a generic auth rejection rather than a clear "malformed token file" error.
2. token.rs:21-23 -- an explicit `--token` value, even if empty/whitespace, is accepted and returned immediately (`if let Some(token) = explicit_token { return Ok(...) }`), skipping env/file fallback sources -- an empty explicit token silently wins over a genuinely-configured fallback token.
3. crate/sinexctl/src/bin/sinex-mcp-server.rs:57 -- `Config::load().unwrap_or_default()` silently collapses any config-load failure (corrupted file, permission error, unsupported schema) into default settings, with no signal to the operator that their configuration was ignored.

Found via a narrate-through audit of crate/sinexctl/src/auth/{mod,tls,token}.rs and crate/sinexctl/src/bin/sinex-mcp-server.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Create a token file with a trailing newline (the common case) -- observe auth fails with a generic error rather than a clear malformed-token message.
2. Pass --token "" (empty) -- observe it's accepted and used instead of falling back to env/file sources.
3. Point sinex-mcp-server at a corrupted config file -- observe it silently starts with defaults instead of erroring.
acceptance_criteria: Token-file contents are trimmed before use. An empty/whitespace explicit token is treated as absent (falls through to env/file sources) rather than winning outright. sinex-mcp-server surfaces config-load failures (at minimum a startup warning) rather than silently defaulting.

title: xtask tls verify.rs: key/cert mismatch, partial NATS client creds, and non-CA-cert-as-CA are all downgraded to warnings instead of invalidating the result
description:
Three issues in xtask's TLS verification helper (xtask/src/tls/verify.rs), a distinct file from the doctor.rs TlsCheck already filed as sinex-xryb -- this is the underlying check_tls_config/check_nats_tls implementation:
1. A key/cert-match verification failure (`Err(e) => { result.warnings.push(...) }`) is recorded only as a warning, never flips `result.valid` to false -- a caller can get valid:true from check_tls_config even though the key/cert pair genuinely doesn't match (encrypted key, unsupported format, or true mismatch), and proceed to a runtime TLS failure.
2. `check_nats_tls`'s client-cert/client-key guard only checks BOTH env vars together (`if let (Ok(cert), Ok(key)) = (...)`); if only one of SINEX_NATS_CLIENT_CERT/SINEX_NATS_CLIENT_KEY is set (or one is misspelled), no warning or error is emitted for the partial/mismatched configuration.
3. A non-CA certificate supplied where a CA cert is expected (`if !info.is_ca { warnings.push(...) }`) is also only a warning, not a hard invalidation -- an operator supplying a leaf cert for SINEX_API_TLS_CLIENT_CA can still see valid:true.

Found via a narrate-through audit of xtask/src/tls/{generate,mod,verify}.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Supply a genuinely mismatched cert/key pair -- observe check_tls_config still reports valid:true.
2. Set only SINEX_NATS_CLIENT_CERT (not the key) -- observe check_nats_tls emits nothing.
3. Supply a leaf certificate as SINEX_API_TLS_CLIENT_CA -- observe valid:true despite is_ca being false.
acceptance_criteria: See Acceptance above.

title: xtask doctor --fix silently drops previously-collected report sections on overwrite; /proc scan errors silently discarded undercounting rust-analyzer processes; --reclaim and footprint-reporting use two independently-computed target dirs
description:
Second narrate-through pass over xtask/src/commands/doctor.rs (the earlier audit-xtask-gates review this session deprioritized the rust-analyzer diagnostic-parser section, ~lines 972-1285, for time). New findings beyond what that review already filed (sinex-xryb TLS vacuity, sinex-aunm Postgres-extensions vacuity):

1. Lines 384-409,391-398,400-429,435-468 -- in --fix mode, after remediation, `if let Ok(fresh) = execute_doctor(...) { result.data = fresh.data; result.status = fresh.status; }` OVERWRITES the result with a freshly-generated base report; sections collected earlier in the same invocation (e.g. runtime diagnostics gathered before remediation) are dropped from the final machine-readable output even though they were explicitly requested, because the fresh report doesn't include them.
2. Lines 853-871 -- `for entry in entries.flatten()` while scanning /proc for rust-analyzer processes silently discards per-entry read errors; on a system with restricted /proc visibility, unreadable PID entries are dropped, undercounting `processes.len()` and potentially suppressing the "multiple rust-analyzer processes" warning path.
3. Lines 540-543 vs 654-657 -- the target directory used for `--reclaim` disk-space cleanup and the one used for rust-analyzer footprint reporting are computed via two independently-written expressions (`workspace_root().join("target")` vs `workspace_target_dir_for(&root)`); if a custom CARGO_TARGET_DIR layout makes these diverge, --reclaim and the footprint report silently operate on different trees.

Found via a second, narrate-through audit pass of xtask/src/commands/doctor.rs (2026-08-11, gpt-5.3-codex-spark).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run xtask doctor --fix --runtime where the runtime check fails and triggers remediation -- observe the final machine-readable result.data lacks the runtime section that was collected earlier in the same invocation.
2. Simulate restricted /proc visibility (e.g. via a container with limited /proc access) -- observe rust-analyzer process count is undercounted and the multi-process warning may not fire.
3. Configure a custom CARGO_TARGET_DIR layout so workspace_root().join("target") diverges from workspace_target_dir_for(&root) -- observe --reclaim and the footprint report operate on different directories.
acceptance_criteria: Fix-mode merges the fresh post-remediation report into the existing result rather than wholesale-overwriting it. /proc entry read errors are logged (not silently dropped) so undercounting is visible. Both target-directory computations are unified into one shared helper.

title: xtask lint_forbidden's DerivedOutput literal-bypass detector has both a false-positive (typed constructors) and false-negative (multiline literals); analytics.rs truncate_str can panic on non-ASCII
description:
Two issues in xtask's forbidden-pattern lint and analytics commands:
1. xtask/src/commands/lint_forbidden.rs:1001-1010 -- check_derived_output_literal_violations_for_file's `DerivedOutput` struct-literal-bypass detector has both a false-positive and a false-negative: (a) it treats `rest.starts_with("::<")` as a raw-literal violation, which flags valid typed constructor calls like `DerivedOutput::<T>::transduced(...)` even though they're not struct-literal bypasses; (b) detection is line-local (only checks if `{` appears on the SAME line as `DerivedOutput`), so a multiline struct literal like `DerivedOutput::<T>\n    { ... }` is never detected, letting the actual bypass this lint exists to catch slip through undetected.
2. xtask/src/commands/analytics.rs:1630 -- `format!("{}...", &s[..max.saturating_sub(1)])` in truncate_str slices by byte index without checking UTF-8 char boundaries, panicking `xtask analytics hotspots` on non-ASCII diagnostic message text -- same UTF-8-boundary bug class as sinex-e6sc/sinex-e6ti.

Found via a narrate-through audit of xtask/src/commands/{lint_forbidden,analytics}.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Write DerivedOutput::<T>::transduced(...) somewhere and run the lint -- observe a false-positive violation.
2. Write a multiline DerivedOutput::<T> { ... } struct literal and run the lint -- observe it's NOT detected (false-negative on the exact bypass the lint exists to catch).
3. Run xtask analytics hotspots against a diagnostic message containing non-ASCII text long enough to trigger truncation -- observe a panic.
acceptance_criteria: The literal-bypass detector no longer flags ::< typed-constructor syntax as a violation, and detects multiline struct literals (not just same-line). analytics.rs's truncate_str clamps to a UTF-8 char boundary.

title: xtask privacy CLI: --generate produces a predictable (not cryptographically random) key, decrypt failures reported as CommandResult::success, unknown --category silently matches everything
description:
Four issues in xtask's privacy command (xtask/src/commands/privacy.rs), all in the encryption-key/decrypt/filter workflow:

1. `--generate` key material: `seed = format!("{}-{}", std::process::id(), SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).unwrap_or_default().as_nanos()); let hash = blake3::hash(seed.as_bytes());` -- the generated key is a hash of PREDICTABLE data (process id + timestamp), not cryptographically random bytes. An attacker with a small pid/time search space can recover or predict generated keys far more easily than a real key-generation routine should allow.
2. Lines 280-297 -- a decrypt failure is wrapped as `CommandResult::success().with_message("Decryption failed").with_data(json!({"error": ...}))` -- the CLI reports SUCCESS even though decryption failed, which can cause automation checking only the top-level success flag to treat a failed decrypt as passed and continue with bad/absent data.
3. Lines 108-114,123 -- an unrecognized `--category` value silently becomes "no filter" (matches everything) rather than erroring, so a typo like `--category=secrt` returns all rules instead of alerting the operator to the typo.
4. Lines 309-310 -- the same SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).unwrap_or_default() pattern as #1: a clock error silently zeroes part of the key-generation seed, silently degrading key entropy/uniqueness under an edge-case clock condition.

Found via a narrate-through audit of xtask/src/commands/{privacy,schema}.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run xtask privacy ... --generate twice in quick succession -- observe the seed is derived from pid+timestamp, not a CSPRNG.
2. Run a decrypt operation with a bad key/corrupted ciphertext -- observe the CLI's top-level success field is still true.
3. Run with --category=secrt (typo) -- observe it silently returns all rules instead of erroring on the unrecognized category.
acceptance_criteria: --generate uses a real CSPRNG (e.g. rand::rngs::OsRng or getrandom) for key material, not a hash of predictable pid/timestamp data. Decrypt failures set CommandResult to a failure state, not success. Unrecognized --category values produce an explicit error listing valid categories rather than silently matching all rules.

title: xtask jobs list/active can panic on non-ASCII command names -- same UTF-8-boundary truncation bug already fixed elsewhere this session (sinex-e6sc)
description:
crate xtask/src/commands/jobs.rs:697 -- `format!("{}...", &s[..max_len - 3])` in the command-name truncation helper (`truncate_str`) slices by byte index computed from a char-count-oriented max_len, without checking UTF-8 char boundaries.

Concrete failure: a job/command name containing non-ASCII text (e.g. a Unicode window title or path fragment surfaced through a job's display name) can have its byte-13 cutoff land mid-codepoint, panicking `xtask jobs list` / `xtask jobs active`. This is the same UTF-8-boundary bug class already found and fixed in sinexctl's sibling shortcuts.rs this session (sinex-e6sc) -- xtask's own jobs.rs never got the equivalent treatment.

Found via a narrate-through audit of xtask/src/commands/{jobs,impact,reap}.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Start a background job whose command/display name contains multi-byte UTF-8 characters (e.g. Unicode text) long enough to trigger truncation.
2. Run xtask jobs list or xtask jobs active -- observe a panic from a mid-codepoint byte slice.
acceptance_criteria: truncate_str in jobs.rs clamps to the nearest valid char boundary (matching the fix pattern used for sinex-e6sc / truncate_str_boundary_safe elsewhere in this codebase) rather than slicing by raw byte index.

title: xtask sandbox test-context helpers: fail_on_delivery ignores its count arg, baseline_events never updated, orphaned material on publish failure, background handles dropped immediately, drop-path quiesce swallows timeout
description:
Five issues in xtask's sandbox test-context/event helpers (xtask/src/sandbox/{hooks,context,events}.rs):
1. hooks.rs:172-178 -- `TestHooksBuilder::fail_on_delivery(n)` ignores its `n` argument entirely and behaves identically to fail_once -- tests relying on "fail on the Nth delivery" get "fail on first delivery" instead.
2. context.rs:440-443,1083-1085 -- `baseline_events` is hardcoded to 0 in with_name and never updated; event_delta() subtracts this from the live count, so a per-test DB that starts with any seeded/fixture rows overcounts events relative to what the test actually produced.
3. events.rs:170-191 -- publish_event_internal creates the source material row before publishing; if the subsequent publish/persistence-lookup fails, the material row is never added to created_events, so Drop-triggered cleanup never removes it, accumulating orphaned test data.
4. context.rs:1198-1206 -- register_background_handle spawns a task that holds the handle for exactly one yield_now() tick then drops it -- a long-lived process/thread handle registered this way is dropped almost immediately, so quiesce() doesn't actually track its lifetime.
5. context.rs:1586-1590 -- Drop-path background quiesce does `let _ = tokio::time::timeout(...).await;`, discarding timeout/error outcome, so cleanup proceeds even if background work is still active, creating a race window between tests.

Found via a narrate-through audit of xtask/src/sandbox/{context,events,evidence,hooks}.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Call fail_on_delivery(3) then deliver once -- observe it already fails (should require 3 deliveries).
2. Seed a test DB with fixture rows before calling with_name -- observe event_delta() overcounts.
3. Force publish_event_internal's post-publish lookup to fail -- observe the material row survives Drop cleanup.
4. Call register_background_handle with a long-lived handle -- observe it's dropped after one tick.
5. Force the background quiesce timeout to fire during Drop -- observe cleanup proceeds silently.
acceptance_criteria: fail_on_delivery actually counts to n before failing. baseline_events reflects the real starting count. Orphaned materials from failed publishes are cleaned up (added to created_events before the fallible step, or tracked separately). register_background_handle genuinely holds the handle until quiesce/drop. Drop-path quiesce surfaces (at minimum logs) a timeout rather than silently proceeding.

title: xtask sandbox snapshot/tether/stack: serialization-failure swallowed to null, TLS config parsed but never applied, panic on zero-count seed, unacked message on channel close
description:
Four issues in xtask's snapshot/tether/stack sandbox test helpers:
1. xtask/src/sandbox/snapshot_helper.rs:52 -- `serde_json::to_value(value).unwrap_or(JsonValue::Null)`: any non-serializable evidence payload silently collapses to null and persists as missing diagnostic data, obscuring the exact failure mode during postmortem analysis.
2. xtask/src/sandbox/tether.rs:71-77 -- TLS config fields (nats_ca/nats_cert/nats_key) are parsed from env but never actually applied to the NATS connection (comment: "In a real implementation, we would set up TLS here..."); only nats_creds is conditionally used. Operators setting SINEX_TETHER_NATS_CA/CERT/KEY expect secure/mTLS behavior that silently doesn't happen.
3. xtask/src/sandbox/stack.rs:376 -- `wait_for_event_persisted(..., *event_ids.last().unwrap())` panics via unwrap() when seed_material_with_events is called with count=0, even though count: usize including 0 is a valid-looking call.
4. xtask/src/sandbox/tether.rs:480-487 -- if the consumer channel closes, the message-forwarding loop exits via `break` without acking the current message, leaving it unacked and subject to redelivery/replay on restart.

Found via a narrate-through audit of xtask/src/sandbox/{snapshot,snapshot_helper,stack,tether,timing}.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Pass a non-serializable evidence payload -- observe it silently becomes null.
2. Set SINEX_TETHER_NATS_CA/CERT/KEY and observe the connection does not actually use TLS/mTLS.
3. Call seed_material_with_events(..., 0) -- observe a panic.
4. Close the tether consumer channel while a message is in flight -- observe it's left unacked.
acceptance_criteria: Serialization failures surface an error rather than silently becoming null. TLS config fields are actually applied to the NATS connection, or the fields/env vars are removed if genuinely unimplemented. seed_material_with_events(0) returns Ok/an explicit error rather than panicking. The forwarding loop acks the in-flight message (or explicitly documents why not) before breaking on channel close.

title: xtask sandbox postgres helper builds ALTER ROLE SQL via raw string interpolation of operation_id (SQL-injection-class bug in test tooling)
description:
xtask/src/sandbox/postgres.rs:143-145 -- `format!("ALTER ROLE {} SET sinex.operation_id = '{}';", config.app_user, config.operation_id)` interpolates `operation_id` directly into a SQL string literal with no escaping or parameterization. `app_user` is presumably validated as an identifier elsewhere but `operation_id`'s literal value is not.

Concrete failure: an operation_id containing a single quote or SQL metacharacters breaks the statement or, in the worst case, injects additional SQL. This is xtask's own dev/test-sandbox tooling (not a production attacker-facing surface), but operation_id may originate from less-trusted contexts (CI-generated identifiers, environment variables) where this is still a real correctness/injection-class bug worth fixing via parameterized SQL (`SET LOCAL`/`set_config()` doesn't support role-scoped ALTER ROLE SET via bind params directly, but the identifier can at minimum be validated/escaped).

Found via a narrate-through audit of xtask/src/sandbox/{orchestrator,postgres,slog}.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Construct a sandbox config with operation_id containing a single quote or SQL metacharacter.
2. Observe the generated ALTER ROLE statement is malformed or allows injected SQL.
acceptance_criteria: operation_id is validated/escaped before interpolation (or the statement is restructured to use a parameterized form, e.g. via set_config() with bind parameters where PostgreSQL permits it for session-local GUCs).

title: xtask sandbox fs guards: path traversal from unsanitized test_name, partial trigger-disable leak, swallowed restore failures, non-UTF8 env silently dropped
description:
Four issues in xtask's sandbox filesystem-guard helpers (test infrastructure), found via narrate-through audit:

1. Path traversal from unsanitized test_name: xtask/src/sandbox/fs/path_validation.rs:61-63 (`format!("sinex-test-{}-{}", test_name, uuid)` then `.join(...)`) and xtask/src/sandbox/fs/resources.rs:132-136 (`format!("{test_name}.txt")` then `.join(...)`) both build paths from caller-supplied `test_name` without sanitizing `/` or `..` sequences -- a test_name containing path syntax can escape the intended sandbox tree.
2. Partial trigger-disable leak: xtask/src/sandbox/fs/guards.rs:260-279 -- if disabling triggers on table B fails after table A succeeded, the function returns Err without restoring A, leaving triggers disabled on already-processed tables.
3. Restore failures silently swallowed: xtask/src/sandbox/fs/guards.rs:191-203, 230-238, 290-303 -- restore methods log a warning and return Ok(()) even when the restore SQL fails, so callers get a successful Result while session state (RLS/replication-role/triggers) is still altered.
4. Non-UTF-8 env values treated as absent: xtask/src/sandbox/fs/guards.rs:92,113 -- `std::env::var(key).ok()` treats a non-UTF8 env value as missing, so restoration on Drop removes the variable instead of restoring its original (non-UTF8) bytes.

Found via a narrate-through audit of xtask/src/sandbox/fs/{mod,guards,path_validation,resources}.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Call the test-file helpers with a test_name containing '/' or '..' -- observe the resulting path escapes the intended temp/sandbox root.
2. Trigger a multi-table disable-triggers call where a later table fails -- observe earlier tables are left with triggers disabled and no rollback.
3. Trigger a restore-guard failure (bad SQL, closed connection) -- observe the guard returns Ok(()) instead of surfacing the failure.
acceptance_criteria: test_name is sanitized (reject or escape path-syntax characters) before path construction. Partial multi-table failures roll back or retry already-processed tables. Restore failures propagate as errors rather than being logged-and-ignored. Non-UTF8 env var values are preserved (e.g. via OsString) rather than silently treated as absent.

title: xtask sandbox DB template-clone advisory lock can leak if the second lock acquisition fails after the first succeeds
description:
xtask's ephemeral-Postgres test-sandbox template-cloning path can leak a shared advisory lock if the second (exclusive) lock acquisition fails after the first (shared) one succeeds.

crate/xtask/src/sandbox/db/pool/provisioning.rs:425-437:
```rust
let template_lock_id = advisory_lock_key(template_name);
sqlx::query("SELECT pg_advisory_lock_shared($1)")
    .bind(template_lock_id)
    .execute(conn.as_mut())
    .await?;

let clone_lock_id = advisory_lock_key(&format!("{template_name}::clone"));
sqlx::query("SELECT pg_advisory_lock($1)")
    .bind(clone_lock_id)
    .execute(conn.as_mut())
    .await?;
```
Unlocks happen unconditionally later (:463-471):
```rust
let _ = sqlx::query("SELECT pg_advisory_unlock($1)").bind(clone_lock_id)...;
let _ = sqlx::query("SELECT pg_advisory_unlock_shared($1)").bind(template_lock_id)...;
```
If pg_advisory_lock_shared succeeds but the subsequent pg_advisory_lock errors (e.g. cancellation, connection fault), the `?` on the second call returns early -- before the unlock section runs. The shared advisory lock on the template can remain held on that DB session; if the connection returns to the pool, later template-clone calls can be blocked, manifesting as provisioning latency buildup or apparent deadlock in CI.

Found via a targeted audit of crate/xtask/src/sandbox/db/pool/provisioning.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11), verified against the quoted code.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Inject a failure (connection fault, statement timeout, cancellation) between the pg_advisory_lock_shared call and the pg_advisory_lock call in the template-clone path.
2. Observe the function returns early via ? without releasing the already-acquired shared lock.
3. Observe the connection, once returned to the pool, still holds that shared advisory lock, and a subsequent clone attempt against the same template can block on it.
acceptance_criteria: The lock-acquisition sequence uses a guard/RAII pattern (or an explicit try/unlock-on-error path) so any failure after the first lock is acquired always releases it before propagating the error. A test simulating a mid-sequence failure confirms no lock is held afterward.

title: xtask sandbox DB reset reports success even when the session-GUC read fails, risking cross-test-run pollution via stale session_replication_role/row_security
description:
xtask's test-sandbox database reset path swallows a failed session-state read and still reports the slot as successfully cleaned, risking cross-test-run pollution.

crate/xtask/src/sandbox/db/pool/reset.rs:426-437, 474:
```rust
let row = sqlx::query_as::<_, (String, String, String)>(...)
    .fetch_one(&mut *conn)
    .await;

if let Ok((role, row_sec, sync_commit)) = row {
    // reset logic...
}

Ok(())
```
If fetch_one fails (e.g. transient connection issue), the reset-decision block is simply skipped -- the function still returns Ok(()). clean_database then continues and seeds fixtures, handing back a slot reported as "clean" even though session-level GUCs like session_replication_role or row_security may still carry state from the PREVIOUS test run.

Failure scenario: a test that depends on session_replication_role or row_security being at their default value silently inherits a dirty value from whatever ran in that slot before, causing flaky/order-dependent test failures that look unrelated to the sandbox pool itself.

Found via a targeted audit of crate/xtask/src/sandbox/db/pool/reset.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11), verified against the quoted code.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Inject a failure into the session-GUC fetch_one query during a sandbox DB reset (e.g. connection drop mid-query).
2. Observe the reset-decision block is skipped but the function still returns Ok(()).
3. Observe the caller (clean_database) proceeds to seed fixtures and hands back the slot as clean, without any signal that the GUC check was skipped.
acceptance_criteria: A failed session-GUC read during reset either propagates as an error (forcing the caller to discard/reprovision that slot rather than reuse it), or is at minimum logged loudly so a pattern of test flakiness can be traced back to it. A test simulating the fetch_one failure confirms the slot is no longer silently reported clean.

title: privacy catalog's built-in rule seeding silently drops rules with unsupported matcher shapes instead of erroring or logging
description:
Built-in privacy-rule seeding in crate/sinex-primitives/src/privacy/catalog.rs silently drops any rule whose matcher shape or structural-detector serialization isn't supported by policy_seed_rule, rather than surfacing an error.

catalog.rs:27-31:
```rust
rules.extend(secret_rules());
rules.extend(pii_rules());
rules.extend(infrastructure_rules());
rules
...
fn policy_seed_rule(rule: PatternRule, enabled: bool) -> Option<PrivacyPolicySeedRule> {
    ...
    Matcher::All(_) | Matcher::Any(_) => return None,
    ...
    serde_json::to_value(detector).ok().and_then(|value| value.as_str().map(str::to_string))?;
```
If a built-in rule uses an unsupported matcher shape (Matcher::All/Any) or a structural detector whose serialization can't become a plain string, policy_seed_rule returns None and the rule is silently omitted from the seeded catalog via filter_map -- no error, no log, no operator-visible signal that seeding was incomplete.

Given this session already established the privacy catalog's emptiness is a critical, hard-to-notice failure mode (sinex-t5sr), a seeding path that can silently under-populate the catalog (rather than fully failing loudly) is a related, compounding risk -- an operator who runs seed-builtin and sees "it ran" has no way to know some rules were silently excluded.

Found via a targeted audit of crate/sinex-primitives/src/privacy/catalog.rs using gpt-5.3-codex-spark (2026-08-11), verified against the quoted code.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Add (or identify an existing) built-in PatternRule using Matcher::All or Matcher::Any, or a StructuralDetector whose serde serialization isn't a plain JSON string.
2. Run the seed-builtin path -- observe policy_seed_rule returns None for that rule and it's silently excluded via filter_map, with no log/error/count discrepancy surfaced.
acceptance_criteria: policy_seed_rule's None-returning paths log a warning naming the dropped rule, or seeding fails loudly on an unsupported built-in rule shape.

A compile-fail test covers the mismatch case.
