title: MEDIUM-HIGH: xtask's own schema-bundle generator is built with a test-only Cargo feature enabled, so a test-only authority enum value (CurationJudgmentActorKind::TestFixture) leaks into the committed, public-repository schema contract file -- and the drift guard is structurally blind since generator and checker are the same testing-enabled binary
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via a capability-flag/test-production-divergence audit, touching the project's own "Public Repository Boundary" doctrine. xtask's Cargo.toml declares its sinex-primitives dependency with feature "testing" enabled -- in the regular [dependencies] section, not [dev-dependencies]. xtask is simultaneously the SCHEMA BUNDLE GENERATOR (generate_schema_bundle), the DRIFT CHECKER (xtask docs schema-bundle --check, wired into release readiness), and the DEV-STACK SEEDER for the checked-in public schema files.

CONSEQUENCE, VERIFIED IN THE TREE: crate/sinex-primitives's CurationJudgmentActorKind::TestFixture is #[cfg(any(test, feature="testing"))]-gated specifically SO IT CANNOT BE CONSTRUCTED FROM ORDINARY JSON DESERIALIZATION IN A PRODUCTION BINARY (per the already-fixed sinex-audit-actorkind, whose whole point was that a doc comment alone wasn't an enforced boundary). Despite that, schemas/v1/curation/curation.judgment.json -- a COMMITTED, PUBLIC-REPOSITORY schema contract file -- contains "const":"test_fixture" in the CurationJudgmentActorKind oneOf, with the cfg-gate doc comment copied verbatim into the schema's own description field.

WHY THE DRIFT GUARD CANNOT CATCH THIS: because the generator and the checker are literally the same testing-feature-enabled binary, --check compares a testing-derived bundle against a testing-derived bundle -- it can never detect this specific class of drift, since both sides of the comparison have the leak.

SCOPE HONESTY (bounds the severity): the LIVE PRODUCTION registry is not directly affected -- the real sinexd binary generates and syncs its own bundle at its own startup, and sinexd is built package-scoped (cargo -p sinexd -p sinexctl in the Nix release build), so Cargo feature unification does NOT pull testing into the deployed binary itself. The actual damage is: (a) a PUBLIC-REPOSITORY committed contract artifact advertising a test-only authority value as a legal external input, (b) a dev stack that gets seeded with this overly-permissive schema, (c) a drift guard that is provably structurally blind to this entire class of leak. Same-shape doc drift already user-visible: sinexctl's curation CLI command help text documents the actor-kind argument as accepting 'user, operator, deterministic_policy, or test_fixture' -- but a real production sinexd/sinexctl pair cannot deserialize test_fixture at all.
acceptance_criteria: Move xtask's sinex-primitives dependency's testing feature to a build-profile-gated or explicitly-separate check (or move the schema-generation logic to not require the testing feature at all), so the committed schema bundle reflects what a production binary can actually construct. Regenerate schemas/v1/curation/curation.judgment.json (and audit siblings for the same leak) once fixed. Correct sinexctl's curation CLI help text to not document test_fixture as a real accepted value.

title: HIGH: the 'production path' source-test harness never instantiates any adapter -- 7 of 8 fixture builders (MockDbusBackend/MockClipboardBackend included) are dead code, and the harness's own module doc claims otherwise; the entire InputShapeAdapter half of every source is untested by this suite
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via a capability-flag/test-production-divergence audit. crate/sinexd/tests/sources/production_path.rs is documented (module doc, "Production-path test harness root") as the harness proving each registered source works end-to-end through its production adapter+parser pair, explicitly naming per-source fixtures like MockDbusBackend/MockClipboardBackend. Reality: no obligation in the harness ever builds or injects a fixture -- adapter_kind is threaded through the whole harness only to be discarded (confirmed: two obligation files explicitly document their adapter_kind parameter as "informational; dispatch is byte-level", underscore-prefixed as unused). Grepped fixtures:: usage outside the fixtures/ directory itself across the whole test tree -- exactly TWO hits, both in one desktop test (unix socket only). So fixtures/{append_only_file,clipboard,dbus,file_drop,journal,sqlite_row,static_file}.rs -- 7 of 8 fixture builders -- have ZERO callers. MockDbusBackend and MockClipboardBackend are never constructed by this harness at all, despite the module doc explicitly claiming they are.

WHAT THE HARNESS WRONGLY APPEARS TO PROVE: that each registered source works end-to-end through its production adapter+parser pair across four obligations (InitialIngestion/Replay/Isolation/Privacy) for its declared AdapterKind.

WHAT IT ACTUALLY PROVES: that MaterialParser (the byte-to-intent half) is deterministic on hand-supplied bytes. The entire InputShapeAdapter half -- the half that produces anchored SourceRecords in the first place -- is NEVER EXECUTED by this harness. Concrete production gaps this cannot catch: cursor advancement, anchor-byte assignment, logical_path derivation, inotify event coalescing in FileDropAdapter, SQLite ROWID cursor semantics, D-Bus ParsedMatchRule filtering. The already-known sinex-h3g class ("AW durations freeze at scan time -- ROWID cursor vs in-place heartbeat growth") lives exactly in the adapter half and is structurally invisible to this harness. A regression that makes DbusStreamAdapter::open drop every signal whose interface doesn't match, or that makes AppendOnlyFileAdapter re-emit the whole file on each scan, would leave every production_path case green.

Secondary hazard in the same area, currently unreachable only because the mocks are never injected: both dbus_stream.rs and clipboard_polling.rs consume their injected backend via slot.take() -- a ONE-SHOT Option. Any second open() on the same adapter instance silently falls back to the REAL backend (RealDbusBackend / ArboardBackend::new()). If the harness is ever wired up as documented, a replay/re-open obligation would attempt a live D-Bus connection mid-test rather than failing loudly.
acceptance_criteria: Wire the obligation layer to actually build and inject fixtures per AdapterKind as the module doc already claims, or correct the doc to state the harness only exercises MaterialParser determinism on hand-supplied bytes, not the adapter layer. Fix the one-shot slot.take() hazard in dbus_stream.rs/clipboard_polling.rs before wiring the harness up for real, so a second open() fails loudly instead of silently falling back to a live backend mid-test.

title: HIGH: double_replay_idempotent is a tautological test -- the fake replay source is told the exact answer to assert, bypassing the entire admission/equivalence-key-dedup pipeline, so it structurally cannot catch the exact class of regression (sinex-ecy) it's named to prevent
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via a capability-flag/test-production-divergence audit. crate/sinexd/tests/api/replay_determinism_test.rs's double_replay_idempotent test (doc: "Double-replaying the same scope is idempotent (event count stable)") is TAUTOLOGICAL -- the fake source used for the second replay is constructed with events_processed set to the CURRENT live count after the first replay, i.e. it is instructed to emit exactly the number of rows already live. The assertion (live_after_1 == live_after_2) is satisfied by construction of the test fixture, not by any property of the replay engine being tested.

The fake (spawn_fake_replay_scan_source, tests/api/common/mod.rs) re-emits via a DIRECT pool.events().insert(event) call -- bypassing the ENTIRE production re-emission pipeline: EventEmitter -> EventBatcher -> NATS raw stream -> admission (parse/schema/plausibility/EQUIVALENCE-KEY DEDUP) -> MaterialReadySet FK gate -> ts_orig resolution -> redact_batch -> persist -> confirmed publish.

Production gap: the archive/cascade/scan-command half of replay IS real in this test (a real ReplayExecutionEngine runs), but the re-emission half is entirely simulated with no equivalence_key ever attached. The already-closed sinex-ecy finding class ("equivalence keys are per-checkpoint COUNTERS -> replay/reset collision -> fail-open dedup silently suppresses fresh derived events") would make a REAL second replay emit FEWER events than the first -- precisely the regression this test is named to catch -- and it is structurally unobservable to this test, since the fake never passes through admission dedup at all. Note the sibling test material_replay_archives_preserve_content (same file) is fine -- it asserts on audit.archived_events content, which the real engine writes."
acceptance_criteria: Rewrite double_replay_idempotent to re-emit through the REAL pipeline (NATS raw stream -> admission -> confirmed publish) rather than a direct DB insert with a foreknown count, so it can actually falsify an equivalence-key-collision regression like the one sinex-ecy fixed. Given sinex-ecy is closed, this is worth an independent live verification that a real double-replay is still idempotent post-fix, since this test never actually checked that.

title: an entire validated runtime-config subsystem (745 lines, full Validate-derive ladder) has zero constructors anywhere in the repo -- yet is actively documented as THE way to load source/automaton config, and an open security bead (sinex-pzo9) cites it as the reference pattern to copy
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via a fallible-validation-discarded audit (adjacent finding, same audit). An entire validated runtime-config subsystem -- crate/sinexd/src/runtime/config.rs, 745 lines -- has ZERO constructors anywhere in the whole repository. RuntimeConfig, EventSourceConfig, AutomatonConfig, MaterialMetadataPolicy, PathClassRule, plus load_from_env and validate_config and four custom validators (validate_service_name, validate_log_level, validate_work_dir, validate_seconds_nonzero) -- confirmed via exhaustive grep across the whole repo, the ONLY references anywhere are the module's own re-exports (runtime/mod.rs, runtime/prelude.rs) and one doc-comment mention. No ::builder(), no load_from_env caller, no serde deserialization site, no test constructor. Last touched by the sinexd-collapse cleanup PR (#1642), which is evidently where the callers were removed without removing the config module itself.

This carries a full #[derive(Validate)] ladder -- nested composition, url/range(min=1,max=1000) constraints, four custom validators, plus a validate_config() that additionally checks the work-dir parent exists on disk. None of it runs, ever.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN ORDINARY DEAD CODE -- two LIVE artifacts point at it as if it's real and working:
1. crate/sinexd/docs/runtime_configuration.md documents RuntimeConfig::load_from_env("my-source") as THE way source/automaton config is loaded -- a reader following the current docs would write code against a function nothing calls.
2. The OPEN bead sinex-pzo9 (the ops.start RCE finding) cites runtime/config.rs's validate_work_dir as "the existing path-validation pattern" that the vulnerable media-worker path should be made to follow -- an active security-fix recommendation is holding up dead code as the reference implementation to copy.

Partial prior coverage: sinex-mi2y point 3 already notes RuntimeConfig::database_pool_size specifically is dead config, scoped narrowly to the pool-threading question -- this finding is that the entire containing module, not just that one field, has never had a caller since the collapse cleanup.
acceptance_criteria: Either wire crate/sinexd/src/runtime/config.rs's RuntimeConfig/EventSourceConfig/AutomatonConfig back into the actual config-loading path (if the collapse cleanup genuinely left a gap), or delete the module and correct docs/runtime_configuration.md and sinex-pzo9's cited reference pattern to point at whatever mechanism actually loads config today. Do not let sinex-pzo9's fix cite this as a model without first confirming it's real.

title: SINEX_NAMESPACE is resolved via 3 independent mechanisms that only agree by env-var coincidence -- a --namespace CLI flag (no export) diverges the scan-pacer and import-progress paths from the real NatsPublisher namespace, live for dev/test invocations though masked in the NixOS deployment
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via a duplicated-independently-resolved-state audit. SINEX_NAMESPACE is resolved via at least THREE independent mechanisms that currently agree only by env-var coincidence, not by shared code:

1. crate/sinexd/src/runtime/runtime_cli.rs -- clap #[arg(long, env="SINEX_NAMESPACE")], threaded into NatsPublisher.namespace -- the canonical, authoritative namespace used for every subject/stream construction in NatsPublisher (10+ call sites).
2. crate/sinexd/src/runtime/parser/adapter_source.rs -- an independent raw std::env::var("SINEX_NAMESPACE") read, feeding ScanPacer's namespace for the sinex-2n9 pacing/progress KV. The code's OWN comment admits the gap: "Matches how RuntimeCli/NatsPublisher resolve namespace elsewhere in the runtime... RuntimeContext does not currently expose the resolved namespace to source drivers."
3. crate/sinexd/src/api/handlers/import_progress.rs -- another independent raw std::env::var("SINEX_NAMESPACE") read, feeding ScanProgressStore::open, bypassing GatewayConfig.namespace that services.config() already exposes.

CONCRETE DIVERGENCE: args.namespace (mechanism 1) can be set by a --namespace <flag> CLI argument, but clap's env= attribute only supplies a value when the flag is ABSENT -- it never writes the resolved value back into the process environment. So launching with --namespace foo (no export) makes NatsPublisher.namespace=Some("foo") while mechanisms 2 and 3's raw reads both still return None -- the scan pacer's progress-KV bucket and the import-progress RPC handler would silently operate under a DIFFERENT namespace than the one actual events are published/subscribed under. Not exploitable in prod today (the NixOS deployment never passes --namespace, confirmed via grep), but live for any dev/test invocation using the flag form.

Second-order edge case: two different "treat blank env var as None" helper flavors exist in the codebase (env::var_optional treats SINEX_NAMESPACE="" as Some(""), env_nonempty_string_optional treats it as None), and SinexEnvironment::nats_stream_name_with_namespace produces a trailing-underscore-suffixed stream name for Some("") vs an unsuffixed one for None -- so these two helper flavors compute DIFFERENT real stream names for the identical blank env var, independent of the three-mechanism divergence above.
acceptance_criteria: Thread the resolved namespace through RuntimeContext (as adapter_source.rs's own comment already suggests) so source drivers and RPC handlers read the SAME resolved value NatsPublisher uses, instead of each independently re-reading the raw env var. Standardize on one blank-vs-None treatment for SINEX_NAMESPACE specifically rather than having two helper flavors disagree.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] Concrete triple-resolution bug (SINEX_NAMESPACE resolved 3 independent ways, agreeing only by env-var coincidence); testable via a test that diverges the env var from a code default.

title: 8 response/view-layer enums declare variants with zero production construction sites anywhere -- SinexObjectKind (11 of 30 unconstructed, including the object-reference type embedded throughout evidence/trace links), PrivacyStateKind (5 of 8, security-relevant states that can never actually occur), plus 6 more
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via a systematic audit for cause F ("API/type surfaces declare more variants/capability than the implementation delivers") of the mechanisms-built-then-discarded pattern. Confirms and extends the SearchMode::Vector/Hybrid instance (already tracked as sinex-ebe2 F3b) with 7 more enums across the response/view layer, all sharing the same shape: a variant is fully declared, has round-trip serde/display support (so it LOOKS wired), but has zero production construction sites anywhere.

MOST SEVERE: SinexObjectKind (crate/sinex-primitives/src/views/common.rs), the generic "kind" tag on SinexObjectRef embedded throughout evidence refs, trace links, and sinexctl show <kind>:<id>. 11 of 30 variants are never constructed anywhere: Document, DocumentChunk, SemanticEntity, SemanticRelation, QueryRun, AdmissionOutcome, Snapshot, MomentCandidate, PrivacySession, Caveat, ExternalRef. public_ref.rs has a COMPLETE bidirectional string<->kind round-trip table for all 30 variants (so an operator CAN type sinexctl show document-chunk:<id> without a parse error), and the TUI has a complete display-label match for all 30 -- but crate/sinexctl/src/commands/show.rs only implements real lookup for SourceMaterial/SourceDriver/Operation/Event (plus Command/RpcMethod), falling through to an "unsupported" response for the other 11 kinds. This is permanently unsupported, not "not found yet," and looks identical to a real gap from the type signatures alone.

PrivacyStateKind (views/common.rs), 5 of 8 variants unconstructed: MetadataOnly, PermissionDenied, PolicyBlocked, TombstonePending, ExportRestricted. The sole production constructor (DisclosureDecision::new_with_policy_refs) only ever produces RawVisible/Suppressed/Redacted. These 5 sound security/privacy-relevant enough that a client reading events.cards' privacy_state.state field could reasonably build logic treating "export restricted" or "tombstone pending" specially -- the server can never emit them.

EventTraceRelation (views/events.rs), 5 of 9 variants unconstructed (QueryRun, Proposal, Judgment, ExternalRef, Policy) -- the sole production constructor only ever produces 4 of the 9.

EventOriginKind (views/events.rs), 3 of 5 unconstructed (Declared, System, ExternalMirror) -- but these are STRUCTURALLY unreachable given the current provenance type system (the internal Provenance enum architecturally has only Material/Derived variants per the XOR provenance model), not just unimplemented. Undocumented as reserved/future in the response-facing type though, despite feeding a live RPC (events.cards).

ActionSideEffect::Compose (views/common.rs) -- zero references anywhere in the entire workspace outside its own declaration, not even a test or display match. The single cleanest/most vestigial instance found.

DebtStage (views/debt.rs), 3 of 9 unconstructed (ArtifactInvalidated, OperationPending, OperationFailed) -- confirmed against the live sinexctl ops debt list implementation.

DesktopContextOutputKind (views/desktop.rs), 2 of 6 unconstructed (EvidenceWindowView, ContextReportArtifact) -- notably, a REAL EvidenceWindow type exists and IS reachable (sinexctl desktop context explain) but routes through an entirely separate metadata registry (output_kind.rs's declared_output_kind string tagging), confirming this specific enum variant is genuinely vestigial rather than "not yet wired."

ActionAvailabilityState (views/common.rs), Loading/Partial unconstructed (minor, 2 of 7).

SEPARATE, RELATED FINDING (parsed-signal discarded, not an enum-variant gap): crate/sinexd/src/runtime/parser/adapters/email_gmail_api.rs's GmailRestMessageList.result_size_estimate is parsed then #[allow(dead_code)] discarded -- Gmail's own estimated total-message-count for the current list query, a natural input to the existing progress-tracking mechanism (scan_progress.rs's events_total/bytes_total for ETA) that nothing wires it through to. A smaller sibling: email_oauth.rs's OAuthErrorBody.error_description is parsed then discarded (though the raw response body is retained as a fallback, so this one is only partially lost).

VERIFIED SOLID, worth noting as the pattern done RIGHT: crate/sinexd/src/sources/package_completeness.rs is a large requirements-matrix generator that could easily have fallen into this same trap, but doesn't -- it's genuinely load-bearing (served live via an RPC + MCP tool + consumed by evidence bundles), and for the one row where a reader might mistake it for real enforcement (criticality_declaration), the code explicitly disclaims in-line: "Non-blocking: this row is informational... The ENFORCED gate is deploy-time, in sinexd::sources::bindings::validate_bindings." Worth using as the template comment convention for the other findings above.

Audit scope: covered the 13 enums in crate/sinex-primitives/src/views/*.rs plus SearchMode (14 total) -- roughly 3% of the workspace's ~437 public enums, deliberately the highest-value slice (enums embedded directly in response/view DTOs). RPC request/response bodies outside the views layer, source_contracts/domain enums, and error enums were NOT covered and could have the same defect shape.
acceptance_criteria: For each enum, either wire a real producer for the currently-unconstructed variants, or mark them clearly as reserved/future in a doc comment (matching package_completeness.rs's good disclaimer pattern) so a reader/client can't mistake type-level presence for actual runtime capability. Prioritize SinexObjectKind (most severe, affects sinexctl show's core UX) and PrivacyStateKind (security-relevant variants that look load-bearing). Consider an xtask check that flags any response/view-layer enum variant with zero non-test construction sites, to catch the next instance of this pattern mechanically rather than requiring another audit.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] 8 dead enum variants -- testable via an exhaustiveness/construction-site assertion per enum.

title: ARCH-EPIC: CLI/TUI rendering-correctness bugs -- sinexctl's own presentation layer, distinct from consumption-boundary security (sinex-1hus)
description:
Consolidating epic, 2026-08-11. Three beads, all found in the same audit pass, all about the terminal rendering layer itself being broken -- distinct from sinex-1hus (consumption-boundary security/sanitization) since these are correctness bugs in sinexctl's own presentation code, not content flowing across a trust boundary.

Children:
- sinex-yumr -- sinexctl's own ANSI color styling measures escape-sequence bytes as visible width (tabled's ansi feature isn't enabled), destroying its own table layout on every interactive terminal -- live-reproduced, up to 97-column drift.
- sinex-8dus -- every truncation helper counts characters not display columns, so CJK content (present in this deployment's real browser/window/media title captures) renders at roughly double its intended budget with no table width constraint to catch the overrun.
- sinex-t9gq -- the TUI has no panic hook to restore terminal state, and enables mouse capture that's never read, disabling native text selection for zero benefit.

All three are genuine, live-relevant bugs in the presentation layer that would be immediately visible to the operator on first use post-wipe (every automaton/source will be in the maximally-affected all-placeholder-cells state for yumr specifically).
acceptance_criteria: Fix as a batch given they're all in the same rendering layer and were found together -- likely touches the same table-building/truncation helper code for at least two of the three.

title: ARCH-EPIC: entity/relation graph subsystem is dormant and internally inconsistent across its own automata
description:
Consolidating epic, 2026-08-11. Five independently-discovered beads about the entity/relation graph subsystem, all converging on the same underlying picture: this subsystem is dormant (the 4-stage chain is default-off, the shadow-lane re-entry path has no operator trigger) and, even where individual pieces work correctly in isolation, they are internally inconsistent with each other in ways that would surface the moment anything activates them.

Children:
- sinex-cel3 -- the live relation extractor cannot observe co-occurrence at all (the entity resolver only emits its output event once per entity, ever), producing spurious cross-gap pairs on every window close and structurally-constant temporal statistics.
- sinex-z3a7 -- the ratified shadow-lane re-entry path is not a faithful port of the (broken) live automaton it's meant to replace, has an unremediated instance of an already-fixed bug class, and its 'byte-reproducible' scope hash is positional rather than content-addressed.
- sinex-cmy -- entity/relation insertion defaults fabricate authority (confidence 1.0, empty source refs), and cross-source entity linking was empirically confirmed to not exist as a mechanism at all -- most source event types never reach entity extraction, and where they do, canonicalization only links at domain granularity.
- sinex-pift -- knowledge-graph path-finding has no node-visited guard on a graph whose normal shape is near-complete cliques, an asymptotic blowup risk the moment it gets its first real caller (currently zero callers).
- sinex-98hg -- no cross-source content dedup/fingerprinting exists, the practical consequence of cmy's cross-source-linking-doesn't-exist finding for the specific 'same URL captured via 4 different sources' scenario.

Net picture: before any decision to activate the entity/relation graph beyond its current dormant state, this cluster of beads should be triaged together -- several of the individual fixes (e.g. z3a7's semantic-divergence finding vs cel3's live-automaton co-occurrence gap) point toward the SAME underlying design decision (which co-occurrence semantics are actually correct) rather than being independently fixable.
acceptance_criteria: Triage this cluster together before any decision to activate the entity/relation chain beyond its current dormant state -- several children point at the same underlying design question (correct co-occurrence semantics) rather than being independently fixable point bugs.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit 2026-08-11] Lane F reviewed: this is an ARCH-EPIC, epic-level not a single-test target -- flagged only, not decomposed this pass.

title: truncation budgets across sinexctl count characters, not display columns -- a CJK title truncated to a 60-char budget renders at ~117 columns, roughly double the intended width, and no table anywhere has an explicit width constraint to catch the overrun
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via temporal/presentation-robustness audit. The mission hypothesis that table ALIGNMENT breaks on CJK is FALSE and verified so -- tabled/papergrid and ratatui both use unicode-width correctly, and a CJK table row's borders were confirmed to line up exactly in a live repro. The REAL defect is truncation BUDGET overrun, not alignment.

Every truncation helper across the codebase counts CHARACTERS, not display COLUMNS: the shared truncate_chars helper in views/common.rs, sinexctl's own truncate_string in query.rs, two verbatim-duplicated copies of the same function in tui.rs and shortcuts.rs, plus call sites in context.rs and query_units.rs. Live-measured: truncating a Japanese title to a 60-character budget keeps 60 CHARACTERS, which renders as 117 display COLUMNS -- the ASCII equivalent of the same budget is 60 columns. The SUMMARY column of sinexctl events query (declared budget 60) therefore renders roughly 120 columns wide on real CJK content, pushing what should be a 5-column table to ~137 columns.

No table anywhere sets an explicit width constraint -- all table-styling call sites across the CLI apply only border styles, never a width-truncate or width-wrap setting. Once total row width exceeds the terminal, the terminal soft-wraps a fixed-width box-drawn table and the borders shred visibly.

This is directly live-relevant, not hypothetical: browser tab titles, window titles, and music/media track metadata are all captured sources on this deployment and routinely carry CJK text.

Sub-case, lower severity: truncation can split grapheme clusters (cutting between a base character and its combining marks in NFD-normalized text), orphaning a combining mark next to the truncation ellipsis -- cosmetic, but means the character-count budget also UNDER-fills for NFD/Indic text in the opposite direction from the CJK over-fill.
acceptance_criteria: Switch truncation helpers to measure/truncate by display width (unicode-width, already a transitive dependency) rather than character count, consolidating the duplicated truncate_string copies in the process. Add an explicit width constraint (truncate or wrap) to table rendering as defense-in-depth even after the budget fix, so a future truncation-budget regression degrades gracefully instead of shredding table borders.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] Char-count vs display-column truncation is directly testable with a CJK (double-width) title fixture asserting the rendered budget isn't overrun. No test yet -- distinct from the already-fixed truncate_str_boundary_safe (that fixes UTF-8 safety, not display width).

title: HIGH, live-reproduced: sinexctl's own ANSI color styling destroys the tables it decorates -- tabled measures escape-sequence bytes as visible width (missing the ansi feature), producing up to 97-column drift on real command output, worst exactly when every field is a styled placeholder
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via temporal/presentation-robustness audit, LIVE-REPRODUCED via standalone rustc builds against the workspace's own compiled tabled/console/unicode-width dependency rlibs (not just static reading). Not the injection class (sinex-e0qo, attacker-controlled content) -- this is sinex's OWN console::style() output breaking sinex's OWN table layout, self-inflicted on every --format table surface on an interactive terminal. Fixing e0qo by sanitizing captured content will NOT fix this, since the escapes here are emitted by sinexctl downstream of any ingest/read sanitization.

Mechanism, each link verified: tabled 0.20 is used with default features -- the "ansi" feature is NOT enabled (confirmed in Cargo.lock, no ansi-str/ansitok dependency present). Without that feature, tabled's underlying width-measurement function counts raw unicode-width on the cell string, and unicode-width maps every char <= U+00A0 (including ESC, 0x1B) to display width 1 -- measured live: an ANSI SGR sequence like the one console emits for "dim" styling measures as width 4 despite rendering as ZERO columns. console::StyledObject::fmt emits the real escape sequences whenever colors_enabled() is true (any interactive TTY). So every style(x)....to_string() cell is measured several columns WIDER than it actually renders.

Live-measured against sinexctl automata list's actual column-formatting shape: border/header rows render at their true width, but a row with 1 styled cell renders 17 columns narrower than the measured/padded width, and a row with 12 styled cells renders 97 columns narrower. An automaton with no metrics yet (which is the state of EVERY automaton on first inspection after the planned fresh wipe + re-import) renders every optional column as a dim placeholder -- the table is not "slightly ragged", it is unreadable.

Confirmed-affected live table builders (each passes a style(...).to_string() into push_record): sinexctl automata list, sinexctl sources list --materials, sinexctl runtime list (LAST HEARTBEAT column), sinexctl ops replay list (STATUS is column 2 of 4, so it shifts every subsequent column), sinexctl events query (dim TIMESTAMP), sinexctl telemetry commands (dim LAST UPDATE). 57 style(...).to_string() call sites total across the CLI; not all feed tables, these six confirmed.

Why it has never been caught: console::colors_enabled() is false when stdout is not a TTY, so piped output -- including every test harness capture and every pipe-to-less -- renders perfectly. The defect exists ONLY on the operator's direct interactive terminal, which is the default, most common path. Operator workaround today: NO_COLOR=1 (honored via console's unix-term handling).

VERIFIED SOLID, same class, do not "fix": passing a StyledObject DIRECTLY to a width format specifier (rather than calling .to_string() on it first) is correct, because console's formatting machinery forwards the Formatter to the inner value so padding applies to the text only, not the escape-inflated length. Reproduced live. sinexctl's timeline/explain/recall line renderers already use this correct pattern -- the bug is specifically the .to_string()-then-measure sites listed above.
acceptance_criteria: Enable tabled's ansi feature (papergrid then strips escapes via ansitok before measuring width), or stop materializing style into cell strings before pushing to the table and apply color through tabled::settings::Color instead -- the second option is strictly better since it also improves the e0qo remediation path. Verify against the six confirmed-affected commands with an automaton/source that has no metrics yet (all-placeholder-cells case), which is the worst case and exactly what every command will show immediately after the planned wipe.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] Already LIVE-REPRODUCED per the bead's own description (standalone rustc build against the real tabled/console rlibs) -- that repro just needs to become a persisted regression test. Not written yet.

title: no relevance-regression protection exists for documents.search -- the entire test suite asserts sortedness/membership/mode, never actual ranking order, so a fix to the already-known ranking bugs (sinex-ebe2/yypi) can land with no way to prove it improved anything
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via verification-tooling meta-audit. There is no test anywhere that would catch a ranking/relevance regression in documents.search. The entire search test surface (crate/sinex-db/tests/document_search_test.rs, 606 lines, 15 tests) asserts only sortedness, membership, mode equality, filter correctness, pagination non-overlap, or emptiness -- never actual relevance ordering:

- The one ordering test asserts scores[i]>=scores[i+1] -- satisfied by any scoring function including a CONSTANT. A change replacing real ranking with a fixed value would pass.
- The multi-word FTS test seeds one chunk with both query terms and another with only one, with a comment noting the two-term chunk should rank first -- but the assertion only checks membership in the hit set, not ordering. An inversion of relevance ordering passes.
- The exclusion-operator test wraps its only assertion in a check for the FTS search mode specifically -- a regression that flips the mode to the trigram-fallback path DISABLES the test rather than failing it, self-suppressing.

No fixed corpus with graded relevance, no expected-ordering assertion, no NDCG/hit@k harness, no snapshot of a ranked result list exists anywhere. Combined with sinex-ebe2/sinex-yypi (which document that ranking is currently WRONG in specific, measured ways), the absence of a golden set means any fix to those beads will land with no way to prove it improved anything, and no way to detect a later regression once fixed.
acceptance_criteria: Add a fixed corpus with graded relevance judgments (even a small hand-curated one) and an expected-ordering assertion for at least the top-K results of a representative query set, so a future fix to sinex-ebe2/sinex-yypi's ranking bugs has a way to demonstrate improvement, and a future regression has a way to get caught. Fix the exclusion-operator test's self-suppressing mode-gated assertion as a smaller, immediate improvement to the existing suite.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] The bead's entire resolution IS writing a real relevance-regression test (current suite only asserts sortedness/membership, not actual ranking order) -- maximally in the O3 category by definition.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] Investigated during db-schema TDD pass. This bead's own resolution is a real relevance-regression test for documents.search (current suite only asserts sortedness, satisfied even by a constant score). Deferred writing it this round -- doing it properly needs a realistic multi-document fixture with known relevance ordering (not just 2-3 trivial docs), which is a bigger lift than the other beads in this cluster. Concrete shape: seed docs with deliberately varying term-frequency/field-match relevance, assert the CURRENT top-ranked result stays top-ranked after a no-op round-trip (locks in present ranking so a future regression is caught), not just satisfied ordering.

title: SINEX_EVENT_ENGINE_CONSUMER_NAME override is honored by the raw-stream backpressure READER but not the event-engine consumer WRITER -- setting it silently disables source-side backpressure entirely, and the module comment claiming symmetry is false
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via SINEX_* startup-validation sweep. crate/sinexd/src/runtime/backlog.rs's event_engine_raw_consumer_name() reads SINEX_EVENT_ENGINE_CONSUMER_NAME with a doc comment claiming it "honors the same override env var the event engine itself uses." FALSE -- grepped the whole workspace: the event engine's actual consumer name is set in exactly ONE place, EventEngineConfig's Default impl, as a fixed format string based on the environment name -- from_args (which reads ~25 other env vars) never touches it, and no NixOS module or doc sets this var either.

Consequence chain: crate/sinexd/src/runtime/nats_publisher.rs resolves the consumer name from the SAME env var for the backpressure gate (wait_for_raw_events_stream_capacity), and on a consumer-not-found error treats "consumer doesn't exist" as "no backpressure" (returns Ok). So setting SINEX_EVENT_ENGINE_CONSUMER_NAME to ANY value permanently and silently disables the source-side raw-stream capacity gate entirely, since the event engine still creates the fixed-name consumer while the backpressure check looks for the overridden name and finds nothing.

The existing test cannot catch this: the adapter-source test creates the test consumer itself via the SAME resolution function used by the reader -- both sides of the test's assertion are the reader, the actual producer (EventEngineConfig) is never involved, so the test would pass even with this bug present.

Currently mitigated: nothing sets this var today (no NixOS module, no docs, no test sets it to a non-default value) -- it is presently an unused, inert knob. Per "unfinished is not obsolete," fix rather than delete.
acceptance_criteria: Either wire SINEX_EVENT_ENGINE_CONSUMER_NAME into EventEngineConfig::from_args so the event engine's own consumer actually honors it (making the doc comment true), or delete both reads and the false comment if this override is genuinely not meant to be supported. Fix the test to exercise the real producer's consumer name, not the reader's own resolution function on both sides of the assertion.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text:
Two related findings 2026-08-11, same audit that confirmed this bead's shape systematically elsewhere in the codebase:

1. SIBLING OF THIS BUG'S SHAPE (currently harmless): the confirmed-events stream name ({base}_CONFIRMED) is reconstructed independently in 3 places -- the canonical JetStreamTopology::for_lane builder (correctly consumed by the event engine's own bootstrap), an independent format!('{raw_stream}_CONFIRMED') inline in runtime/jetstream_consumer.rs's run_inner() (used by EVERY automaton's per-automaton confirmed-event consumer), and a third independent reconstruction inside the same dead preflight code this bead already covers. They currently agree (all derive the suffix identically), so no live bug today -- but it's the exact same 'one canonical typed builder plus hand-rolled string reconstructions' shape this bead's own consumer-name finding has, and would silently go stale the moment the canonical builder's naming convention changes (e.g. a new lane-specific suffix) without the hand-rolled copies being updated too.

2. NEW, RELATED DORMANT FINDING: the per-automaton confirmed consumer (jetstream_consumer.rs, the same file as finding 1) hardcodes the literal 'SINEX_RAW_EVENTS' base-stream key with NO lane parameter at all -- unlike JetStreamTopology's lane-aware activity()/reflection() constructors which correctly derive different base streams per lane. Currently harmless since crate/sinexd/src/automata/registry.rs has zero reflection-lane automaton entries (confirmed via grep) -- but if a reflection automaton is ever registered through the standard automaton runtime rather than a bespoke path, it would silently subscribe to the ACTIVITY-lane confirmed stream instead of the reflection one, with no error.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] Concrete override-inconsistency bug (SINEX_EVENT_ENGINE_CONSUMER_NAME honored by the reader but not the sibling path); testable via a divergence test.

title: sinexctl ops verify baseline's closure-verification health check is structurally incapable of passing since the beads migration -- wrong substrate (still queries GitHub Issues, retired a month ago) and wrong id type (passes numeric issue ids to a verifier that requires bead string ids)
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via verification-tooling meta-audit. crate/sinexctl/src/commands/verify/baseline.rs's discover_and_verify_recent_closures() shells out to a GitHub issue-list query against a 30-day closed-issue window -- but GitHub Issues were retired as the task substrate and ALL issues were bulk-closed as not-planned on 2026-07-10, now outside the sliding 30-day window. Steady state: returns (0,0) -> CheckStatus::Skipped.

Second, independent breakage: even if the issue query DID return results, the code runs xtask verify closure against a NUMERIC issue id -- and the bead-native verifier hard-rejects that with "closure verification requires a Bead string id such as sinex-e7e9" (live-confirmed via direct invocation). So verified would stay 0, pct=0, and the check would report CheckStatus::Fail ("Multiple closure verifications failing") -- a GUARANTEED false FAIL if the gh query ever does return issues again.

Net: the "Closure verification health" baseline check can only ever be Skipped or falsely Fail. Skipped scores 0 but is excluded from the denominator in compute_score, so the composite baseline score silently drops this dimension entirely rather than reflecting its absence. This is the ONLY automated consumer of the closure verifier anywhere in the tooling, and it has been inert for a month with nothing noticing.
acceptance_criteria: Rewrite the closure-health discovery step to query bd (recently-closed beads) instead of gh issue list, and pass bead string ids to xtask verify closure instead of numeric ids -- matching the actual current task substrate. Consider whether the baseline composite score should visibly flag when a dimension is Skipped for a month+ rather than silently excluding it from the denominator forever.
close_reason: Closure Evidence Manifest: Merged via PR #2616 (squash-merged 2026-08-11), Lane L (sinexctl/TUI). Fix: discover_and_verify_recent_closures() was querying the retired gh issue list substrate instead of bd list --closed-after, and was passing numeric GitHub issue ids instead of bead string ids to xtask verify closure; both corrected. Verified via xtask test -p sinexctl -E 'test(closure)' on the merged commit.

title: sinexctl shortcuts status reads private-mode state from a local file instead of the gateway RPC (unlike every other privacy-mode consumer) -- silently reports false 'disabled' when run against a remote/different-host gateway
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via deployment/multi-context-robustness audit. crate/sinexctl/src/commands/shortcuts.rs (private_mode_signal) calls load_private_mode_state(&state_dir) -- a direct std::fs::read_to_string off LOCAL disk -- where state_dir resolves via an override, then /realm/project/sinex/.sinex/state env var, then a hardcoded default. Critically, if the path simply doesn't exist (the common case on any machine other than the one physically running sinexd, or with a different/unset SINEX_STATE_DIR), load_private_mode_state returns Ok(RuntimePrivateModeState::disabled()) -- NOT an error, no warning surfaced -- so shortcuts status will silently report 'private-mode: healthy -- disabled' even when the real, remote daemon currently has private mode ENABLED.

Contrast with the correct pattern used everywhere else: commands/privacy.rs goes through GatewayClient RPC exclusively for every read/mutation, and the TUI correctly calls self.client.private_mode_status().await (an RPC call) rather than touching the filesystem. Scenario matching this operator's own documented multi-machine agent-worktree workflow: running sinexctl shortcuts status from a second machine or a differently-configured shell against the same remote gateway gives a false 'disabled' reading for a privacy-relevant control, with zero indication the read is unreliable -- exactly the kind of false-confidence signal that matters most for a privacy control specifically.
acceptance_criteria: Route shortcuts status's private-mode check through the same GatewayClient RPC every other consumer already uses (private_mode_status()), matching the TUI's already-correct pattern, instead of reading local disk state directly.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] private_mode_signal reading local disk state instead of the gateway RPC is directly testable: assert the command consults the gateway, not a local file, for multi-host/multi-session correctness. No test yet.

title: sinexctl error output is not automation-friendly: no JSON error contract regardless of --format, the dead error-classification module (enhance_rpc_error) never runs, and error text ignores NO_COLOR/non-TTY detection
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via CLI/automation-surface-consistency audit. Three related gaps, all in the same error-handling path:

1. No structured/JSON error contract anywhere in sinexctl, and --format has ZERO effect on error rendering. crate/sinexctl/src/main.rs's main() returns color_eyre::Result<()>; every command handler propagates Err up through ? to this single point. No ErrorView/error-envelope type exists anywhere in sinex-primitives::views. Live-verified across multiple commands with --format json: every failure (connection refused, auth missing, not-found, validation) produces the identical human-oriented color-eyre chain on stderr regardless of requested format -- a script asking for --format json gets no JSON on the error path, ever, from any command.

2. enhance_rpc_error (crate/sinexctl/src/error.rs:10) -- the module whose entire purpose is classifying errors (connection/auth/timeout/not-found) and attaching machine-relevant help text -- is DEAD CODE. Exactly one grep hit for its call site: the definition itself. Only two of its helpers are actually wired up (is_not_found_error used once in audit.rs, format_public_rpc_error_details used in gateway.rs for one sub-case). Live-verified: an unreachable-gateway call prints the raw reqwest error chain with NONE of connection_error_help()'s troubleshooting text ever appearing. The classification logic that would let a script (or human) programmatically distinguish 'gateway down' from 'auth failed' from 'not found' simply never executes for the vast majority of commands.

3. Error output ignores both TTY detection and NO_COLOR, unlike success output. Hex-dumped stderr from a failed command redirected to a plain file (non-TTY): literal ANSI escape sequences present in the file bytes, both with and without NO_COLOR=1 set. Contrast: success-path table output (console crate) correctly auto-detects non-TTY and suppresses color -- but color_eyre::config::HookBuilder (installed in main.rs with no theme/color override) does not. Any automation capturing sinexctl stderr into a log/grep gets raw escape codes polluting the text, on top of having no JSON alternative to fall back to (item 1).

Separately verified (NOT a bug, noted for completeness): the exit-code convention is coarse but internally consistent -- 0 success, 2 for clap usage errors, 1 for everything else uniformly via explicit std::process::exit(1) calls -- so a script CAN distinguish 'malformed invocation' from 'ran but failed', just not distinguish failure classes within the '1' bucket, which compounds with items 1-3 (no structured output to fall back on for that distinction either).
acceptance_criteria: Wire enhance_rpc_error into the actual error path so its classification/help text is reachable. Add a JSON error envelope emitted when --format json is requested, even on failure. Make color_eyre's error rendering respect the same non-TTY/NO_COLOR detection the success-path console rendering already correctly does.

None have tests yet.

title: MEDIUM: automaton input checkpoint (last_input_event_id) has no monotonicity guard -- written unconditionally on delivery order, but consumed as a strictly monotonic resume cursor derived from mint order, causing either duplicate reprocessing or permanent skip depending on which direction the reorder goes
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via crash-only-design audit (Opus). crate/sinexd/src/runtime/automaton/adapter/state_io.rs:380-401: last_input_event_id is set unconditionally to whatever event arrived last (:385), while the sibling max_input_ts_orig field two lines below is correctly guarded to only advance monotonically (:392-398) -- an inconsistency within the same function. last_input_event_id is then consumed as a strictly monotonic resume cursor (Cursor::after_id) for catch-up, but confirmed-stream delivery order is PUBLISH order (post-persist, post-NAK/redelivery, post-batching across concurrent admission work) -- not id-MINT order (UUIDv7 assigned at EventBuilder::build()). These orders can diverge under concurrent admission.

Two distinct failure consequences from the one defect: (1) REGRESSION -> duplicate reprocessing: if a lower-id event is delivered after a higher-id one, the checkpoint moves backward, and the next restart re-scans and re-feeds the whole intervening window into stateful automata (session detector, analytics accumulators, interval-lift) -- admission's equivalence_key dedup is fail-open, so suppression is best-effort only. (2) ADVANCE-PAST -> permanent skip: the confirmed consumer acks on mpsc enqueue, not on processing (a 1024-deep channel) -- SIGKILL with a high-id event already processed (checkpoint saved past it) while a lower-id event still sits acked-but-unprocessed in the channel loses that event from the stream entirely AND places it below the resume cursor, so nothing ever re-reads it.
acceptance_criteria: Guard last_input_event_id the same way max_input_ts_orig already is -- only advance when the new event's id is actually greater than the current checkpoint, matching the pattern already correctly implemented two lines below it in the same function.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] Concrete missing invariant: last_input_event_id written unconditionally with no monotonicity guard. Directly testable (assert checkpoint doesn't regress on out-of-order event arrival); not written yet.

title: public-repository-boundary enforcement relies almost entirely on manual review -- the one automated secret scanner is opt-in (not in default xtask check), not wired to any git hook, and only covers 3 provider-shaped patterns
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via host-level security audit. Confirms CLAUDE.md's own self-assessment is accurate, not just cautious wording: .githooks/ contains ONLY pre-push (no pre-commit hook exists at all in this repo), and pre-push runs only xtask check --changed-strict (a schema-bundle/API-drift guard) -- it never invokes any secret-scanning check.

There IS a real secret-literal scanner: check_provider_shaped_secret_literals() (xtask/src/commands/lint_forbidden.rs:1333-1356), regex-matching GitHub classic PATs (ghp_...), GitHub fine-grained PATs (github_pat_...), and AWS access keys (AKIA...) across *.rs/*.md/*.toml/*.yml/*.yaml via a repo-wide (not diff-scoped, not commit-scoped) rg scan. But it's explicitly OPT-IN, not default: check.rs's own comment says 'Forbidden patterns (optional, off by default)', gated by --forbidden; plain xtask check does not run it, only xtask check --full does (a manual, periodic, broad-gate invocation per CLAUDE.md's own stated cadence, NOT something that runs automatically on every commit or push). The pre-push hook's own invocation of xtask check --changed-strict does not forward --forbidden either.

No gitleaks/trufflehog/detect-secrets/ggshield/pre-commit-hooks-style tool is integrated anywhere in the repo -- the only hits for those tool names are in .agent/scratch/ external research notes explicitly recommending adoption, never acted on.

What the existing check would NOT catch: generic API keys/JWTs not matching the three known provider shapes, PEM private key blocks, database connection strings with embedded credentials, passwords, and -- most relevant to CLAUDE.md's actual stated worry -- any prose, fixture, or commit-message content encoding real personal/financial/health/identity data. CLAUDE.md's text ('Path and regex checks cannot decide whether prose, fixtures, or commit messages are appropriate') is confirmed as an accurate limitation, not aspirational caution -- there is genuinely no automated backstop for that class at all.
acceptance_criteria: Wire the existing --forbidden provider-shaped-secret check into the pre-push hook by default (cheap, already exists, just needs forwarding), and/or add a real pre-commit hook running it diff-scoped rather than full-repo-scoped for faster feedback. Consider adopting a maintained secret-scanning tool (gitleaks or similar, already recommended by prior external research in .agent/scratch/) for broader pattern coverage than the current 3 hardcoded provider shapes. The prose/personal-data class explicitly cannot be automated reliably -- document that this remains a manual-review-only category rather than implying otherwise.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] Confirmed true: .githooks/ has only pre-push, no pre-commit hook. The negative claim (no automated enforcement exists) is trivially testable/already-verified; but 'how to actually enforce the repo boundary automatically' is an undesigned mechanism, not yet AC-shaped -- partial, not full.

title: ARCH-EPIC: make per-field privacy metadata coverage universal and load-bearing (not just declarative-only, not just an audit artifact)
description:
Scoped redesign following the sinex-tzqt correction (2026-08-11). A real per-field privacy metadata mechanism already exists (ParserFieldPrivacyMetadata, DeclarativeFieldSpec.sensitivity, the generated privacy-coverage.generated.json matrix) -- this epic is NOT about building it from scratch, it's about closing the two gaps that make it currently incomplete and inert:

1. COVERAGE GAP: only declarative-macro-based source contracts get real per-field metadata; 30 of 31 imperative parsers (impl MaterialParser directly) get a silent empty default, including browser/history.rs's URL field -- one of the single most revealing fields in the whole capture surface. atuin_history.rs already demonstrates the fix pattern (delegate field_privacy_metadata() to an underlying declarative-derived record type, or hand-implement the trait method directly).

2. ENFORCEMENT GAP: even a source with COMPLETE field-level metadata gets zero automatic benefit -- the coverage matrix is explicitly documented as audit-only ('does not apply DB/user privacy policy'). Nothing reads a field flagged CredentialBearing/PersonNameCandidate/etc to suggest or auto-bind a scoped privacy.rules row. This connects directly to sinex-4kbm's auto-convergence theme (schema-apply-style declarative convergence) -- the natural shape is: per-field sensitivity metadata becomes an INPUT to the same auto-converging catalog-seeding mechanism proposed there, not a separate dead-end artifact.

3. CLEANUP: the record-level sensitivity_hints field (crate/sinex-primitives/src/privacy/mod.rs, PatternRule's sibling concept applied at record granularity via collect_sensitivity_hints in source_record.rs) is a lossy flattening of the same per-field data that already exists with full granularity elsewhere -- once per-field coverage is universal, either retire the flattened field or clearly document it as a coarse rollup only, so nobody mistakes it for the real per-field signal.
acceptance_criteria: Every source contract (declarative or imperative) reports real field_privacy_metadata() -- browser/history.rs's URL field specifically gets a correct SensitivityHint declaration as the concrete first target. Field-level metadata flagged with a given hint drives at least a suggested (not necessarily auto-applied without review) scoped privacy.rules binding, wired into the sinex-4kbm auto-convergence mechanism rather than remaining a static documentation artifact. The lossy record-level sensitivity_hints flattening is either removed or explicitly documented as coarse-only.

title: SensitivityHint is dead: declared at whole-record granularity (not per-field), populated by only 6/35 source contracts, and has ZERO consumers anywhere -- browser/history.rs's URL field specifically carries none despite being maximally revealing
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via operator follow-up on the privacy-architecture discussion (sinex-4kbm). SensitivityHint (crate/sinex-primitives/src/privacy/mod.rs:79-92) was presumably meant to be a real per-field sensitivity-annotation mechanism ('may propose or bind rules', doc comment references pre-Beads issue numbers #1042 AC3/#1611) but is functionally dead on every axis:

1. GRANULARITY: declared at the WHOLE-RECORD level via a single Vec<SensitivityHint> per source contract's record builder, not per-field. crate/sinexd/src/sources/source_contracts/desktop/window_manager.rs:154-156 sets [FreeText, PotentiallySensitive] for an entire window-activation record -- there's no way to say 'window_title is sensitive but window_class isn't' within the same record.

2. COVERAGE: only 6 of ~35 source contracts populate it at all (window_manager, activitywatch, email, media x2, document/staging). Every other source contract -- including browser/history.rs, finance.rs, messaging.rs, social.rs, bookmark.rs, ALL terminal-history sources (bash/zsh/fish/text/atuin/kitty_osc/asciinema), dbus.rs, journald.rs, git.rs, health.rs, knowledgebase.rs, library.rs, ai_session.rs, music.rs, clipboard.rs, fs/parser.rs, system/notification*.rs, system/udev.rs, system/systemd.rs -- sets sensitivity_hints: Vec::new() (confirmed via grep, ~30 exact hits).

3. CONCRETE SEVERE INSTANCE: browser/history.rs:225 sets sensitivity_hints: Vec::new() -- the URL field carries ZERO sensitivity annotation despite being one of the single most revealing fields in the entire capture surface (health searches, financial sites, adult content, everything a browsing history reveals about a person).

4. ZERO CONSUMERS: grepped every SensitivityHint reference workspace-wide -- every hit is the type definition, a source contract SETTING the field, or macro plumbing (crate/sinex-macros/src/source_record.rs) carrying it through generated structs. No API handler, no privacy engine code (event_engine/policy.rs never reads it), no CLI/sinexctl tooling ever reads sensitivity_hints back out anywhere. This is the third instance this session of the 'declared metadata, zero enforcement' architectural pattern, alongside DisclosureContext (sinex-wtkk) and occurrence_identity doc-string drift.

Relates to and reframes sinex-4kbm's point 3 (Secret-category context-scoping default) -- see that bead's 2026-08-11 amendment for the fuller architectural analysis: ProcessingContext is really a capture-modality taxonomy, and SensitivityHint was presumably meant to be the complementary content-sensitivity axis, but since it has zero consumers ProcessingContext ends up carrying the whole weight of both jobs it wasn't designed for.
acceptance_criteria: Either give SensitivityHint (or a successor mechanism with real per-field, not per-record, granularity) an actual consumer -- e.g. a sinexctl/API surface that lists fields carrying a given hint so an operator can review/bind rules to them, matching the type's own original stated intent -- or retire it and fold its intent directly into per-field rule scoping. At minimum, populate it correctly on browser/history.rs's URL field and any other high-sensitivity field currently at Vec::new() before treating this as resolved either way.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text:
CORRECTION 2026-08-11, verified by reading further before the operator acted on this: my 'zero consumers anywhere' claim was WRONG for the per-field mechanism specifically -- retracting that part.

A real, separate, per-field privacy metadata system already exists and IS wired to a live consumer: crate/sinex-primitives/src/parser/declarative.rs:223 (DeclarativeFieldSpec.sensitivity: Vec<SensitivityHint>, per FIELD in the declarative source-definition DSL) flows through crate/sinex-macros/src/source_record.rs:490-509 (collect_field_privacy_metadata) into ParserFieldPrivacyMetadata { field_name, effective_privacy_context, sensitivity_hints, ... } -- genuinely per-field, not per-record. This IS consumed: crate/sinexd/src/sources/privacy_coverage.rs's build_privacy_coverage_matrix() reads it via field_privacy_metadata() (dispatch.rs:52,70-71) and generates a real committed artifact, crate/sinexd/docs/sources/privacy-coverage.generated.json.

What's still genuinely broken (narrower and more precise than my original claim):

1. This per-field mechanism ONLY auto-populates for DECLARATIVE-macro-based source contracts. Confirmed via grep: 31 of ~32 source contracts implement MaterialParser IMPERATIVELY (impl MaterialParser for X directly, hand-written, not the declarative DSL) -- and of those 31, only ONE (atuin_history.rs:232-234) overrides field_privacy_metadata() at all, and even that one just delegates to an underlying declarative-macro-derived record type. The other 30 imperative parsers -- including browser/history.rs, the URL-field example -- get a silent EMPTY default. privacy_coverage.rs's own generated caveat text confirms this exact gap: 'field-level metadata unavailable; imperative parsers must declare rows before coverage can be inferred.'

2. Even where fully populated, the matrix is explicitly self-documented as audit-only, not enforcement: 'static matrix only; does not apply DB/user privacy policy... records safe-surface evidence, not a global payload-redaction guarantee' (privacy_coverage.rs:135-138). So even a source WITH complete field-level metadata gets zero automatic benefit toward actual redaction -- nothing reads this matrix to suggest or auto-bind privacy.rules scoped to a flagged (source, field_path).

3. The RECORD-level sensitivity_hints field (the one my original finding focused on) is a genuinely lossy, separate, redundant flattening of the same per-field data (collect_sensitivity_hints, source_record.rs:476-488) -- it throws away exactly the granularity the parallel per-field mechanism already preserves. This part of the original finding stands.

See the follow-up epic bead for the actual scoped redesign work this correction implies.

title: silent, undetectable size-cap drops: document_parser (4MiB) discards the entire document with only a log line, journald (256KiB) drops the whole entry as a parse error -- same 'operator had no idea this existed' shape as the ts_orig lower bound
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via a dedicated audit for arbitrary hardcoded limits, prompted directly by the operator's surprise at discovering the ts_orig_lower_bound_unix default (sinex-oq7j). This is the closest match to that same failure shape found in the sweep, and arguably worse: the ts_orig bound at least routes rejected data to the DLQ (visible via sinexctl ops dlq list); these two caps leave NOTHING but a log line.

1. HIGH CONFIDENCE, live-reachable: crate/sinexd/src/automata/document_parser.rs:45,48,197-205,337-344 -- MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES = 4 * 1024 * 1024 (4MiB). Hit at two call sites: the Dendron-markdown/knowledgebase-vault corpus (line 197) and the terminal-output corpus (line 337, stdout.len() from a command.canonical event). Both paths return Ok(Vec::new()) on exceeding the cap -- the PARENT event (document.ingested / command.canonical) was already admitted fine, but document-parser (confirmed live/registered in automata/registry.rs:157-158) silently emits ZERO derived output, with only a tracing::warn!(...'Document exceeds size cap, skipping'). A large pasted chat export saved as a markdown note, a long financial CSV pasted into a document, or capturing the stdout of any command producing >4MiB (a big cat, find /, build log, git log -p) loses the ENTIRE document/chunk set with no operator-facing signal at all -- not even a DLQ entry. Terminal-output capture via the shell canonicalizer is confirmed live (corroborated by sinex-kix9).

2. MEDIUM CONFIDENCE: crate/sinexd/src/sources/source_contracts/system/journald.rs:28,124-128 -- MAX_JOURNAL_LINE_BYTES = 256*1024 (256KiB). Any single journald JSON record (not just the MESSAGE field -- the WHOLE journalctl -o json line, all metadata fields included) over 256KiB is dropped via a hard Err (parse failure), not just the message content. A long single-line structured-JSON application log, a giant stack trace piped through systemd-cat, or verbose service output logged without newlines would be lost entirely. Confidence is medium because it's unverified whether systemd-journald's own field/entry limits (SystemMaxUse/rate-limiting/LineMax) already truncate before this ever sees the bytes -- worth an empirical check (journalctl -o json | jq '. | length' distribution) before prioritizing, since if journald itself already caps around a similar value this check may be largely redundant rather than the actual loss point.
acceptance_criteria: At minimum, both size-cap drops should route through the same visibility mechanism as other admission-time rejections (DLQ, or an explicit skipped-content event/counter) rather than a bare log line -- matching the standard this project already applies elsewhere (schema-reject-to-DLQ, plausibility-reject-to-DLQ). Consider whether 4MiB is actually the right document-parser cap given this project's stated comprehensive-capture mission (large pasted content, build logs, long CSVs are all plausible legitimate inputs) -- if raised, verify memory/resource impact given this host's documented earlyoom-at-<15%-free behavior. For journald: first empirically verify whether journald's own limits already truncate before this cap is ever the actual loss point.

title: no page-level data-corruption detection anywhere in the deployment stack -- Postgres data_checksums off, btrfs nodatacow disables filesystem checksums too, no scrub, no app-level integrity verification -- nothing would catch silent corruption during or after the imminent full re-import
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via infrastructure/transport/tooling config audit, verified across three independent layers (a standing, cross-cutting deployment gap, not a code regression):

1. PostgreSQL data_checksums is not enabled: neither the dev initdb invocation (xtask/src/infra/services/postgres.rs:193-202, no -k/--data-checksums) nor the NixOS-managed prod cluster (nixos/modules/database.nix, no initdbArgs set at all) turns this on.
2. Filesystem-level protection is also off: /realm/project/sinnix/modules/services/sinex/bridge.nix:214-219 places sinex's Postgres data directory on the nodatacow @sinex btrfs subvolume -- the module's own comment explicitly says 'the nodatacow @sinex subvol has no btrfs checksums, so FPW [full_page_writes] is the remaining torn-page defense.' nodatacow disables COW AND checksumming together on btrfs (they're coupled) -- a deliberate, documented tradeoff at the time (avoiding COW fragmentation on a write-hot DB), but full_page_writes only protects against torn writes during a crash MID-WRITE, not against bit-rot/silent corruption of already-committed pages.
3. No pg_verify_checksums, no periodic scrub, and no application-level content-hash verification of core.events/audit.archived_events rows exists anywhere in the codebase.

Net effect: a corrupted page in a compressed chunk (where blast radius per page is LARGER than uncompressed, since columnstore packs many rows per page) has no verification layer between it and a reader. Depending on where corruption lands, TimescaleDB's decompression may throw a structural error (loud, safe) or -- for corruption that doesn't violate the compressed stream's syntax, e.g. a bit-flip inside a delta-encoded integer array -- may silently decompress to a WRONG VALUE with no error at all. This is not a regression -- it was clearly a conscious tradeoff (nodatacow's performance win vs detection loss) -- but it means there is currently NO WAY TO DETECT that the imminent full re-import itself corrupted data on write, or that anything corrupts on read afterward. No existing bead covers data-checksum/corruption-detection posture specifically (sinex-mvs2/sinex-u5g are adjacent but don't mention integrity/checksums).
acceptance_criteria: Decide deliberately whether to accept this tradeoff going forward (nodatacow performance vs corruption-detection) or add a mitigation -- e.g. enabling Postgres data_checksums (independent of the filesystem layer, catches page-level corruption on read with a real perf cost worth measuring), a periodic pg_verify_checksums / btrfs scrub-equivalent, or application-level content hashing on a sample of rows. At minimum, document this as a known, accepted gap so a future 'why did we lose data' investigation doesn't waste time assuming it would have been caught.

title: xtask dev-NATS port derivation collides across checkouts (100-slot hash) and the stale-process cleanup kills WHATEVER process holds that port with zero checkout-ownership check -- one checkout's xtask infra start can silently kill another's live NATS server
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via infrastructure/transport/tooling config audit. Directly relevant given this project's own documented workflow of concurrent agent worktrees/parallel subagent fanout sessions.

nats_port_for_checkout() (xtask/src/infra/stack.rs:105-113) derives the dev NATS port as 4222 + (SHA256(checkout_root_path)[0] % 100) -- a deterministic hash into only 100 possible ports, with NO collision detection, no retry, and no bind-then-fallback (contrast the ephemeral per-test sandbox NATS, which correctly does true OS-assigned port allocation via bind-to-0-and-read-back). Two different worktree paths can and, per the birthday paradox, WILL with non-trivial probability (~10% with 5 concurrently-active checkouts, ~26% with 8) hash to the same port.

Worse than a mere bind failure -- ACTIVE FRIENDLY FIRE: NatsManager::start() (xtask/src/infra/services/nats.rs:306-344) unconditionally calls cleanup_stale_nats_processes(port, verbose) on every start, which does a SYSTEM-WIDE pgrep -f nats-server, checks via lsof whether each found PID is bound to the target port, and if uses_target_port is true ALONE (line 45: if uses_target_port || is_old) SIGTERMs then SIGKILLs that process -- with ZERO check for whether the process belongs to THIS checkout. If two checkouts collide on the same hash-derived port, starting or restarting one FORCIBLY KILLS THE OTHER'S live, actively-serving dev NATS daemon, corrupting or interrupting whatever dev session/test run that other checkout had in flight. The cleanup function's own doc comment frames this as intentional ('helps prevent port-already-in-use errors and cleans up accumulated processes') but has no notion of checkout ownership at all.

Concrete repro: two worktrees whose paths hash to the same 4222+n offset, both running xtask infra start / xtask run core --bg in the same session -- the second one silently kills the first's NATS server.
acceptance_criteria: Bind-and-verify with fallback-to-next-port for dev NATS, matching the pattern already correctly used in the ephemeral sandbox NATS (xtask/src/sandbox/nats/ephemeral.rs). At minimum, scope cleanup_stale_nats_processes' kill decision to PIDs recorded in THIS checkout's own pid file, never a global port-based pgrep scan that can hit another checkout's process.

title: documents.search (LIVE, reachable via MCP): trigram fallback is arithmetically unreachable for real chunks yet forces a full table scan every miss; pagination past FTS exhaustion silently switches ranking systems mid-page-sequence; ranking has no length normalization
description:
Discovered 2026-08-11 via derived-intelligence algorithmic-quality audit (Opus), MEASURED against the live dev Postgres (not just reasoned statically). This is the one part of the derived-intelligence layer that is actually LIVE and reachable today (documents.search RPC, MCP sinex_documents_search) -- the embedding/vector lane and 4-stage entity chain are both dormant/default-off, so this is the highest-value finding in the report.

F1 -- trigram fallback threshold is unreachable AND costly. crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/document_search.rs:34,384 uses similarity(dc.text, ) > 0.15 (TRIGRAM_SIMILARITY_THRESHOLD, comment says 'catches common typos'). pg_trgm's similarity() is the SYMMETRIC Jaccard ratio -- the denominator is dominated by the chunk's own trigram count, and chunks are paragraph-sized up to 64KiB. MEASURED on the live DB against a realistic 862-char paragraph with query terms present verbatim: similarity('informer', chunk)=0.0207, similarity('informer cache resync', chunk)=0.0482, similarity('readiness probe health endpoint termination grace', chunk)=0.1149 -- ALL below the 0.15 threshold despite every query term being present in the chunk. A typo LOWERS the numerator while the denominator stays chunk-sized, so the documented 'catches typos' purpose is unachievable as implemented. Compounding: similarity(x,y)>c is not an indexable form -- confirmed via EXPLAIN with enable_seqscan=off forcing a Seq Scan computing trigram sets over up-to-64KiB texts on every miss, versus the correct word_similarity(query,text) %> operator form (also measured: word_similarity('informer cache resync', chunk)=0.70), which DOES use the index the module's own docstring claims is used.

F2 -- pagination silently switches ranking systems mid-sequence. document_search.rs:184-196 runs the FTS query WITH the caller's OFFSET, and treats 'zero FTS rows AT THIS OFFSET' as 'FTS matched nothing at all', falling into the trigram path at the SAME offset against a COMPLETELY DIFFERENT result set. Concrete: query matches 3 chunks by FTS, limit=2 -- page 1 and 2 return FTS rows correctly, but page 3 (offset=3, past FTS's own result count) falls into trigram_fallback AT OFFSET 3 OF THE TRIGRAM RESULT SET, which (per F1) is almost always empty -- so today this mostly costs two full table scans per exhausted page rather than returning wrong rows, but fixing F1 alone turns F2 into a live correctness bug (wrong rows returned on late pages). Also: search_mode is reported as 'trigram_fallback' even when the trigram path itself found nothing -- the field misdescribes what actually ran.

F3 -- ts_rank_cd runs with normalization=0 (no division by document length), so a 64KiB terminal-log chunk that incidentally repeats a term outranks a 200-char note that is actually about it -- 'most relevant first' does not hold as implemented. Ordering IS fully deterministic otherwise (ORDER BY score DESC, document_id ASC, chunk_index ASC -- verified solid).

F3b -- SearchMode::Vector/Hybrid and VectorSearchParams are unreachable dead wire-states: search() never reads vector_params, the API handler hardcodes vector_params:None, and these two SearchMode variants are never constructed anywhere in the workspace -- so 'search_mode: vector|hybrid' is a documented possible response value that cannot ever occur. Per this project's 'unfinished is not obsolete' doctrine, complete this rather than deleting it, but consumers should not be told those modes exist yet.
acceptance_criteria: Replace the trigram-fallback predicate with word_similarity(query, text) %> threshold (index-usable via the existing trgm index, asymmetric and correct for short-query-vs-long-document matching). Fix pagination to not silently switch ranking systems mid-sequence -- either compute both FTS and trigram result sets once and merge/dedupe properly, or clearly signal a ranking-system change to the caller rather than silently blending offsets across two different result sets. Add length normalization to ts_rank_cd (normalization=32 or =2). Either wire vector_params/SearchMode::Vector|Hybrid to something real, or don't document them as reachable response values yet.

VectorSearchParams (document_search.rs) has ZERO constructions anywhere in the entire workspace -- not just SearchMode::Vector/Hybrid being unconstructed, the PARAMETER STRUCT itself has no caller anywhere, including all 13 test call sites, which all pass None. This is the plumbing gap between this bead's search-quality bugs and the separately-audited embedding/hybrid-search algorithm bugs (sinex-bksb, sinex-yypi) -- documents.search declares a vector/hybrid capability on its result contract that literally no code path can produce or supply parameters for.
