title: Remaining source-adapter findings: dbus default rules capture nothing, udev watches wrong path, library mtime fabrication, hledger date formats, weechat timezone
description:
Batch of findings from the 2026-08-10 remaining-sources audit (bash/text-history timestamp handling was verified CORRECT, no fabricated ts_orig -- do not re-litigate):

1. system.dbus's default match rules (dbus_stream.rs:81-101) subscribe to interfaces (UPower.Device, bluez.Device1, NetworkManager.Device, UDisks2.*, mpris.MediaPlayer2.Player) that modern implementations don't actually emit signals on -- real state changes go through DBus.Properties.PropertiesChanged/ObjectManager.InterfacesAdded, neither of which is subscribed. Verified live: 25s of dbus-monitor on both system and session bus produced ~1000s of PropertiesChanged/UnitNew/UnitRemoved events and ZERO matches to any default rule -- this source captures essentially nothing as currently configured. Compounding: if PropertiesChanged WERE captured, classify_dbus_event (system/dbus.rs:64-84) checks interface.contains('DBus') before any payload-specific branch, so it would all misfile as generic method.called anyway. Also dead NixOS config knobs: sources.nix:1547-1571 exposes systemd_config/dbus_config fields (monitor_services, include_interfaces, etc) that have ZERO readers anywhere in crate/ -- operator-facing settings that silently do nothing, including the exact include_interfaces knob that would fix this.

2. system.udev's device-type inference (udev.rs:57-70) is written for /sys path substrings (/usb, /block, /net, /input) but the adapter actually watches /dev (recursive:false) -- on this host only 4/201 /dev entries could ever match, and only as directories, so every real device event classifies as DeviceType::Other. Module doc still claims 'over /sys'.

3. library.rs:322-331 fabricates an mtime: when file modified() or the nanos conversion fails, it substitutes Timestamp::now() but STILL emits TimingEvidence::InferredMtime{mtime:<now>} -- presenting a synthesized clock as real filesystem evidence. The adjacent Err arm correctly uses Atemporal; this fallback should too.

4. hledger parser (finance.rs) only recognizes YYYY-MM-DD dates (:183) -- ledger/hledger also commonly use YYYY/MM/DD and YYYY.MM.DD, and a slash-dated journal parses to ZERO transactions SILENTLY. Also only matches 'include ' (:134), missing !include and tab-separated forms. Transaction anchors are ordinal indices, not byte offsets (:~425), so anchors shift when a transaction is inserted mid-file. No real hledger journal exists on this host to verify against live data.

5. weechat.rs:53 does dt.assume_utc() on WeeChat's local-time log timestamps -- every IRC message timestamp is shifted by the host's UTC offset and labeled Intrinsic (claiming full confidence in a value that's actually wrong by the timezone offset). No real WeeChat logs on this host to verify against.
acceptance_criteria: 1. dbus default match rules actually subscribe to PropertiesChanged/InterfacesAdded (the real signal shape modern DBus services use), classify_dbus_event dispatches on the actual changed property/interface rather than defaulting generic method.called for anything DBus-related, and the dead systemd_config/dbus_config NixOS knobs either get real readers or are removed. 2. udev either watches /sys (matching its own classification logic) or the classification logic is rewritten for /dev's actual entry shape. 3. library.rs's fallback mtime path uses Atemporal like its sibling Err arm, not a fabricated InferredMtime. 4. hledger date parsing accepts the common slash/dot date formats hledger/ledger actually use in practice, and anchors use real byte offsets. 5. weechat timestamps are parsed with the correct local timezone (or explicitly flagged low-confidence if the true zone is unknowable) rather than a wrong-by-construction UTC assumption labeled Intrinsic.

title: API/gateway medium findings: SSE reconnect doesn't resume, unauthenticated health/ready leak DB errors, SSE bypasses rate limiting
description:
Batch of 3 related MEDIUM findings from the 2026-08-10 API/gateway audit (the chokepoint itself -- RpcRegistry::dispatch's scope enforcement, role derivation, token handling -- was independently verified SOLID, no findings there):

1. SSE accepts Last-Event-ID but never actually resumes from it: sse_handler.rs:166-182 parses/validates the header, but SubscriptionSlot::new (sse_bus.rs:153-155) uses resume_from ONLY to seed a recent-delivered dedup set with that single id -- there is no NATS/DB backfill of missed events. Events published while a client was disconnected are silently absent from the resumed stream, with no gap signal (SseMessage::Gap only fires for live channel-full drops, sse_bus.rs:224-229, never for reconnect). Browser EventSource clients auto-send this header and will incorrectly assume a true resume happened.

2. /health and /ready are unauthenticated (rpc_server.rs:926-927) AND /ready's error path leaks raw sqlx Display text: service_container.rs:488 builds format!('Database ping failed: {error}') from raw sqlx error Display, returned verbatim in the unauthenticated response body (handlers/system.rs:62) -- the exact 'Display may leak paths/SQL' pattern this project's own CLAUDE.md flags as internal-only. /ready also runs a DB query plus a NATS round-trip per unauthenticated request with no rate limiter.

3. SSE subscriptions bypass rate limiting entirely -- handle_sse_stream never calls state.rate_limiter. The only bound is a process-global MAX_ACTIVE_SUBSCRIPTIONS=512 (sse_bus.rs:37) with no per-token share, so a single readonly token opening 512 SSE connections locks out every other subscriber.
acceptance_criteria: 1. SSE reconnect either performs a real backfill from the resume point (NATS replay or DB query) or explicitly signals a gap to the client rather than silently omitting the missed window. 2. /ready's error response uses a sanitized public-facing message (matching the public_payload() pattern used elsewhere), not raw error Display text; consider adding a lightweight rate limit even for unauthenticated health endpoints. 3. SSE subscription creation is rate-limited per-token, or MAX_ACTIVE_SUBSCRIPTIONS is enforced per-token rather than globally.
close_reason: Duplicate of sinex-7ffg (filed 19 min later, same audit pass): findings 1-3 (SSE Last-Event-ID doesn't resume, /health+/ready unauthenticated error-text leak, SSE bypasses rate limiting) are near-verbatim identical, and 7ffg is the strict superset (adds 3 more: distributed rate-limiter window-reset gap, SSE gap-frame id/seq mismatch, native_messaging default-role inversion). Closing as duplicate rather than tracking the same findings twice; all follow-up work belongs on sinex-7ffg.

title: Replay minor findings: 24h default window clock mismatch, wall-clock non-determinism in interval_lift replay
description:
Two smaller findings from the 2026-08-10 replay-execution audit:

1. crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/replay.rs:49-57 silently defaults an unwindowed replay scope to the last 24h; build_filter_query (:69-73) filters on ts_coided, yet that same window end gets shipped downstream as a WORLD-TIME horizon TimeHorizon::Historical{end_time} (replay_writer.rs:493-495). For historical imports where ts_coided (interpretation time) diverges heavily from ts_orig (when it actually happened), these are genuinely different clocks -- a 24h-ts_coided-windowed replay scope combined with a ts_orig-interpreted horizon downstream can produce a mismatched/confusing scope boundary.

2. crate/sinexd/src/automata/interval_lift.rs:967,989 pass Timestamp::now() as max_end_time (clamped at :632). An interval whose observed end exceeded processing wall-time at ORIGINAL processing time will re-derive with a LONGER end_time/duration on replay (since 'now' at replay time is later than 'now' at original processing time) -- genuine replay non-determinism baked directly into a derived payload, violating the general expectation that replaying the same input through the same code produces the same output.
acceptance_criteria: Item 1: the 24h-default window and the downstream TimeHorizon it feeds use a consistent clock (both ts_coided-based or both ts_orig-based), or the mismatch is documented as intentional with clear rationale. Item 2: interval_lift's max_end_time clamp uses a value derived from the input data (or the replay's own declared horizon) rather than wall-clock Timestamp::now(), so replay is deterministic for this automaton.

title: Privacy: small correctness items from the 2026-08-10 redaction audit (non-string fields, silent no-ops, stale invariant comment)
description:
Batch of smaller findings from the 2026-08-10 pre-wipe privacy audit, each independently minor but worth fixing together:
1. Stale invariant comment: crate/sinex-db/src/postgres_copy.rs:739-742 and crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/events/persistence/types.rs:94-98 both claim content_hash is computed 'BEFORE redact_batch could mutate payload' -- false, redact_batch runs at persist.rs:630 and the hash (admission.rs:1094) hashes the already-redacted payload. Behavior is self-consistent (supersession compares redacted-vs-redacted), but the documented sinex-w1w7 invariant doesn't match what ships -- fix the comment or verify/fix the actual intended invariant.
2. Non-string payload fields never redacted: PrivacyEngine::process_json (sinex-primitives/src/privacy/engine.rs:287-315) recurses into strings/arrays/objects only -- a numeric {"ssn": 123456789} or a PII-bearing object KEY passes through untouched.
3. Silent no-op on unresolved field paths: apply_scoped_engine_to_json (event_engine/policy.rs:1316-1324) uses value.pointer_mut(...) and does nothing (no warn, no metric) when absent -- a payload-schema rename silently disables an operator's redact rule with zero signal.
4. External recognizers skip nested fields: apply_external_rule_to_json (policy.rs:1035-1044) only processes a field-bound target when it's JsonValue::String -- an object/array at that pointer passes unchanged. Local rules recurse; inconsistent.
5. Latent, no live impact: policy_seed_rule silently drops Matcher::All/Any builtins (catalog.rs:62) and discards rule contexts (compile_rules sets contexts: Vec::new(), policy.rs:490) -- no builtin currently uses All/Any so this hasn't bitten anyone yet.
acceptance_criteria: Each of the 5 items either fixed or explicitly triaged/deferred with rationale. At minimum: item 3 (silent no-op) should get an operator-visible warn/metric so a schema rename doesn't silently disable redaction with zero signal -- this is the one with the worst 'looks fine, isn't' failure mode of the batch.

comments.text: Additional small finding 2026-08-11 via verification-tooling meta-audit, same function family as this bead's items: Presidio-backed rules parse entity_type and score from the recognizer response (PresidioAnalyzeResponse in event_engine/policy.rs) but both fields are #[allow(dead_code)] -- only start/end offsets are used. replace_external_spans/external_replacement derive the redaction label purely from rule.name, never from the detected entity type, so a rule configured with multiple entity types (PERSON, CREDIT_CARD, EMAIL_ADDRESS in one rule's entities list) redacts all three to the identical <RULENAME> token, and the recognizer's own per-match confidence score is discarded entirely -- the privacy engine has a confidence model elsewhere and this is the one external-recognizer path that receives a real confidence signal and throws it away.

title: Unlimited-scan negative-control test for sinex-2n9 pacing deterministically caps backlog at 40, cause unidentified
description:
While building sinex-2n9 (historical-import pacing), a companion negative-control test (unlimited_historical_scan_lets_backlog_grow_past_paced_bound, proving RateBudget::unlimited() genuinely lets backlog exceed the paced bound, as the inverse of the paced positive-control test) failed deterministically: observed_max backlog capped at EXACTLY 40 across multiple runs on fresh sandboxes, including after widening the tail sampling window from 3s to 8s (ruling out a sampling-race explanation, the value was byte-for-byte identical both times, not just close). The pacing implementation itself was independently verified correct via direct code review. RateBudget::unlimited() (crate/sinex-primitives/src/pacing.rs) nulls both rate and backlog threshold fields. merged_with_override does a whole-struct override, not field-level merge, per its own passing unit test merged_override_wins_when_present. BacklogGate::from_budget returns None for an unlimited budget. ScanPacer::after_batch (crate/sinexd/src/runtime/pacing.rs) skips the wait_for_capacity call entirely when the gate is None. The positive-control test (paced_historical_scan_holds_raw_backlog_below_threshold) passes reliably. TOTAL_RECORDS in the test fixture is 240, the observed cap of exactly 40 does not match any configured threshold in either test (paced test used backlog_pause_threshold=15/resume=5, the failing test explicitly set RateBudget::unlimited()). The test was removed from crate/sinexd/src/runtime/parser/adapter_source_test.rs (see the comment left in its place) rather than shipped broken or silently ignored (this codebase has no ignore-attribute precedent).

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run the negative-control test unlimited_historical_scan_lets_backlog_grow_past_paced_bound on a fresh sandbox.
2. Observe observed_max backlog caps at exactly 40, deterministically, across multiple runs.
3. Widen the tail sampling window from 3s to 8s and rerun -- observe the value is byte-for-byte identical (40), ruling out a sampling-race explanation.
4. Read crate/sinex-primitives/src/pacing.rs's RateBudget::unlimited() -- confirm it nulls both rate and backlog threshold fields, and BacklogGate::from_budget returns None for an unlimited budget, so nothing in the reviewed pacing code should impose a 40-item cap -- root cause of the observed 40 is not yet identified.
acceptance_criteria: Root-cause the deterministic 40-cap in the negative-control scenario (see removed-test comment in adapter_source_test.rs for exact repro steps: real JetStreamConsumer with WorkQueue-retention stream, a slow simulated puller at 30ms/msg, RateBudget::unlimited() passed to scan_historical, sampling raw_events_consumer_pending().num_pending every 20ms). Investigate: (a) whether num_pending as reported by consumer_info() has some interaction with max_ack_pending:0 client-default that server-side resolves to a smaller effective cap than expected for WorkQueue-retention streams specifically, (b) whether the tee/publish path in settle_and_publish_events has its own bounded concurrency/channel capacity independent of RateBudget that naturally throttles publish rate to roughly match the 33msg/s consumer, (c) whether another stream/consumer with a similar name is being queried by mistake. Once root-caused, either fix the real bug (if backlog truly cannot exceed 40 under production conditions, unlimited is not actually unlimited and needs a real fix) or restore a corrected version of the negative-control test with an accurate methodology.

title: fn_document_projection DO UPDATE (documents + newly-fixed document_chunks) has no ts_orig/occurrence-quality ordering guard -- shares the systemic unconditional-overwrite pattern already flagged elsewhere
description:
PR #2571 (fix/sinexd, merged 59edc0505) correctly fixed sinex-audit-docchunks-replay-redaction-bypass by changing core.fn_document_projection()s document.chunked branch from ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING to ON CONFLICT (document_id, chunk_index) DO UPDATE SET text=EXCLUDED.text, ... -- matching the pre-existing document.parsed -> core.documents branch, which was already DO UPDATE. Both branches now share the same property: the AFTER INSERT trigger fires at core.events INSERT time and unconditionally overwrites core.documents/core.document_chunks with whatever arrived LAST in insertion order, with no comparison against ts_orig (occurrence time) or any revision/quality signal on the incoming vs stored row. This is the identical anti-pattern already identified as a HIGH-severity systemic bug class in this same pre-wipe audit campaign: sinex-audit-outoforder-pattern (closed via PR #2556, 6 Rust automata fixed to guard on ts_orig before overwriting last-seen state) and sinex-audit-telemetry-health-view-staleorder (still open, same pattern in a SQL view). fn_document_projection is a SQL trigger, not a Rust automaton, and was not in scope for either of those beads, and is not covered by any currently-open bead. Concrete failure sequence: two overlapping replay/backfill operations touching the same document occurrence, where the run producing the OLDER/lower-quality text (e.g. a broader unrelated backfill still using a stale privacy ruleset) happens to have its document.chunked event ADMITTED (inserted into core.events, which is what fires this trigger) after a separate, already-corrected replay for the same chunk -- possible given at-least-once NATS delivery/redelivery and the documented in-flight emission-ordering gaps already tracked under bd epic r6d. The result would silently reintroduce stale/under-redacted text into core.document_chunks.text after a correct replay had already fixed it, with no error or staleness signal -- structurally the same operator-facing failure mode PR #2571 just closed for the DO NOTHING case, reopened via a different ordering path.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Confirm PR #2571 (merged 59edc0505) changed core.fn_document_projection()'s document.chunked branch from ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING to ON CONFLICT (document_id, chunk_index) DO UPDATE, matching the pre-existing document.parsed -> core.documents DO UPDATE branch.
2. Read the trigger definition -- confirm it fires on core.events INSERT and unconditionally overwrites core.documents/core.document_chunks with whatever arrived LAST in insertion order, with no comparison against ts_orig or any revision/quality signal.
3. Insert two document.chunked (or document.parsed) events for the same document/chunk out of ts_orig order (a later-occurring, lower-quality event inserted after an earlier-occurring, higher-quality one).
4. Observe the projection reflects whichever arrived last in insertion order, not the higher-quality/more-recent-by-occurrence-time row -- the same anti-pattern already fixed for 6 Rust automata in sinex-audit-outoforder-pattern (PR #2556), but not yet applied to this SQL trigger-driven projection path.
acceptance_criteria: core.fn_document_projection() (both the document.parsed and document.chunked branches) either compares an ordering signal (ts_orig on the incoming core.events row vs. the currently-stored projection row, or an equivalent monotonic revision marker) before overwriting, or an explicit design note records why insertion-order-wins is acceptable here (e.g. because upstream replay orchestration already guarantees serialized, non-overlapping replay windows per document) -- in which case that guarantee should be verified and cited, not assumed. VERIFY: a test that inserts two document.chunked events for the same (document_id, chunk_index) out of ts_orig order (the chronologically-older-content event admitted SECOND) demonstrates the projection ends up with the correct (by whatever policy is chosen) text, not silently whichever arrived last.
notes: Found during independent adversarial review of PR #2571/#2572 (pre-wipe hardening pass, 2026-08-02). The PR itself is correct and necessary -- DO NOTHING was a strictly worse, deterministic bug (leaked text never self-heals at all). This finding is about the residual risk in the DO UPDATE it (correctly) adopted, inherited from the pre-existing document.parsed branch and now extended to document_chunks. Lower urgency than the closed redaction-bypass bug: requires two overlapping replay operations to race, whereas the fixed bug fired on every ordinary single replay.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] Testable per its own Steps to Reproduce: insert two document.chunked events out of ts_orig order, assert projection reflects the higher-quality one, not last-inserted. No test yet.

title: scribe-tap keylog source: portfolio verdict + staged JSONL import contract
description: The constellation doctrine (operator global CLAUDE.md project diagram) states sinex captures events from scribe-tap, and target-vision report/data-landscape.md lists it as a source ("5.77M keystroke lines across 155 daily JSONL files — Keylog ingestor (designed, not built)"). Live evidence 2026-08-02: /realm/data/captures/keylog/logs holds 290 daily JSONL files, 1.5 GB, current through today — the capture side runs; the sinex side does not exist. Verified: no source contract (nixos/modules/source-catalog.generated.json has 65 entries, none keylog/keystroke; rg keylog|scribe-tap|keystroke over crate/ + nixos/ matches only threat-model prose), and no bead (bd sql LIKE scribe/keylog/keystroke returns only rkv.12/k53x tangents). Old GH #1065/#1071 framed keylog as a privacy-gated source decision; that decision never migrated to beads, and because keylog has no contract at all it is invisible to the sinex-5j8 capture-domain census (which enumerates existing contracts). Scope: (1) decision leg — record a keep/defer/prune verdict for the keylog domain alongside the 5j8 census; (2) if keep: DirectoryWalk/StaticFileAdapter contract over the daily JSONL files, maximum privacy_tier with sensitivity declaration per sinex-rkv.12 posture, deployment through the sinex-stm static-import glue, equivalence keys for re-import idempotence, and a named consumer derivation per catalog extension rule 1 (candidate: typing-activity intervals feeding attention composites, sinex-a4w.3). The material is backfillable forever (daily files persist), so per the rkv irreversibility note there is no capture urgency — P3, not P2.
design: Follow the rkv.6 template: land on the ORIGINAL capture artifacts (daily JSONL under /realm/data/captures/keylog/logs), never on derived summaries. Occurrence identity from (file, line/offset) anchors; the daily-file shape fits the existing DirectoryWalk adapter. Privacy posture is a capture-instrument declaration (rkv.12), not a redaction feature.
acceptance_criteria: A recorded verdict (bead note or 5j8 census row) exists for the keylog domain. If keep: contract + binding registered (catalog row present); events queryable on the live host from a staged import of at least one real daily file; re-import of the same file produces no duplicate occurrences; sensitivity declaration and blast-radius statement recorded per rkv.12. If defer/prune: rationale recorded and this bead closed as deferred citing the census row.
notes: Filed 2026-08-02 from sinex-target-vision triage (report/data-landscape.md; old GH #1065/#1071 did not survive the beads migration).

title: Live browser capture client: WebExtension + qutebrowser producer for browser.capture_batch
description: The server surface for live browser capture is fully built and has zero producers. browser.capture_batch RPC exists (crate/sinexd/src/api/handlers/browser.rs; BrowserNavigationObservedPayload / BrowserTabActivatedPayload / BrowserDownloadObservedPayload; request types in crate/sinex-primitives/src/rpc/browser.rs) behind native-messaging auth with per-extension capability ACLs and per-extension rate limiting (crate/sinexd/src/api/native_messaging.rs, SINEX_NATIVE_MESSAGING_CAPABILITIES). Verified 2026-08-02: rg capture_batch / native_messaging across sinex and sinnix matches only the server, its tests, and the RPC catalog — no WebExtension, no qutebrowser userscript, no client of any kind. No bead mentions capture_batch, WebExtension, or native messaging (bd sql LIKE checks). Grounded in target-vision report/data-landscape.md: "No live browser capture: Gateway has native messaging support (server-side ready) but the WebExtension client does not exist yet — #847" and the qutebrowser primary-browser live gap (#1449); neither GitHub issue survived the 2026-07-03 beads migration. Current browser capture is snapshot-only: Chrome via the manual Sky History export (multi-day lag noted in data-landscape §Data Quality) and qutebrowser via history.sqlite snapshot (browser.history contract). Scope: a minimal Chromium WebExtension speaking native messaging to the existing endpoint, plus a qutebrowser leg (userscript/IPC hitting the same RPC), deployment glue in nixos/sinnix, and occurrence identity / equivalence keys so the live leg and the snapshot leg dedup per the sinex-908 idempotence matrix. Relates: sinex-rkv.3 (browser content crawl is a consumer of live visit events), sinex-rkv.16 (historical backfill), closed sinex-60r (attention-source quality).
design: Client artifacts can live in-repo (a small extension dir + qutebrowser userscript) with the native-messaging host manifest generated by the NixOS module; reuse the existing extension-id capability ACL rather than inventing new auth. Live leg registers as its own binding on the existing browser.history contract or a sibling live contract — decide against the catalog, do not fork the web namespace.
acceptance_criteria: A live browser session produces browser navigation/tab events on the live host through browser.capture_batch (per-source event counts via sinexctl sources / store analytics); the producing extension identity is authenticated through the native-messaging capability ACL; overlap between the live leg and the browser.history snapshot leg creates no duplicate occurrences (equivalence-key evidence recorded); the catalog carries a binding row for the live leg; deployment wiring is committed with the client build/install path documented.
notes: Filed 2026-08-02 from sinex-target-vision triage (report/data-landscape.md). Old GH #847/#1449 did not survive the beads migration.

title: sinex-db database test suite: intermittent uk_derivation_product_event_output duplicate-key failure (6/377)
description:
Discovered incidentally during PR #2565 verification (sinex-audit-forbidden-pattern-blind-spots / sinex-96fg fix): a full xtask test -p sinex-db --all run surfaced an unrelated pre-existing flake -- a uk_derivation_product_event_output unique-constraint duplicate-key violation in 6 of 377 sinex-db::database tests. Not investigated further (out of scope for that PR); root cause unknown -- could be a genuine test-isolation gap (tests sharing a fixture id/key that should be randomized per-test) or a real constraint-design issue.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Run `xtask test -p sinex-db --all` (a full, non-impact-scoped run).
2. Observe roughly 6 of 377 sinex-db::database tests intermittently fail with a uk_derivation_product_event_output unique-constraint duplicate-key violation.
3. Root cause not yet investigated -- could be genuine test-isolation (tests sharing a fixture id/key that should be randomized per-test) or a real constraint-design issue; first step for whoever picks this up should be identifying which specific tests flake and whether they share a fixture.
acceptance_criteria: Root cause identified: either a test-fixture ID-generation gap (fix: randomize/uuid the colliding key per test) or a genuine constraint-design bug in the derivation.lane_outputs (or wherever uk_derivation_product_event_output lives) uniqueness rule. VERIFY: xtask test -p sinex-db --all run multiple times shows zero uk_derivation_product_event_output failures.
notes: Discovered by the sinex-96fg/sinex-audit-forbidden-pattern-blind-spots fix agent during verification (2026-08-02); could not file directly because bd create was broken for it at the time (Error 1105, Field id doesnt have a default value -- same known bd write-path incident). title: SOURCE_MATERIAL stream max_message_size cap is set in Rust bootstrap but not mirrored in the Nix-managed stream config
description:
Audit wave 3 finding (NixOS-other lane). crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/material_assembler/pipeline.rs:170-184 sets max_message_size=512*1024 when the Rust bootstrap owns SOURCE_MATERIAL. nixos/modules/nats.nix:191-196 defines SOURCE_MATERIAL in defaultBootstrapStreams WITHOUT maxMessageSize (option exists, defaults null -- no --max-msg-size flag passed to nats stream add/edit). In the actual deployment mode (SINEX_NATS_STREAMS_MANAGED_EXTERNALLY=true), the Rust bootstrap for this stream is SKIPPED entirely, and verify_externally_managed_streams_present() only checks the stream EXISTS, not that its field-level config matches -- this fields drift is invisible at every startup check that exists today. The declaratively-provisioned stream ends up with NATS servers default (much larger) max payload instead of the 512KiB cap the Rust code assumes.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Read crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/material_assembler/pipeline.rs:170-184 -- Rust bootstrap sets max_message_size=512*1024 when it owns the SOURCE_MATERIAL stream.
2. Read nixos/modules/nats.nix:191-196 -- SOURCE_MATERIAL is defined in defaultBootstrapStreams WITHOUT maxMessageSize (the option exists but defaults to null, so no --max-msg-size flag is passed to nats stream add/edit).
3. Deploy with SINEX_NATS_STREAMS_MANAGED_EXTERNALLY=true -- the Rust bootstrap for this stream is skipped entirely, so the field-level 512KiB cap the Rust code assumes is never applied by the Nix-managed provisioning path.
4. Read verify_externally_managed_streams_present() -- confirm it only checks the stream EXISTS, not that its max_message_size matches, so this drift is invisible at every startup check that currently runs.
acceptance_criteria: nats.nix SOURCE_MATERIAL stream config sets maxMessageSize=512KiB matching the Rust-side assumption, and the externally-managed-streams verification checks field-level config parity (at least for max_message_size), not just stream existence.
notes: Discovered by pre-wipe audit wave 3 (NixOS-other lane). Medium severity: silently changes the accepted-frame-size contract between in-process and Nix-managed deployment modes. Distinct from sinex-n23.3 (aggregate memory budget arithmetic) -- this is per-field config parity between two topology sources. All other stream configs (retention/max_age/max_bytes/discard, reflection-lane set) verified byte-for-byte matching -- this is the one field-level gap found.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] No config-consistency test found between pipeline.rs:170-184's Rust-side max_message_size=512*1024 and nixos/modules/nats.nix:191-196's Nix default. Testable via a drift-check test/lint comparing the two values.

title: redact_batch string-length mutation invalidates the just-fixed pre-redaction byte offsets on document.chunked
description:
Audit wave 3 finding (document search/FTS lane), follow-on to PR #2554 (sinex-audit-docparser-offsets, closed). That fix made byte_offset_start/end and source_anchor_start/end exactly match real byte positions in the PRE-REDACTION text. But redact_batch (crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/policy.rs:752) runs DOWNSTREAM of the parser (persist.rs:630) and, for global built-in catalog rules using Strategy::Redact with a fixed-length replacement label (e.g. =<REDACTED>), can change the byte length of text. The offsets are NEVER recomputed after this mutation. Scenario: a chunk containing an email/token gets its matched span replaced with a different-length label -- persisted document_chunks.text (and documents.text_byte_len, summed PRE-redaction) no longer agrees with byte_offset_start/end/source_anchor_start/end. Any future consumer trusting source_anchor_* to byte-slice back into raw source-material bytes (none exists yet in-repo, but its the documented purpose of the field) would get a wrong/garbage slice for any redacted chunk.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Confirm PR #2554 (sinex-audit-docparser-offsets) made byte_offset_start/end and source_anchor_start/end exactly match real byte positions in the PRE-REDACTION text.
2. Read crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/policy.rs:752 vs persist.rs:630 -- redact_batch runs DOWNSTREAM of the parser, after offsets were already computed against pre-redaction text.
3. Configure a global built-in catalog rule using Strategy::Redact with a fixed-length replacement label (e.g. "<REDACTED>") whose length differs from the matched span.
4. Parse a document.chunked chunk containing an email/token matching that rule.
5. Observe the persisted document_chunks.text (post-redaction) and documents.text_byte_len (summed pre-redaction) no longer agree with byte_offset_start/end/source_anchor_start/end, since the offsets are never recomputed after the redaction mutation changes the string length.
acceptance_criteria: byte_offset_*/source_anchor_* are recomputed (or invalidated with a clear signal) after redact_batch mutates chunk text length, so the documented byte-exact-anchor contract holds for redacted chunks, not just unredacted ones.
notes: Discovered by pre-wipe audit wave 3 (document search/FTS lane). Medium severity: no active in-repo consumer exploits source_anchor_* for byte-exact slicing yet, but the field is exposed via documents.get_chunks API/MCP and documented as byte-accurate, so the contract is silently broken the moment redaction fires -- a second independent mutator of the same string that PR #2554s fix did not account for.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] Testable: redact a chunk with a length-changing replacement label, assert byte_offset_start/end still match the persisted text. No test yet.

title: command_frequency_hourly/current_window_focus mix ts_coided bucketing with ts_orig value selection inside the same CAGG
description:
Audit wave 3 finding. current_window_focus (apply.rs:3002-3016) buckets by time_bucket(5min, id) [ts_coided] but selects last(window_class, ts_orig) WITHIN that bucket -- a self-contradictory mix of the two clocks in one derived value: for a bucket with a live event plus a late-arriving backfilled one, the last focus shown may not correspond to what was actually last-focused within that processing-time window. command_frequency_hourly (apply.rs:3024-3067) buckets purely on ts_coided over sources that include bulk-importable shell.atuin/shell.history.* -- for a bulk backfill, every historical command lands in whatever hour corresponds to IMPORT time not execution time, making it an hourly import-throughput view rather than the hourly execution pattern its name/purpose implies.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Read apply.rs:3002-3016 (current_window_focus) -- buckets by time_bucket(5min, id) using ts_coided, but selects last(window_class, ts_orig) within that bucket -- a self-contradictory mix of interpretation-time bucketing and occurrence-time value selection.
2. Produce a live event and a late-arriving backfilled event that both land in the same ts_coided-defined 5-minute bucket -- observe the "last focus" the view reports may not correspond to what was actually last-focused within that processing-time window.
3. Read apply.rs:3024-3067 (command_frequency_hourly) -- buckets purely on ts_coided over sources including bulk-importable shell.atuin/shell.history.*.
4. Run a bulk historical backfill of shell history -- observe every historical command lands in whatever hour corresponds to IMPORT time, not execution time, making the view an hourly import-throughput chart rather than the hourly execution-pattern chart its name implies.
acceptance_criteria: Either document these views explicit ts_coided semantics (accepting the implication for backfilled sources), or rework them to bucket on ts_orig with an appropriate CA-refresh strategy for non-monotonic historical data.
notes: Discovered by pre-wipe audit wave 3 (telemetry/CAGGs lane). Medium severity, silently misleading data for imported/backfilled sources; live-only sources unaffected (ts_orig approx ts_coided there). Distinct from sinex-u5g (strict-diff detection gap) and sinex-8m8 (CA churn/hand-tuning loss) -- this is a bucketing-choice correctness bug, not a drift-detection or churn issue.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] The self-contradictory clock-mixing within one CAGG bucket is directly demonstrable now via a live-plus-backfilled-event-in-same-bucket test, independent of which fix direction is eventually chosen. O3.

title: Media capture session-state never reconciles with actual capture health -- stays enabled/idle forever after the driver starts failing
description:
Audit wave 3 finding (session-state lane). crate/sinexd/src/sources/media_screen_capture_driver.rs:462-466 and media_audio_capture_driver.rs:509-513: when capture_once() fails inside the continuous-run loop, the driver only warn!s and continues -- never writes back to core.source_session_state. lifecycle_state/visibility_state are written ONLY by the operator-facing execute_session_control, driven purely from the REQUESTED action, never from observed driver outcome. Scenario: operator issues resume, row reads enabled/idle; the screenshot/audio binary starts failing every cycle (permission revoked, Wayland portal denied, binary missing) -- the row stays enabled/idle indefinitely, sinexctl inspect reports this stale never-corrected state as current truth. Also: visibility_state doc-comments visible_capture_active|idle|suspended but the only writer never emits visible_capture_active -- structurally no way to distinguish enabled-and-actually-capturing from enabled-but-idle.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Read crate/sinexd/src/sources/media_screen_capture_driver.rs:462-466 and media_audio_capture_driver.rs:509-513 -- when capture_once() fails inside the continuous-run loop, the driver only warn!s and continues, never writing back to core.source_session_state.
2. Issue sinexctl ... resume for media screen or audio capture -- confirm the session-state row reads enabled/idle.
3. Force the underlying capture binary to fail every cycle (revoke permission, deny the Wayland portal, or remove the binary).
4. Observe the session-state row stays enabled/idle indefinitely -- sinexctl inspect reports this stale, never-corrected state as current truth, with no operator-visible signal beyond a repeating WARN log line.
5. Read the visibility_state doc comment (visible_capture_active|idle|suspended) -- confirm the only writer never emits visible_capture_active, so there is structurally no way to distinguish enabled-and-actually-capturing from enabled-but-idle.
acceptance_criteria: Repeated capture failures update session_state (e.g. a failure_class/degraded lifecycle_state, or visibility_state actually distinguishing live-capturing from idle) so sinexctl inspect reflects reality, not just requested intent.
notes: Discovered by pre-wipe audit wave 3 (session-state/media-control lane). Medium severity -- direct instance of the state-drift class the audit was scoped to check for (sinex believes X, OS-side reality diverged, nothing reconciles).

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] concrete numbered repro steps (force capture failure, observe stale enabled/idle state) map directly to an integration test; not yet written

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 follow-up 2026-08-11] Confirmed live: 'visible_capture_active' (crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/source_session_state.rs:24 doc comment) is grepped nowhere else in the codebase as a string literal -- no writer ever emits it. capture_once() failures in the continuous run loop (media_screen_capture_driver.rs:462-466, media_audio_capture_driver.rs:509-513) only warn! and continue; nothing calls back into SourceSessionStateRepository on failure. A faithful red test needs to drive the real continuous-run loop (async, DB-gated, backend-injectable) through N forced capture failures and then assert the session_session_state row is unchanged -- that requires more runtime/DB scaffolding (a working RuntimeContext + injectable failing ScreenCaptureBackend wired through the full loop, not just capture_once in isolation) than this lane's bounded time budget covers. Left as tdd:open-o3-could-be-full (still feasible in principle); not attempted this pass rather than shipping a shallow/vacuous test.

title: No rate limiting on the gateway auth-verification path -- unlimited unauthenticated bearer-token guess attempts
description:
Audit wave 3 finding (gateway auth lifecycle lane). GatewayAuth::verify() (crate/sinexd/src/api/rpc_server/auth.rs:225-239) does a constant-time compare against the single configured token and returns AuthError::Missing/Invalid with no throttling of any kind -- no per-IP limiter, no failure-counter, no backoff. The existing RateLimiter is only invoked AFTER successful token verification (rpc_server.rs:320-321,574-575), keyed by the valid token -- it caps authorized callers throughput, does not stop guessing. A client with network access to the RPC listener can send unlimited guess attempts at zero cost beyond one constant-time comparison per attempt.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Read crate/sinexd/src/api/rpc_server/auth.rs:225-239 -- GatewayAuth::verify() does a constant-time compare against the single configured token and returns AuthError::Missing/Invalid with no throttling, per-IP limiter, failure counter, or backoff.
2. Read rpc_server.rs:320-321,574-575 -- confirm the existing RateLimiter is only invoked AFTER successful token verification, keyed by the valid token, so it caps authorized-caller throughput but does nothing to stop guessing.
3. Send unlimited bearer-token guess attempts to the RPC listener from a client with network access -- observe each attempt costs only one constant-time comparison, with no mechanism anywhere on the path slowing or blocking repeated failed attempts.
acceptance_criteria: A coarse IP-or-global rate limiter applies to the auth-verification step itself (before role/token validity is known), independent of the existing per-valid-token limiter.
notes: Discovered by pre-wipe audit wave 3 (gateway auth lane). Low-medium severity: mitigated by require_mtls_for_remote() mandating a client CA for any non-loopback bind (an attacker needs a valid client cert before reaching the bearer-token check at all), and token entropy is operator-controlled. Real defense-in-depth gap given CLAUDE.md doctrine explicitly flags exposure-beyond-localhost as the relevant threat scenario. Verified CLEAN in the same lane (not new findings): timing-attack resistance already fixed (constant_time_eq via subtle crate), token expiry matches the already-documented no-revocation doctrine (not re-reported), and a full RpcRole census across all ~120 RPC methods found zero mutating-method-gated-at-ReadOnly outliers -- single dispatch chokepoint (RpcRegistry::dispatch) shared by both HTTP and native-messaging transports, no bypass path.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] Crisp and testable: send repeated invalid-token requests and assert no throttling/backoff kicks in before successful auth (currently true per GatewayAuth::verify()). No test yet.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2-impl 2026-08-11] Investigated: GatewayAuth::verify() confirmed to have zero throttling state (AuthError enum only has Missing/Invalid, no rate-limited variant, no per-attempt counter anywhere in auth.rs). Not reduced to a test this pass: the bead doesn't specify the intended throttle shape (per-IP? per-process? what threshold?), so a red test would require inventing fix semantics rather than testing a defined AC. Needs a design decision first.

title: NativeImapSyncClientConfig derives plaintext Debug, unlike GmailOAuthCredentials which manually redacts
description: Audit wave 3 finding (email/OAuth lane). NativeImapSyncClientConfig (email_imap_sync.rs:252-270) is #[derive(Debug, Clone)] with plaintext password: String and access_token: Option<String> fields -- no redaction. NativeImapSyncClient (email_imap_sync.rs:304-307) wraps and re-exposes the same via its own derived Debug. Contrast: GmailOAuthCredentials (email_oauth.rs:58-67) has a MANUAL Debug impl explicitly redacting client_secret/refresh_token, with a doc comment stating Secrets never appear in emitted records or errors. No current call site formats via {:?} and no #[tracing::instrument] auto-captures it, so nothing leaks TODAY -- but the codebases own established redact-on-Debug convention for credential-bearing structs is inconsistently applied, a latent landmine for a future debug!/instrument/panic path.

title: Activity vs reflection storage-lane routing is convention-only, not structurally enforced -- violates own type-enforcement-ladder doctrine for a load-bearing invariant
description:
Audit wave 2 finding (reflection-lane lane). storage_lane (crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/admission.rs:458) is fixed ONCE per AdmissionService instance at consumer construction (based on which JetStream consumer -- Activity vs Reflection -- is running), never re-derived per event, then insert_stream_batch_into(self.storage_lane, &rows) applies it uniformly to the whole batch. The high-throughput batch/COPY path (persistence.rs:1248-1364, the one actually used by JetStream consumers) has NO per-row source_role(row.source) check anywhere. Contrast: the single-event insert path (persistence.rs:283-286/679-682, used by API handlers/tests) DOES re-derive lane per-event from source_role -- the safety property exists in one path but not the one carrying production ingestion volume. publish_intent/publish_telemetry (runtime/nats_publisher.rs:328-341/479-487) each only debug_assert on the class enum, neither checks event.source against SourceRole. Currently safe only because exactly one call site ever invokes publish_telemetry with hardcoded sinex.*-sourced payloads -- a future automaton/adapter/refactor reusing either function for the wrong source class would silently misroute with no compile-time/lint/DB-constraint/admission-time check catching it.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Read crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/admission.rs:458 -- storage_lane is fixed ONCE per AdmissionService instance at consumer construction, never re-derived per event.
2. Read persistence.rs:1248-1364 -- the high-throughput batch/COPY path (the one JetStream consumers actually use in production) applies self.storage_lane uniformly to the whole batch with no per-row source_role(row.source) check.
3. Contrast persistence.rs:283-286/679-682 -- the single-event insert path (used by API handlers/tests, not production ingestion volume) DOES correctly re-derive lane per-event.
4. Read runtime/nats_publisher.rs:328-341/479-487 -- publish_intent/publish_telemetry each only debug_assert on the class enum, neither checks event.source against SourceRole.
5. Construct a scenario where a single AdmissionService/consumer instance processes events whose source doesn't match its fixed storage_lane (e.g. via a future consumer misconfiguration or a reflection-tagged event reaching the Activity consumer) -- the batch path has no per-row check that would catch or prevent the resulting lane misrouting, unlike the single-event path.
acceptance_criteria: Storage-lane routing is enforced structurally (a DB CHECK constraint on source-prefix vs table, or a per-row source_role assertion in the batch/COPY insert path, or a stronger type-level guarantee) rather than resting on the invariant that only one call site ever calls each publish function. VERIFY: a test that attempts to route a sinex.*-sourced event through publish_intent (or a non-sinex.*-sourced event through publish_telemetry) is rejected rather than silently misrouted.
notes: Discovered by pre-wipe audit wave 2 (reflection-lane lane). sinex-bor confirmed RESOLVED (nats.nix now declares all 5 reflection streams correctly, no reopen needed) -- this is a NEW, distinct finding. Medium severity: no live evidence of misrouting today, but the reverse-direction failure mode (a real activity event silently routed into reflection.events, which is excluded outright not filtered, so it would be silently LOST to activity consumers) is exactly the CLAUDE.md doctrine self-observation must not pollute activity surfaces sitting at type-enforcement rung 6 (convention only) for something the doctrine calls load-bearing.

title: Phone and SSN recognizers miss common unstructured formats (pre-filter anchor excludes entire format classes)
description: Audit wave 2 finding. PHONE_RE (crate/sinex-primitives/src/privacy/detector.rs:100-113) requires the candidate to start with either a + international prefix or a parenthesized area code -- a bare dash/space/dot-separated number with neither (555-867-5309, 555.867.5309, 5558675309) never reaches is_plausible_phone at all; not a validation-strictness issue, a pre-filter anchor that excludes the entire common unstructured format class outright. SSN_RE (detector.rs:408-412, \b\d{3}[-\s]\d{2}[-\s]\d{4}\b) requires a dash-or-space separator between every group -- a bare unseparated 9-digit SSN (123456789, common from OCR/forms) never matches the pre-filter, so is_valid_ssns checksum logic (which itself correctly strips non-digits and would validate a bare run) never gets a chance to run. Existing tests (detector_test.rs:67-79) only cover the prefixed/separated cases, no regression coverage for either gap.
acceptance_criteria: PHONE_RE and SSN_RE pre-filters match the common unstructured/unseparated formats too (bare dash-separated phone numbers, unseparated 9-digit SSNs), routing them into the existing plausibility/checksum validation logic rather than excluding them before that logic ever runs. Tests cover both previously-missed formats.
notes: Discovered by pre-wipe audit wave 2 (privacy engine lane). Medium severity false-negative gap -- common PII shapes (OCRd documents are literally one of this platforms own capture sources) go completely undetected whenever the phone_number/ssn recognizer rules are active.
close_reason: Fixed by PR #2590 (feature/fix/privacy-recognizer-unstructured-phone-ssn). PHONE_RE widened with two new alternatives (bare NANP-shaped NNN-NNN-NNNN/NNN.NNN.NNNN, bare unseparated 10-digit) alongside the existing +/parens branches; is_plausible_phone gained a NANP structural check (area/exchange code cannot start with 0/1) applied to unseparated bare-10-digit candidates without a + prefix, to bound the false-positive surface opened by removing the structural anchor requirement. SSN_RE group separators made optional ([-s]? instead of [-s]) so a bare unseparated 9-digit run reaches is_valid_ssn; that function's existing area/group/serial range checks were left as the plausibility filter (SSNs have no real checksum digit) -- same pattern as NIP/REGON bare-digit acceptance elsewhere in this file. Closure Evidence Manifest: AC1 (both previously-excluded formats now caught, prefixed/separated cases still pass) satisfied -- new tests phone_finds_bare_dash_separated, phone_finds_bare_dot_separated, phone_finds_bare_unseparated, ssn_finds_bare_unseparated added alongside existing phone_finds_international/phone_finds_parens/ssn_finds_in_text which still pass (135 passed, 0 failed). AC2 (false-positive sanity check) satisfied -- phone_rejects_bare_unseparated_with_invalid_nanp_prefix (order-ID-shaped 1234567890 rejected via NANP check) and ssn_rejects_bare_unseparated_invalid_area (999123456, area 999 rejected via existing range check) added; residual false-positive risk on NANP-valid-shaped random numbers documented explicitly in PR body as an accepted tradeoff (no real checksum exists for either format). AC3 (xtask check -p sinex-primitives passes, targeted tests pass) satisfied -- verification commands and output in PR Verification section. Verification: DATABASE_URL=... nix develop --command xtask check -p sinex-primitives (success); DATABASE_URL=... nix develop --command xtask test -p sinex-primitives -E test(detector) or test(privacy) (135 passed, 0 failed); pre-push drift guard xtask check --changed-strict origin/master passed.

title: privacy.field_rules.priority column is fetched, documented, and completely ignored by rule application
description:
Audit wave 2 finding. crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/privacy_policy.rs:159-172 queries priority (ORDER BY fr.priority DESC); crate/sinexctl/src/commands/privacy.rs:302-304 CLI docstring explicitly promises higher values win earlier when scopes overlap. But compile_rules (crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/policy.rs:435-542) groups rules into a HashMap<ScopeKey,ScopeRules> and iterates it (policy.rs:512) -- HashMap iteration order is UNSPECIFIED, can vary between process restarts/cache refreshes. Within one scopes rule vector, ordering comes from the rules query ORDER BY name (alphabetical), not priority. priority is read into FieldRuleRecord.priority and then dropped -- zero references to .priority anywhere in rule compilation/application.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Read crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/privacy_policy.rs:159-172 -- the query fetches priority (ORDER BY fr.priority DESC).
2. Read crate/sinexctl/src/commands/privacy.rs:302-304 -- the CLI docstring explicitly promises "higher values win earlier when scopes overlap."
3. Configure two overlapping field-scoped privacy rules with different priority values.
4. Read compile_rules (crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/policy.rs:435-542) -- rules are grouped into a HashMap<ScopeKey,ScopeRules> and iterated (line 512) in unspecified HashMap order; within one scope's rule vector, ordering comes from the rules query's ORDER BY name (alphabetical), not priority.
5. Observe which rule actually applies is determined by HashMap iteration order and alphabetical name, not by the configured priority -- priority is read into FieldRuleRecord.priority and never referenced again anywhere in rule compilation/application (zero references confirmed by grep).
acceptance_criteria: Overlapping rules within/across scopes apply in priority order (higher wins) as documented, deterministically across process restarts -- not HashMap-iteration-order-dependent or alphabetical-by-name.
notes: Discovered by pre-wipe audit wave 2 (privacy engine lane). Medium severity: silent contract violation, non-deterministic across engine refreshes rather than merely wrong-but-stable -- an operator relying on the documented priority precedence gets unpredictable results.

title: Field-scoped privacy rules silently bleed across fields within a scope
description:
Audit wave 2 finding (privacy engine lane). compile_rules (crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/policy.rs:435-542) groups DB policy rules into ONE PrivacyEngine per (event_source, event_type) scope -- not per field. apply_scoped_engine_to_json (policy.rs:1296-1327): if any rule in the scope has field_path=NULL (global rule), the early-return branch runs the ENTIRE scopes compiled engine over the WHOLE payload. Otherwise, for each declared field path in scope.field_paths, the FULL scope.engine (all rules regardless of which field each was bound to) is applied to that one field. The module doc comment promises per-rule field scoping; the implementation only guarantees scope-level (source+type) isolation, not field-level isolation once more than one field-scoped rule shares a scope. Existing tests dont catch this because each test rules literal matcher text happens to be unique to its intended field by construction.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Read compile_rules (crate/sinexd/src/event_engine/policy.rs:435-542) -- DB policy rules are grouped into ONE PrivacyEngine per (event_source, event_type) scope, not per field.
2. Read apply_scoped_engine_to_json (policy.rs:1296-1327) -- for each declared field path in scope.field_paths, the FULL scope.engine (all rules regardless of which field each was originally bound to) is applied to that one field.
3. Configure two field-scoped rules in one scope: rule A bound to /summary with matcher text "X", rule B bound to /window_title with matcher text "Y".
4. Admit an event whose /summary field contains "Y" (rule B's matcher text) but whose /window_title does not contain "X".
5. Observe rule B's matcher fires against /summary too, because the compiled engine for the scope contains both rules and is applied wholesale to every declared field path -- the module doc comment's promise of per-rule field scoping does not hold once more than one field-scoped rule shares a scope. Existing tests miss this because each test's rule matcher text happens to be unique to its intended field by construction, never exercising the cross-field bleed.
acceptance_criteria: A rule scoped to field /summary never fires against a different field /window_title in the same scope, and vice versa -- field_paths is actually consulted to filter WHICH rules apply to WHICH field, not just which fields get the full engine applied. Test: two field-scoped rules in one scope, each with content that would trigger the OTHER rules pattern in the WRONG field -- confirm no cross-field bleed.
notes: Discovered by pre-wipe audit wave 2 (privacy/redaction engine lane). Framed per repo doctrine as a feature-correctness bug (over-redaction, not under-redaction -- errs toward hiding more not less), not a security vulnerability, consistent with privacy being a presentation feature not a security boundary.

comments.author: Sinity
comments.text: [TDD-audit-v2 2026-08-11] Directly testable per its own Steps to Reproduce: two field-scoped rules sharing a scope, assert no cross-field bleed. No test yet.

title: Replay scope time_window filters ts_coided (interpretation time), not ts_orig (occurrence time)
description:
Audit wave 2 finding. crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/replay.rs:70-73 (build_filter_query, used consistently by both collect_scope_root_ids and generate_preview_summary -- no preview/execute drift) filters on ts_coided, not ts_orig. Per this repos own doctrine (query by ts_orig for what happened, ts_coided for what sinex interpreted when -- and the #2182 incident root cause was exactly a ts_coided-bucketed CA making historical imports invisible), a replay scope built around the day this happened will silently miss late/backfilled material admitted after that window and/or pull in unrelated real-world-time events merely interpreted inside that processing window.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Read crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/replay.rs:70-73 (build_filter_query, used by both collect_scope_root_ids and generate_preview_summary) -- the time_window filter applies to ts_coided (interpretation time), not ts_orig (occurrence time).
2. Admit a historical/backfilled event whose ts_orig falls within a target day but whose ts_coided (interpretation time) falls outside it, because it was admitted late.
3. Build a replay scope with a time_window around that target day.
4. Observe the replay scope silently misses that late-admitted event (it would have needed a ts_coided within the window), and/or silently includes unrelated real-world-time events that merely happened to be interpreted inside that processing window -- directly analogous to the #2182 incident root cause (a ts_coided-bucketed continuous aggregate making historical imports invisible).
acceptance_criteria: Replay time_window scoping is either explicitly documented as ts_coided-based with the implication stated (an operator building a scope around historical occurrence dates would get wrong results), or the scope gains a ts_orig-based option. VERIFY: a test with a late-admitted historical event (ts_orig in-window, ts_coided out-of-window at admission time) shows whether it is included or excluded from a time_window replay scope, matching the documented/chosen semantics.
notes: Discovered by pre-wipe audit wave 2 (replay control lane). Medium severity -- undocumented semantic gap on the replay surface specifically, distinct from the general ts_coided-CA doctrine which IS documented elsewhere. Also noted but not filed separately (low priority, table-wide lock held during cascade expansion in archive_replay_cascade_atomically -- LOCK TABLE core.events IN SHARE MODE for the whole select+archive sequence, could stall ingestion for a very large cascade): worth a follow-up if cascade sizes grow large post-rebuild.

title: Embedding model dimension change silently orphans the HNSW index; subsequent writes hard-fail
description: Audit wave 2 finding. register_model (crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/embeddings.rs:17-46) upserts core.embedding_models via ON CONFLICT (provider, model_name) DO UPDATE SET dimensions=EXCLUDED.dimensions -- updates in place, same model_id. trg_embedding_model_create_index (crate/sinex-schema/src/apply.rs:2521-2532) fires AFTER INSERT only, never on UPDATE, so the partial HNSW index for that model_id is never rebuilt. create_embedding_model_index derives the index name purely from model_id and uses CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS with the OLD dimension baked into the vector(N) cast expression -- even a full xtask schema apply convergence pass is a no-op, cannot self-heal. Meanwhile validate_embedding_for_model reads the NEW dimensions value and happily validates+accepts new-dimension vectors under the same model_id; the subsequent INSERT then hits the stale-dimension index cast and Postgres raises a hard runtime error on every write for that model until an operator manually intervenes (no code path calls drop_embedding_model_index anywhere).
acceptance_criteria: Re-registering an existing (provider, model_name) with a changed dimensions value either (a) fires index (re)creation on AFTER INSERT OR UPDATE OF dimensions with DROP+CREATE (not IF NOT EXISTS) when dimensions actually changed, or (b) register_model rejects a dimension change on an existing row and requires a genuinely new model row. VERIFY: a test that re-registers a model with a different dimension count and then successfully writes+queries an embedding at the new dimension.
notes: Discovered by pre-wipe audit wave 2 (embedding/vector-search lane). Currently a LATENT bug, not urgent: the entire embedding write/search plane is dead code today (embedding_producer.rs explicitly never calls store_event_embedding, gated behind sinex-5v6 which is not yet activated). File this as a landmine for whoever implements sinex-5v6 -- it will fire the first time a model gets a dimension revision, and xtask schema strict-diff would not catch it (only checks trigger presence, not that it covers UPDATEs).
close_reason: Fixed and merged via PR #2591 (squash). Original mission-proposed fix (drop+recreate the HNSW index on UPDATE OF dimensions, purging old-dimension rows first) does NOT work: plain CREATE INDEX (non-CONCURRENTLY) scans with SnapshotAny, so a same-transaction DELETE of old-dimension rows does not make them invisible to the index rebuild (still physically present until VACUUM, which cannot run inside a trigger ambient transaction). Confirmed empirically via a minimal standalone repro outside sinex schema: DELETE-then-CREATE-INDEX in one transaction still fails with a pgvector dimension-mismatch error against an otherwise-empty table. Pivoted to Option B: register_model now rejects a dimension change on an existing (provider, model_name) pair (UPDATE SET clause no longer touches dimensions at all, so the invariant holds even under a check-then-write race). Verification: xtask check -p sinex-db -p sinex-schema pass; xtask test -p sinex-db -E test(embedding) -- 3/3 passed including new embedding_repository_rejects_dimension_change_on_reregister regression test.

title: desktop.notification occurrence key drops body/timestamp from its own declared identity, colliding on (app_name, summary) reuse; notification_closed/action are collision-prone by design (D-Bus id reuse)
description:
Audit wave 1 finding. system/notifications.rs declares occurrence_identity = Uuid5From((app_name, summary, body, ts)) but the ACTUAL OccurrenceKey (lines 117-123) only includes fields app and summary -- body and ts are silently dropped, a load-bearing doc/code mismatch (not cosmetic like the bookmark.rs case, which is already fixed on master). Any app reusing a fixed summary across notifications with varying body (chat apps using contact/channel name as summary, message text as body; download managers using "Download complete" as summary, filename as body) collides on the equivalence key -- admission-time fail-open dedup silently suppresses the second/subsequent distinct notification. Separately, notification_closed.rs/notification_action.rs correctly implement what they declare (Uuid5From(notification_id[, action_key])) but D-Bus notification daemons (dunst/mako) recycle small integer notification_ids once a notification closes within the same session -- with RetentionPolicy::Forever and no timestamp component, two unrelated notifications months apart can collide.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Read system/notifications.rs's declared occurrence_identity comment: Uuid5From((app_name, summary, body, ts)).
2. Read the actual OccurrenceKey construction at lines 117-123 -- confirm it only includes app and summary; body and ts are silently dropped.
3. Trigger two distinct desktop notifications from an app that reuses a fixed summary with varying body (e.g. a chat app using the contact/channel name as summary and the message text as body, or a download manager using "Download complete" as summary and the filename as body).
4. Observe the second notification collides on the equivalence key with the first and is silently suppressed by admission-time fail-open dedup, despite being a genuinely distinct notification.
5. Separately, confirm notification_closed.rs/notification_action.rs correctly implement their declared Uuid5From(notification_id[, action_key]) keys, but D-Bus notification daemons (dunst/mako) recycle small integer notification ids, making these keys collision-prone by design across sessions.
acceptance_criteria: desktop.notification OccurrenceKey construction matches its declared identity (includes body and a timestamp component, or the declaration is corrected to match a deliberately narrower key with documented rationale). notification_closed/action gain a coarse timestamp bucket or session-scoping component to bound D-Bus id-reuse collision risk given Forever retention.
notes: Discovered by pre-wipe audit wave 1 (source-adapters lane). notification finding is Medium (plausible for common chat/messaging notification patterns); closed/action finding is Low-Medium (narrower blast radius, long-horizon design gap not implementation bug).

title: Tombstone GC can delete CAS blob content while an orphan-check race leaves the material row alive
description: Audit wave 1 finding. crate/sinexd/src/api/handlers/lifecycle.rs:1007-1150: material_ids_for_archived_events (read) -> execute_cascade_tombstone -> find_orphan_materials (fresh recheck) -> per-material: get_by_id -> content_store.drop_content(...) (irreversible) -> delete_material (DB row delete, several round-trips later, no spanning transaction). If a new/redelivered event referencing the material lands between the orphan check and delete_material (e.g. slow-arriving multi-slice material event, or JetStream redelivery deferred in MaterialReadySet at check time), the FK constraint correctly blocks delete_material (row survives, logged as best-effort/GC-sweeper-will-recover) -- but drop_content already ran uncompensated. The surviving material row now has optional_blob_id pointing at deleted CAS content, for a material with a LIVE event still referencing it. Raw-material data loss in the durable-witness layer.
acceptance_criteria: Either defer drop_content until after delete_material succeeds (so a blocked delete never orphans live content), or re-verify orphan status under a lock immediately before drop_content. VERIFY: a test that races a redelivered event against tombstone-GC for the same material shows the material row, if it survives, still has retrievable content -- never a live event pointing at deleted CAS bytes.
notes: Discovered by pre-wipe audit wave 1 (concurrency/TX lane). Narrow race window (requires shared/wrapped materials with in-flight late events) and the code already documents this path as best-effort, so the author was aware of partial-failure risk generally -- this finding is the specific ordering hazard (drop-then-delete instead of delete-then-drop) that was not covered.
close_reason: Fixed via PR #2589 (fix/sinexd/tombstone-material-drop-order). Root cause: handle_tombstone_approve dropped CAS blob content before delete_material, using a stale find_orphan_materials recheck; a redelivered event referencing the material between recheck and delete left the row alive (correctly blocked by the real core.events.source_material_id FK) but its blob already dropped. Fix: new SourceMaterialRepository::delete_material_if_orphan bakes the NOT EXISTS(core.events)/NOT EXISTS(audit.archived_events) recheck into the DELETE statement itself and returns optional_blob_id only on actual deletion; handle_tombstone_approve now calls this FIRST and only runs the existing CAS-blob-drop transaction (PR #2577 lock_by_id_for_update path) when it confirms the row is gone (Option A from the AC, not Option B -- the real FK plus baked-in NOT EXISTS checks make the single DELETE authoritative, no separate row lock needed). VERIFY criterion satisfied by new test concurrent_event_insert_race_never_orphans_deleted_material (crate/sinex-db/src/repositories/source_materials_test.rs), Barrier-synced against a real core.events insert: passed. Also reran full tombstone_approve suite (5/5) and broader source_material/tombstone/cascade/orphan filter (104/104), all passing.

title: Whole-file-as-one-record source retries forever with no DLQ/quarantine when a single member event never settles
description:
For a StaticFileAdapter-backed source (one-shot file read, the whole file is ONE materialized record fanned out into many events via parse_record), if even a SINGLE event among potentially thousands never reaches a progress-unlocking EmissionReceiptState -- reproduced concretely with a deliberately-malformed/truncated CSV whose trailing record is unparseable -- the whole records unlocked check in adapter_source.rs (span.iter().all(item.state.is_progress_unlocking())) is false, so cursor/checkpoint never advances for ANY event in that record, including the ones that individually succeeded. On the next poll cycle (30s later), the ENTIRE file is re-registered as a fresh source material and re-scanned from scratch -- forever, with no DLQ entry, no quarantine, no partial-progress mechanism, and no operator-visible signal beyond a repeating WARN log line ("record did not fully unlock progress") and a repeating checkpoint-KV WARN ("Checkpoint KV is ahead of this save").

Discovery: found 2026-08-01 while independently re-investigating sinex-9qkm (which turned out to be a false positive from a wc -l row-count miscount, not a real bug -- see its closure notes). During that investigation, a deliberately-truncated CSV test file (head -n cut mid-record, corrupting the final logical row) reproduced this exact endless-retry-with-no-progress pattern cleanly and repeatedly (6+ consecutive 30s poll cycles observed, zero forward progress, zero DLQ entries). This is DISTINCT from sinex-9qkm: no data was lost or falsely claimed as settled -- the successfully-processed events genuinely correctly re-suppress as duplicates on each retry (verified: no double-counting, no phantom rows) -- but the source can never COMPLETE and never surfaces which specific row(s) are the problem.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Register a StaticFileAdapter-backed source pointing at a deliberately-malformed/truncated CSV whose trailing record is unparseable, among otherwise-good records earlier in the file.
2. Let the source materialize and parse -- the whole file becomes one materialized record fanned out into many events via parse_record.
3. Read adapter_source.rs's span-unlock check: span.iter().all(item.state.is_progress_unlocking()) -- confirm it requires EVERY event in the record to unlock, including the one that will never settle because it's unparseable.
4. Observe cursor/checkpoint never advances for ANY event in that record, even the ones that individually succeeded.
5. Wait for the next poll cycle (30s) -- observe the entire file is re-registered as a fresh source material and re-scanned from scratch, repeating forever with no DLQ entry, no quarantine, and no operator-visible signal beyond a repeating WARN log line.
design: Undecided, needs a design pass. Candidate directions: (1) per-event isolation within a whole-file record -- treat each event within a materialized batch as independently retryable/DLQ-able rather than gating the WHOLE records cursor advancement on ALL events unlocking; (2) a bounded-retry-then-DLQ-the-whole-material escape hatch specifically for the one-shot StaticFile case, since unlike a continuous/live source there is no expectation the failing content will ever change; (3) surface the actual per-event failure reason (which event, why) rather than only the aggregate did not fully unlock progress WARN, so an operator/agent can diagnose without re-implementing this investigations reproduction from scratch.
acceptance_criteria: AC: a StaticFile-backed source containing one perpetually-unparseable/perpetually-failing record among many otherwise-good ones reaches a terminal, operator-visible state (DLQ entry or equivalent) within a bounded number of retries, rather than retrying forever; the good records in the same file are NOT blocked from persisting by the one bad record (or, if per-record atomicity for the whole file is intentional/required for a different reason, that constraint is explicit and documented, and the bounded-retry-then-DLQ escape hatch still applies to the whole material). Regression test: a fixture StaticFile source with N good + 1 permanently-bad row proves bounded convergence to a terminal state, not infinite retry.
notes: Filed via bd sql direct INSERT workaround (bd create broken this session -- events.id has no default, DB schema 1.1.0 vs CLI 1.0.4 mismatch). Lower severity than a data-loss bug: no data is lost or double-counted, this is a liveness/completeness + observability gap for a specific failure shape (perpetually-bad content in a whole-file source), not a correctness bug in the common case.
